## **1 Decision problem, description of the technology and clinical care pathway** 

## _**Disease overview and burden**_ 

- Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) refers to inflammation of the paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity, with symptoms that persist beyond 12 weeks.[1,2] There are two broad CRS subtypes defined by the presence or absence of nasal polyps which are non-cancerous soft tissue growths within the sinonasal passages or sinuses.[1] 

- CRS with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) is the result of a chronic type 2 inflammatory phenotype, driven by the cytokines interleukin [IL]-4 and IL-13.[2] The estimated prevalence of CRSwNP among adults living in the UK in 2013 was 1.6/100,000 (0.16%).[3] 

- People with uncontrolled CRSwNP suffer from significant and debilitating symptoms including loss of sense of smell and taste, sinonasal obstruction, chronic infections and facial pain.[2,4] These persistent symptoms have a substantial adverse impact on the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of patients, affecting sleep quality, mood and activities of daily living.[5-7] CRSwNP is associated with a high rate of polyp recurrence despite surgical intervention and revision surgery is common (~15% of patients within 5 years).[2,8] 

- Treatment of CRSwNP is associated with important healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU); in England between 2010 and 2020, CRSwNP-related costs totalled £86.3 million (cost year unavailable).[9] The burden of sinonasal surgery for CRSwNP was £174 million during this time, including £66.7 million attributable to revision surgeries.[9] 

## _**Clinical pathway of care**_ 

- Established clinical management (ECM) for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP consists of maintenance therapy with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) combined with saline rinses, in addition to short-term use of systemic corticosteroids (SCS; for the treatment of exacerbations) and endoscopic sinonasal surgery (ESS).[1,10] 

## _**Unmet need**_ 

- ECM does not target the underlying aetiology of CRSwNP (type 2 inflammation), meaning the clinical benefits of ECM are limited and diminish over time:[10,11] 

   - Recurrence following ESS is common, with a 5-year revision rate of ~15%, which increases among people who had one or more previous surgeries.[8] The clinical benefits of revision surgery are not only temporary but may also be unsatisfactory, with no assurance that sense of smell will return, and limited gains in HRQoL.[5,12] 

   - Extensive (cumulative courses >300 mg within one year) use of SCS is associated with adverse events such as osteoporosis, hypertension and glaucoma,[10,12,13] while ESS carries a risk of potentially serious post-operative complications.[10,14,15] For patients requiring revision surgery, the risk of complications increases with each subsequent surgery.[8,16] 

- National Health Service (NHS) waiting lists for ESS (50% of which represent revision surgery) range from 6 months up to 3 years following specialist referral.[12] This long waiting time negatively impacts people with uncontrolled CRSwNP who, as a result of persistent type 2 inflammation, experience worsening of their disease and prolonged loss of smell and use of SCS.[12] 

## _**Proposed population for dupilumab**_ 

- It is anticipated that dupilumab will be used in line with its licensed indication, as an add-on therapy with INCS for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control.[17,18] 

- In alignment with phase 3 clinical trials for dupilumab, the population considered in this submission is people with uncontrolled CRSwNP following one (or more) surgeries.

## _**1.1 Decision problem**_ 

This technology appraisal evaluates the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of dupilumab as a treatment for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP. Dupilumab (Dupixent[®] ) is indicated in the United Kingdom (UK) ‘as an add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control.’[17,18] 

The final scope for dupilumab in uncontrolled CRSwNP was issued by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in November 2024.The key evidence in this submission is based on the results of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 which are two replicate phase III randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the efficacy and safety of dupilumab as an add-on to intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) versus INCS alone in adults with uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). The decision problem addressed in this submission is summarised in Table 1.

## _**1.2 Health condition and position of the technology in the treatment pathway**_ 

## **1.2.1 Disease overview** 

## _**1.2.1.1 Pathophysiology of CRSwNP**_ 

Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is defined as a symptomatic inflammation of tissues in the paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity; it may be localised (unilateral) or diffuse (bilateral) and is characterised by symptoms that persist beyond 12 weeks.[1,2] CRS can be diagnosed with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) or without nasal polyps (CRSsNP), which are non-cancerous soft tissue growths that develop along the mucosal layer of the sinonasal passages or sinuses.[1,19] Nasal polyps grow and protrude into the nasal cavities, causing partial or total obstruction.[19] 

The underlying pathophysiology of CRSwNP is a type 2 inflammatory phenotype.[1,2,20,21] Type 2 inflammation is driven by type 2 cytokines interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 which promote the infiltration of immune cells such as eosinophils into sinonasal tissue, and stimulate B- lymphocytes to produce immunoglobulin E (IgE) (Figure 2).[1,2] The type 2 inflammatory environment in CRSwNP leads to sinonasal mucosal damage, overproduction of mucus and the remodelling of sinonasal tissue resulting in nasal polyp formation (Figure 1).[1,2] Epithelial cells lining the sinonasal passages become more permeable, allowing foreign antigens and infectious agents to enter the submucosa.[2] This increased permeability, combined with deficiencies in mucociliary clearance, allows the accumulation of bacteria and fungi which can lead to chronic upper airway infection.[2]

Type 2 inflammation is involved not only in the aetiology of CRSwNP, but also drives the pathophysiology of comorbidities associated with this disease.[1,2,4,20] As discussed in Section 1.2.1.4.2, asthma, allergies and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug-exacerbated respiratory disease (NSAID-ERD) are more common in people with CRSwNP than the general population, which is aligned with the concept of unified airway disease.[23,24] 

## _**1.2.1.2 Presentation and diagnosis**_ 

CRSwNP is characterised by chronic inflammation which leads to epithelial damage, mucous membrane thickening and nasal polyp formation.[1] For the majority of people with CRSwNP, polyps occur bilaterally and most commonly arise in the ethmoid, maxillary and sphenoidal sinuses.[19] Uncontrolled CRSwNP can have significant and debilitating symptoms that include:[2,4,25,26] 

- Loss of senses of smell and taste 

- Sinonasal congestion/obstruction and discoloured discharge 

- Impaired breathing 

- Facial pain/pressure 

- Fatigue and sleep disturbance 

- Recurrent upper and lower respiratory infections 

- Eustachian dysfunction and hearing impairment 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 14 of 171 



<!-- page 17 -->

- Post-nasal drip (possibly with bronchial aspiration and associated lower respiratory infection) 

Initial patient presentation to a general practitioner (GP) is usually triggered by symptoms of sinonasal inflammation.[4] Compared with the general population, people with CRSwNP produce greater amounts of sinonasal mucus, with sinonasal congestion and/or obstruction that lead to loss of both sense of smell and taste, fatigue and sleep disorders (such as sleep apnoea).[1,2,4] 

Diagnostic criteria for CRSwNP are described in the European Position Paper on Rhinosinusitis and Nasal Polyps (EPOS) published in 2020 (Table 3).[1] 

Coexisting inflammatory disorders should also be considered during the diagnosis of CRSwNP.[4] Nasal polyps develop as a result of the type 2 inflammatory process associated with these coexisting conditions, and therefore an assessment of nasal polyps is important for effective treatment choices.[1,2,4]

The severity and duration of a person’s symptoms are considered during diagnostic 

evaluation.[1] CRSwNP severity is currently reported utilising a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) where patients are asked to rank the severity of their symptoms from 0 to 10, with ratings of 0 to 3, >3 to 7 and >7 to 10 indicating mild, moderate and severe symptoms, respectively.[27] A definition of disease severity in people with CRSwNP was published in the 2020 EPOS and is based on the level of disease control:[1]

<!-- page 18 -->

- **Controlled disease:** ‘A disease state in which the patients do not have symptoms, or the symptoms do not adversely affect quality of life (QoL), if possible combined with a healthy or almost healthy mucosa and only need for local medication.’ 

- **Uncontrolled disease:** ‘Partially or uncontrolled patients will have symptoms of nasal blockage, discharge, facial pain/pressure, reduced sense of smell and sleep disturbance of >5 in addition to nasal endoscopy findings and the need for rescue medication.’ 

A person with uncontrolled CRSwNP whose symptoms persist despite treatment may be referred to an Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) or specialised Rhinology clinic for further investigation and treatment.[12] Persistent symptoms leading to referral can include loss of sense of smell, nasal obstruction and mucus that have not resolved with INCS or, in some cases, SCS (Section 1.2.2.1).[12] GP referral rates are variable, with some patients estimated to spend 2 to 3 years in primary care without satisfactory improvement before being referred to a specialist.[12] 

## _**1.2.1.3 Epidemiology**_ 

Epidemiological studies for CRSwNP are limited and prevalence estimates are impacted by the heterogeneity of CRS and the diagnostic criteria that are applied.[27] In 2013, analysis of Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) and Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) data collected from over 700 primary care practices in the UK estimated the prevalence of CRSwNP in the adult population to be 1.6 per 100,000 individuals (0.16%).[3] 

The peak incidence of CRSwNP occurs in working-age adults between 45 to 60 years.[2] The prevalence of CRSwNP in the UK is greater in males compared with females, and increases with age.[3] In 2013, the prevalence of CRSwNP in the UK was highest among individuals aged 55 to 64 years (Table 4).[3]

## _**1.2.1.4 Clinical burden**_ 

## _**1.2.1.4.1 Symptomatic burden**_ 

People with uncontrolled CRSwNP experience substantial symptomatic burden and have high levels of morbidity.[23,32] One study compared 36-item Short-Form Health Survey (SF-36) results for 445 people with CRSwNP (in whom the mean duration of symptoms was 12.8 years) with those of the age-adjusted population norm.[5] People with CRSwNP had worse general health, bodily pain and physical functioning (all p<0.0001 and all exceeded the minimum clinically important difference [MCID]) than the age-adjusted population norm.[5] 

The 22-item Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) is a patient-reported outcome (PRO) measure designed to assess symptomatic burden in people with CRS.[7] Baseline SNOT-22 data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 show that loss of sense of smell/taste is the most burdensome symptom experienced by people with CRSwNP (Section 2.6.3), followed by nasal blockage, post-nasal discharge, thick nasal discharge and poor sleep quality.[7] Sinonasal obstruction/congestion can greatly impact the physical and emotional functioning of people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, particularly through impaired sleep which increases fatigue and reduces daytime productivity.[26,33,34] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 18 of 171 



<!-- page 21 -->

Some severe cases of CRSwNP are associated with orbital and intracranial complications.[12,19] For example, polyps that cause orbital compression may lead to ocular symptoms (such as diplopia [double vision] and ophthalmoplegia [paralysis or weakness of eye muscles]), while the presence of sinonasal mucoceles (mucus-filled cysts) can cause further obstruction of the sinuses.[1,12] 

## _**1.2.1.4.2 Comorbidities associated with type 2 inflammation**_ 

People with CRSwNP are frequently diagnosed with comorbidities associated with type 2 inflammation, which include comorbid refractory persistent asthma, inhalant allergy and NSAID-ERD.[9,16,32,35-38] 

The association between CRSwNP and asthma is well-established. One systematic review reported baseline data from 5 clinical trials (representing 1,748 participants), showing that comorbid asthma occurred in 62.3% of people with CRSwNP (range: 56.0% to 71.0%).[39] Additional support includes a multicentre cross-sectional study of 869 people by the Global Allergy and Asthma European Network (GALEN) which documented comorbid asthma in 49.6% of people with CRSwNP, and a UK-based survey study (N=1,470) which documented comorbid asthma in 46.9% of people with CRSwNP.[23,38] When viewed from the opposite perspective, registry data from the Severe Asthma Network Italy (SANI) have recorded CRSwNP in 40.6% of people with severe asthma.[40] 

The estimated prevalence of inhalant allergy among people with CRSwNP in the UK is significantly higher than the prevalence among matched normal controls (31.0% vs. 13%; respectively, p<0.001).[38] Common allergens reported in the UK study included house dust mites and grass pollen.[38] 

NSAID-ERD is defined as the presence of CRSwNP with asthma and NSAID sensitivity; NSAID-ERD is a progressive condition with increased prevalence among people over 40 years of age.[27,37,41] A study in the UK documented aspirin sensitivity in almost 10% of people with CRSwNP (62/651 people; mean age of 56 years).[38] 

The presence of comorbidity correlates with increased severity of CRSwNP symptoms and increased need for revision ESS.[9,42] In particular, the severity of CRSwNP has been correlated with the presence of comorbid asthma (p<0.0001), inhalant allergy (p=0.0017) and aspirin sensitivity (p<0.0001).[42] In a study of 724 people with CRSwNP, when compared with people without comorbid asthma, those with comorbid asthma had higher mean LundMackay- (LMK-) Computed Tomography (CT) scores (indicating greater opacification (‘clouding’) of sinuses), higher mean SNOT-22 scores and higher mean total symptom scores (all p<0.001).[35] Comorbid asthma is also more common among people with CRSwNP

<!-- page 22 -->

## _**1.2.1.4.3 Recurrence and the clinical burden of revision surgery**_ 

Several types of ESS exist for the treatment of people with CRSwNP including polypectomy, ‘functional’ ethmoidectomy (conserves the mucosa) and radical ethmoidectomy (removes some or all of the mucosa).[44] Functional ESS (FESS) refers to surgeries aiming to restore the normal physiology of the sinuses, such as ethmoidectomy.[1,44] Based on the criteria described in Section 1.2.2.1.2, people with uncontrolled CRSwNP may be offered ESS with the intention of removing nasal polyps and improving aeration of the occluded paranasal sinuses, along with opening up the ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses and improving drainage from the maxillary antrum (i.e. spheno-ethmoidectomy with middle meatal antrostomy).[10,12,19] ESS can alleviate sinonasal symptoms and improve the delivery of INCS; however the 5- year revision rate for sinonasal surgery has been estimated at ~15% and increases among people who had one or more previous surgeries (20.2% vs. 9.8% in patients with and without prior sinonasal surgery, respectively).[8] The clinical benefits of surgery are not only temporary but may also be unsatisfactory for the patient. For example, there is no assurance that a person’s sense of smell will return following multiple surgeries.[12] During consultation between Sanofi and UK clinical experts, it was estimated that 75% to 80% of people with CRSwNP do not achieve satisfactory improvement in their sense of smell following ESS, and the likelihood of gaining an improved sense of smell further diminishes following a second and third sinonasal surgery.[12,45] In CRSwNP, loss of smell may be caused by the degeneration of olfactory neurones and shedding of the olfactory epithelium due to type 2 inflammation, which explains this decreasing likelihood of smell improvement with increasing numbers of surgeries as surgery does not address inflammation.[45] 

People with CRSwNP who require revision surgery must be re-referred by their GP to a rhinology clinic. Revision sinonasal surgeries are rarely prioritised in the NHS (with the exception of severe cases, such as those involving bone erosion), and a duration of 2 to 3 years may elapse between recurrence and revision surgery.[12] During this delay to surgery, ongoing type 2 inflammation promotes upper airway remodelling in the nose and sinonasal cavities (Figure 4), causing compression of the olfactory nerves and reducing the likelihood that a person will ever regain their sense of smell.[12] Patients on the waiting list for revision surgery are also exposed to the cumulative toxicity of both SCS and high dose INCS (Section 1.2.2.2.1).[12]

The burden of invasive surgical procedures for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP involves a period of recovery for the patient (approximately 14 days in the UK), in addition to carrying a risk of post-operative complications.[10,12] For patients requiring revision surgery (Section 1.2.2.2.2), the risk of complications increases with each subsequent surgery.[8,16] Additionally, some patients may receive SCS in the postoperative setting, which amplifies the cumulative SCS burden.[30] 

The risk of recurrence following surgery increases among people with type 2 comorbidities indicative of a severe type 2 inflammation burden, such as asthma or NSAID-ERD.[9,12,16,35,36] A retrospective UK-based study using ten years of data from the HES database (April 2010 to March 2020) analysed the rates of revision ESS among people with CRSwNP with or without comorbidities (Table 5).[9] Multiple surgeries were required by ~20% and ~35% of people with CRSwNP and comorbid asthma or CRSwNP and comorbid NSAID-ERD, respectively, compared to ~10% for people with CRSwNP and no comorbidity.[9] The study also identified a shorter median time to first revision surgery for people with CRSwNP and comorbid asthma (7 years) or NSAID-ERD (5 years) vs. people with CRSwNP and no comorbidity (9 years; both p<0.001).[9] Over the 10-year study period, the median number of non-surgical events (i.e., any encounter with an ENT or respiratory specialist) ranged from 6.0 for people with no comorbidity up to 14.9 for people with comorbid NSAID-ERD.[9] This high number of non-surgical events in people with CRSwNP and comorbid NSAID-ERD is indicative of the transient clinical benefit of surgical intervention and the disease burden incurred between revision surgeries.[9] People with CRSwNP and comorbid NSAID-ERD or CRSwNP and comorbid asthma represent a population with uncontrolled disease, who may be at the highest risk of surgical failure.[9,12,16,35,36]

## _**1.2.1.5 Humanistic burden**_ 

The impairment in HRQoL experienced by people with CRS (CRSwNP or CRSsNP) is comparable to that associated with other serious chronic diseases.[47] When assessed using SF-36, mean scores for physical functioning in patients with CRS (CRSwNP or CRSsNP; 87.3) have been found to be similar to those for patients with chronic conditions such as migraine (82.4) and epilepsy (78.9).[47] The persistent symptoms of CRSwNP have a substantial adverse impact on patients’ HRQoL, affecting their sleep quality, mood and activities of daily living.[5-7] 

Analysis of data collected by GALEN show that compared with age-matched population norms, people with CRSwNP have significantly lower SF-36 scores in the domains of mental health, emotional functioning, social functioning and vitality (all p<0.0001).[5] Further worsening of SF-36 scores is noted for patients with CRSwNP and comorbid asthma or NSAID-ERD.[5] 

For people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, symptoms reported to have the greatest impact on HRQoL are sinonasal congestion and/or obstruction, loss of sense of smell and sleep impairment.[4,6,7] The impact of CRSwNP on patients mental health is also evident, as patients are at greater risk of neuropsychiatric conditions (such as anxiety and depression) compared with the general population (p<0.0005).[32] 

During patient interviews in the UK (see Appendix S for the full Patient Insights Workshops Report), several patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP mentioned that sinonasal 

congestion/obstruction associated with nasal discharge had a substantial negative impact on their daily life.[26] Patients reported embarrassment and anxiety in work and social settings due to the constant need to blow their nose and changes in their voice caused by these symptoms.[26] This anxiety leads some patients to avoid social situations and public speaking, with two patients explaining:[26] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 22 of 171 



<!-- page 25 -->

- _‘I lost confidence in social situations. I started to avoid some social situations because I felt like I sounded strange when I spoke.’_ 

- _‘There were times when I was asked to speak in a meeting or a conference and I declined because I couldn't speak in front of everybody [as a result of her CRSwNP] and especially strangers, I couldn't have done it.’_ 

Loss of smell associated with the presence of nasal polyps is an often underappreciated symptom that increases with disease severity and adversely influences daily life in many ways.[7,26,48] Most people with CRSwNP find that loss of smell negatively impacts their mental health and their ability to perform and/or enjoy multiple daily activities.[48] Living with CRSwNP may also mean people experience an impaired ability to enjoy food due to impaired olfaction and taste, experience decreased appetite and poorer well-being, suffer from anxiety and depression, and have reduced awareness of personal hygiene.[2,12,26,48] People with CRSwNP can also face danger through an inability to smell rancid food, smoke or fire.[1,48] 

Sleep disorder due to the inability to breathe through the nose along with post nasal drip is also a driver of reduced HRQoL in people with nasal polyposis and may be twice as likely (odds ratio [OR] 2.25; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.54, 3.29) to occur in people with CRSwNP compared with healthy controls.[49,50] Based on interviews with UK patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP, some patients experience panic attacks due to not being able to breathe through their nose while falling asleep, they were:[26] 

- _‘I was almost having panic attacks at night because of drifting off to sleep and instinctively trying to breathe through my nose and remembering that I couldn’t.’_ 

- _‘Sometimes when you're just drifting off to sleep. I try and breathe through my nose. And you can't. And then I just would go into panic mode.’_ 

During consultation with clinical experts in the UK, it was mentioned that CRSwNP does not only impact the patients’ sleep but may also disturb their partner’s sleep due to snoring and snorting.[12] Interviews of patients in the UK confirmed this detrimental effect on partners; a patient said ‘ _my wife and I have not been in the same bedroom for a good number of years now because of the snoring.’_[26] 

Surgical removal of nasal polyps can improve HRQoL for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, as measured by SNOT-22 and European Quality of Life Scale-5 dimension (EQ-5D) scores.[51] However, this improvement in HRQoL generally lasts only up to 6 months based on interviews with people with CRSwNP in the UK.[26] Studies investigating HRQoL among patients who require revision surgery are sparse, however one US-based study found that 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 23 of 171 



<!-- page 26 -->

mean EQ-5D VAS scores decreased with increasing number of sinus surgeries (mean EQ5D VAS scores for patients with 1 prior surgery, ≥1 surgery and ≥2 surgeries were 68.6, 66.4 and 60.8, respectively).[51,52] Data collected in a study by GALEN support this observation, with lower SF-36 scores among people with CRSwNP and a history of sinus surgery compared to people with CRSwNP and no history of sinus surgery.[5] 

Notably, the impact of CRSwNP on patients’ HRQoL may be underestimated. As CRSwNP is a chronic condition, people with CRSwNP typically adapt to their disease and underestimate the severity of their symptoms.[12] For instance, the underestimation of the negative impact that loss of smell/taste has on patients’ HRQoL was captured by a quote from interviews with UK patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP: ‘ _The hardest thing is the no smell and no taste. You adjust to it, and you live with it, but that's the thing I miss most, smelling and tasting food.’_[26] Patient interviews also demonstrated that symptoms are continuous, which potentially magnifies the underestimation of the HRQoL impact; a patient said about CRSwNP _‘can be a bit depressing because it's relentless. There's no escape from it. It gets you down, combine that with tiredness and it does get a bit depressing after a while.’_[26] The poor reliability of nasal polyp score (NPS; Appendix M) as a method of assessing patient outcome is illustrated by cases of CRS with multiple polyps; while a person with a high NPS may adjust to impaired breathing (i.e., breathing through their mouth rather than their nose), they can remain distressed by their loss of sense of smell.[12] 

## _**1.2.1.6 Economic burden**_ 

CRSwNP is associated with productivity loss due to absenteeism and presenteeism, as well as substantial healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU) largely attributable to outpatient care.[1,9,51,53] A high proportion of people with CRSwNP are of working age, therefore indirect costs make a greater contribution to the overall economic burden of CRSwNP compared with direct costs.[1,53] The substantial burden of reduced work productivity in CRSwNP was reflected in patient interviews in the UK, during which patients reported difficulties following a normal working schedule.[26] Some patients had to reduce their working hours and some had to completely stop working.[26] 

In a Dutch cross-sectional analysis of productivity cost questionnaire (iPCQ) responses from 115 people with CRSwNP, total indirect costs incurred by people with CRSwNP amounted to €5,659.30 per patient per year (PPPY; cost year: 2014).[53] People with CRSwNP reported a mean of 10.6 (standard deviation [SD]: 44.4) missed days of work per year, and about one third (34.9%) of people reported reduced effectiveness when at work.[53] Mean absenteeism and presenteeism costs represented €1,441.20 and €1,447.30 PPPY, respectively.[53]

## **1.2.2 Clinical pathway of care** 

## _**1.2.2.1 Current treatment options in the UK**_ 

Guidance on the diagnosis and management of CRS in England is based on recommendations published by the European Rhinologic Society (published as the EPOS, 2020).[54] Supportive recommendations are provided by the British Rhinological Society (BRS) and European Forum for Research and Education in Allergy and Airway Disease (EUFOREA).[1,6,10,55] As detailed below, these recommendations include use of an INCS at each step of the treatment pathway, while only short-term use of SCS is recommended for the alleviation of acute exacerbations (i.e., worsening of symptoms back to baseline severity) in people who do not respond to an INCS, with the aim of reducing nasal polyp size and providing rapid relief.[1,10] ESS may be recommended for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, with the goal of alleviating sinonasal symptoms and improving the delivery of INCS.[10] Following surgery, people are advised to continue use of an INCS with saline rinses in order to maintain the clinical benefits of ESS.[10] Short courses of SCS may be used for acute exacerbations both before and after ESS.[1] When waiting for revision surgery, patients commonly receive SCS in clinical practice,[12] despite a strong recommendation from the European Academy of Allergy & Clinical Immunology (EAACI) against the use of SCS in people with CRSwNP in the preoperative setting.[56] 

## _**1.2.2.1.1 Definition of sinonasal surgeries in EPOS and EUFOREA**_ 

EPOS 2020 guidelines define FESS as ESS aiming to restore the normal physiology of sinuses, while full FESS is defined as ESS with complete sinus opening, anterior/posterior ethmoidectomy, middle meatal antrostomies, sphenoidotomy and frontal opening.[1] Extended and radical ESS have a similar definition to full ESS, but extended ESS may involve areas beyond the sinuses and radical ESS includes significant removal of mucosa.[1] Updated EPOS/EUFOREA 2024 guidelines state that there is no consensus on the extent of ESS, except for the recommendation against polypectomy alone without a complete ESS.[10] 

## _**1.2.2.1.2 EPOS and EUFOREA recommendations**_ 

According to EPOS 2020 guidelines, people who are diagnosed with uncontrolled CRSwNP who do not show clinical improvement after 6 to 12 weeks of appropriate medical treatment may be offered primary ESS, unless surgery/anaesthesia are contraindicated (Figure 5).[1] Updated guidance (2024) from EPOS and EUFOREA also now state that people with CRSwNP are eligible for primary ESS if:[10] 

- They have severe CRSwNP symptoms despite nasal rinses, INCS and 1 to 2 course(s) of OCS in the last 12 months

- The patient is willing/able to undergo surgery 

For people with no improvement at 6 to 12 weeks following appropriate medical treatment and ESS, and who have evidence of type 2 inflammation, EPOS recommend either aspirin de-sensitisation (for people with comorbid NSAID-ERD only), revision ESS or a treatment with a biologic (Figure 5).[1] EPOS highlight that the time between revision ESS decreases with increasing numbers of revision ESS.[30]

## _**1.2.2.2 Limitations of current treatment options**_ 

CRSwNP is characterised by a long disease duration and resistance to therapy.[2] As described in Section 1.2.2.1, the standard of care (hereafter described as ‘established clinical management’ or ECM) for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP includes INCS with saline rinses, SCS for exacerbations and, for patients whose disease remains uncontrolled (defined as per EPOS 2020 guidelines; Section 1.2.1.2), surgery.[1,10] Despite being part of ECM, SCS and surgery provide only limited clinical benefit to some people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, and can be associated with high morbidity.[12] 

In people with comorbid NSAID-ERD, treatment may also include aspirin de-sensitisation.[1,10] However, only a few centres offer this treatment in the UK, so it is not considered part of the ECM for the purpose of this submission. Aspirin desensitisation is also associated with a limited efficacy and poor safety profile in comparison to biologics.[57] Based on a systematic literature review (SLR) with network meta-analysis (NMA) including 29 RCTs in patients with CRSwNP (N=3,461), aspirin desensitisation was associated with an increased incidence of adverse events and lower clinical benefit compared with biologics, including dupilumab.[57] 

## **1.2.2.2.1** _**Limitations of SCS**_ 

Therapy with SCS reduces type 2 inflammation by suppressing the immune system but is limited by its inability to only target the type 2 pathways specifically, which underlies the pathogenesis of CRSwNP.[11] It is not possible therefore to provide a sustained response, and the clinical benefits of SCS diminish over time.[10] 

Extensive (cumulative courses >300 mg within one year) use of SCS in people with CRSwNP is also associated with an increased risk of adverse events, including but not limited to bruising, osteoporosis, diabetes, hypertension, myocardial infarction (if used at high doses over a long period), sleep and mood disturbances, cataracts and glaucoma.[10,12,56,58] Despite this, clinicians may prescribe longer courses of SCS, as reported during patient interviews in the UK ( _‘Well, for a long time I would get three months of steroids and then I would stop for a month or two and then I'd get another three months’_ ), reflecting a 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 30 of 171 



<!-- page 33 -->

lack of alternative options.[10,26] Clinicians estimate that following surgery, ~10% of people with uncontrolled CRSwNP develop reliance on SCS as a maintenance therapy.[12] A UK study with a minimum follow-up of 2 years found use of SCS in people with asthma and/or chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) increased the risk of osteoporosis (diagnosis or fracture), pneumonia, heart failure, cardio- or cerebro-vascular disease and cataracts.[59] Notably, comorbid asthma in people with CRSwNP may increase the risk of adverse events associated with SCS (Table 10).[13]

## _**1.2.2.2.2 Limitations of Surgery**_ 

Surgical intervention for uncontrolled CRSwNP provides partial and temporary relief of some sinonasal symptoms, however the underlying driver of disease (type 2 inflammation) remains, with the potential for polyps to recur.[8,10] Based on patient interviews conducted in the UK, symptoms return quickly following sinonasal surgery; one patient said regarding their symptoms post-surgery: _‘So, within two months it was just full polyps everywhere.’_[26] Furthermore, surgery may not be appropriate for all people with CRSwNP and is contraindicated in those with severe uncontrolled asthma due to the risks associated with anaesthesia.[10] Although people with CRSwNP without previous surgery are outside of the patient population considered in this submission, those with CRSwNP and comorbid severe uncontrolled asthma may be able to benefit from dupilumab within the asthma indication.[60] 

Invasive surgical procedures for uncontrolled CRSwNP also carry a risk of complications.[10,14] Minor complications, occurring in up to ~21% of patients, include perioperative bleeding, post-operative infection and synechiae in the nose.[15] Severe complications occur in up to 1.5% of patients and include cerebral spinal fluid leaks, haemorrhage, orbital complications (which may include blindness in most severe cases) and intracranial complications.[15,30] 

For patients requiring revision surgery, the risk of complications increases with each subsequent surgery.[8,16] It has been found that, before undergoing ESS, patients are most concerned about the risk of revision surgery and wait time for surgery.[30] Based on interviews 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 31 of 171 



<!-- page 34 -->

with UK patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP, surgery was a very negative experience for some patients ( _‘My body went into shock over it. I mean, the pain was horrific. It was just the most horrific experience’_ ).[26] Thus, some patients are reluctant to undergo revision surgery; for instance a patient said ‘ _It is not something I would relish, the thought of having an operation again to be honest with you. If anything, I'd rather not have surgery again, to be honest with you.’_[26] As described in Section 1.2.2.2.2, revision surgeries may not address some of the CRSwNP symptoms (e.g., smell) and offer only temporary symptomatic benefit and limited improvement in patient HRQoL.[5] One patient currently treated with dupilumab for CRSwNP through the Compassionate Use Scheme in the UK said that, prior to initiating dupilumab, he _‘suffered constant inflammation, congestion, pressure headaches, migraines, and the loss of smell and taste’_ despite six surgeries over the course of ten years.[61] 

## _**1.2.2.3 Proposed positioning of dupilumab**_ 

Dupilumab targets the underlying type 2 inflammation driving the pathophysiology of CRSwNP.[17,18] Specifically, type 2 inflammation is targeted by dupilumab through selective inhibition of IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, which is a central and key driver of type 2 inflammation.[17,18] The clinical relevance of type 2 inflammation in people with CRSwNP, particularly in people who require revision surgery, was illustrated in a retrospective study of 33,107 patients in the UK CPRD Aurum database (January 2007 to June 2019), in which investigators documented increasing levels of blood eosinophils (biomarker for type 2 inflammation) in patients requiring multiple rounds of revision surgery for nasal polyps.[16] 

While dupilumab and other biologics have received regulatory approval for the treatment of people with uncontrolled CRSwNP in the UK, none are available to patients through the NHS. Of the other biologics, mepolizumab and omalizumab also target the type 2 inflammatory pathways but at different points further downstream compared to dupilumab.[17,18,62-64] Mepolizumab targets IL-5 which, although it may contribute to the increase in blood eosinophils (biomarker for type 2 inflammation), plays a minor role in the type 2 inflammation response relative to that of IL-4/IL-13.[62] Omalizumab targets IgE,[63 ] which is produced only in response to upstream IL-4/IL-13 signalling (Figure 2).[64] In contrast, dupilumab targets IL-4 and IL-13 which play several major driving roles in type 2 inflammation (Table 11).[17,18,64] Accordingly, treatment with dupilumab has a comprehensive effect, suppressing type 2 inflammation and causing significant reductions in multiple type 2 inflammatory biomarkers, including IgE and eotaxin-3 (both in the blood and nasal secretions).[64]

The proposed positioning of dupilumab in the treatment of people with uncontrolled CRSwNP is depicted in Figure 8. In line with pivotal studies, it is anticipated that dupilumab will be used in combination with INCS in people who have received one or more prior sinonasal surgeries, with the goal of reducing type 2 inflammation, improving sinonasal symptoms and HRQoL, and reducing the risk of revision surgery and need for rescue SCS.[68] As described in Section 1.3, current ECM for patients following one sinonasal surgery consists of INCS (combined with saline rinses) and SCS, with the goal of decreasing the requirement for revision surgeries.[1] Therefore the most appropriate comparator for dupilumab as an add-on therapy to INCS, based on current clinical practice guidelines, is ECM consisting of SCS and revision surgery.

## _**1.3 Equality considerations**_ 

It is expected that introduction of dupilumab in ECM will reduce existing inequalities in the care of patients with CRSwNP, as described below. 

Although biologics targeting type 2 inflammation have regulatory approval in the UK for CRSwNP (including dupilumab), none are currently reimbursed.[17,18,62,63] People with uncontrolled CRSwNP are therefore at a significant disadvantage compared to people with other forms of chronic type 2 inflammatory conditions, such as asthma and atopic dermatitis (AD), for whom targeted biologic therapies are already reimbursed.[17,18,60,69] A NICE recommendation for dupilumab in uncontrolled CRSwNP could positively impact this inequality. 

Consultation with physicians in the UK indicates that people with uncontrolled CRSwNP are likely to remain on a waiting list for ESS for a duration of 6 months up to 3 years depending on where they live, and ~50% of these people are waiting for revision surgery.[12] Based on the evidence presented in this submission, adding dupilumab to ECM (i.e., INCS) is expected to reduce the number of people with uncontrolled CRSwNP who require revision ESS.[12] Thus, the addition of dupilumab to ECM has the potential to alleviate CRSwNP burden on the NHS and reduce wait times for ESS, while the number of patients on waiting lists for treatment in England is currently increasing.[12,70] The benefits of including dupilumab as part of ECM for patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP have been demonstrated in Scotland (NHS Tayside) where, in response to long wait times for elective surgery (>9 months), use of

<!-- page 38 -->

dupilumab among ~30 patients with severe asthma and CRSwNP led to a 50% decrease in the rate of nasal polyp recurrence within 12 months of ESS.[12] 

## **2 Clinical effectiveness** 

_**An SLR identified two high-quality clinical trials for dupilumab in the relevant patient population as defined by the NICE scope (SINUS-24 and SINUS-52)**_ 

- SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are phase 3, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised, parallel group, multicentre international trials, evaluating the efficacy and safety of dupilumab 300 mg added to standard of care in adult patients with severe CRSwNP versus placebo group. 

- In both trials, the co-primary endpoints were the change in bilateral endoscopic NPS; range 0 to 8) and nasal congestion/obstruction (NC) score (range 0 to 3) from baseline to Week 24. 

- Individual results from both trials and results from the prespecified pooled analysis are presented in this submission and have informed the economic analysis. 

- _**SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 have robustly demonstrated the efficacy of dupilumab in uncontrolled CRSwNP**_ 

- In both trials, dupilumab resulted in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the co-primary endpoints of NPS and NC score at Week 24 compared to placebo. Improvements were observed as early as the first post-baseline assessment and continuously improved through Week 24. In SINUS-52, these results were maintained through Week 52 in patients treated with dupilumab once every 2 weeks (Q2W). 

- In both trials, dupilumab resulted in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in each hierarchically tested secondary endpoint at Week 24, compared to placebo. In SINUS-52, these results were maintained through Week 52. 

- Quality of life, as measured by the SNOT-22, was significantly better with dupilumab compared to placebo. 

- CRSwNP symptoms, as measured by the total symptom score (TSS), University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) and loss of smell (LoS), were significantly improved with dupilumab compared to placebo. 

- Analysis of pooled data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 showed that the proportion of patients who required SCS or sinonasal surgery during the treatment period was significantly lower for those receiving dupilumab vs. placebo (9.6% vs. 33.9%, respectively, p<0.0001). 

_**The safety profile of dupilumab for the treatment of CRSwNP is acceptable and consistent with existing safety data in patients with AD, asthma, COPD and prurigo nodularis (PN)**_ 

- Dupilumab has an established and robust safety profile, validated by an extensive clinical development programme involving 15,834 participants and further supported by real-world safety data across multiple indications, with no new safety signals identified in patients with CRSwNP. To date over 1 million patients have been treated with dupilumab for licenced indications worldwide. 

- Dupilumab demonstrated a favourable benefit-risk and tolerability profile in CRSwNP in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. 

- Dupilumab has the potential to generate a significant step-change in the effective treatment of uncontrolled CRSwNP in England, providing meaningful benefits to a burdened patient population with limited treatment options. 

## _**2.1 Identification and selection of relevant studies**_ 

An SLR was conducted with a cut-off date of 01 October 2024 to identify all relevant RCTs reporting on the clinical efficacy and safety of dupilumab and other relevant treatments in adults with uncontrolled CRSwNP.

A total of 16,856 publications were identified in the database searches, and following removal of duplicates, 15,359 publications underwent title and abstract screening. Overall, 465 publications were selected for full-text screening, along with 6 publications identified through grey literature searches, and 141 publications were included in the SLR. These 141 publications reported data from 39 unique RCTs. Among the RCTs identified, 19 investigated biologics (including dupilumab, omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab and CM310), four investigated surgery and 16 investigated other interventions (including corticosteroids [CSs], leukotriene receptor antagonists [LTRA] and implants comprising CSs). The two RCTs which investigated dupilumab, LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 (i.e., SINUS-24) and LIBERTY NP SINUS-52 (i.e., SINUS-52), are described in detail below. 

Full details of the SLR methodology, study selection process, inclusion and exclusion criteria and results are presented in Appendix D.1. 

## _**2.2 List of relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

The relevant clinical effectiveness evidence for dupilumab in CRSwNP was generated from the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials which are summarised in Table 12. The two trials had similar designs, except for the study duration and the number of dupilumab treatment arms:[68] 

- The trial duration was 24 weeks for SINUS-24 and 52 weeks for SINUS-52. 

- SINUS-24 included one dupilumab treatment arm (Q2W), while SINUS-52 included two dupilumab treatment arms with a different dosing to SINUS-24 in one of the arms (Arm A: Q2W; Arm B: Q2W to Week 24, then once every four weeks [Q4W] to Week 52). 

Both studies were multinational, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group phase 3 trials evaluating the efficacy and safety of dupilumab 300 mg in adult patients with severe CRSwNP receiving standard of care (defined as 100 μg mometasone furoate nasal spray [MFNS] in each nostril twice daily).[68]

## _**2.3 Summary of methodology of the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

## **2.3.1 Trial Design** 

SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were both multinational, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group phase 3 trials evaluating the efficacy and safety of dupilumab 300 mg added to standard of care in adult patients with severe CRSwNP.[68] 

The SINUS-24 study included a 4-week run-in period (±3 days), a 24-week treatment period (±3 days) and a 24-week post-treatment follow-up period (±3 days; no dupilumab/placebo received).[68] Patients were randomised (1:1) to receive dupilumab or placebo until Week 24; all patients also received standard of care treatment with MFNS (100 µg in each nostril twice daily) until Week 24 (Figure 9).[68]

## **2.3.2 Patient eligibility** 

Eligible patients enrolled in SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 comprised adults with bilateral sinonasal polyposis and symptoms of CRS despite INCS therapy and who had received SCS in the preceding two years (or had a medical contraindication or intolerance to SCS) or previous surgery for nasal polyps.[68] Key inclusion and exclusion criteria for SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are presented in Table 15. 

**Table 15. Inclusion and exclusion criteria for SINUS-24 and SINUS-52[68,71,72]**

- Patients with bilateral sinonasal polyposis that persisted despite prior treatment with SCS within the past 2 years; and/or had a medical contraindication/intolerance to SCS; and/or had prior sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps, and had: o An endoscopic bilateral NPS ≥5 at Visit 1 (maximum score of 8) with a minimum score of 2 in each nasal cavity 

- o Ongoing symptoms (for at least 8 weeks before Visit 1)* of nasal congestion or obstruction (moderate or severe: score 2 or 3 at Visit 1 and a weekly average severity of >1 at Visit 2), and either loss of smell (partial or total) or rhinorrhoea (anterior or posterior) 

- **Exclusion criteria** • Aged <18 years • Had taken:

## **2.3.3 Settings and locations** 

SINUS-24 was conducted at 79 centres in 13 countries (Bulgaria, Republic Czech, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Ukraine, Russia, the UK and the US).[71] Of these 79 centres, 67 randomised at least one participant.[71] Six sites were located in the UK which included a randomised total of 19 patients; two of these 19 patients withdrew prematurely from the study. 

SINUS-52 was conducted at 119 centres in 14 countries (including Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Chile, Israel, Mexico, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Sweden, Turkey, Japan and the US).[72] Of these 119 centres, 117 randomised at least one participant.[72] 

## **2.3.4 Trial drugs and concomitant medications** 

Patients in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 studies were randomised 1:1 to receive either dupilumab or placebo, with randomisation stratified by history of asthma, history of NSAID-ERD, for nasal polyps and country.[68,71,72]

In SINUS-24, patients were randomised (1:1) to receive 300 mg of dupilumab subcutaneously (SC) Q2W or placebo Q2W until Week 24,[68] while in SINUS-52, patients were randomised (1:1:1) to receive the following treatment regimens:[68] 

- Dupilumab 300 mg SC Q2W until Week 52 (Arm A) 

- Dupilumab 300 mg SC Q2W until Week 24, then SC Q4W until Week 52 (Arm B) 

- Placebo Q2W until Week 52 (Arm C) 

In both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, all patients were receiving standard of care which consisted of 2 self-administered actuations of MFNS (50 μg/actuation) in each nostril twice daily (400 μg per day total) from the beginning of the run-in period and throughout the study.[68,71,72] If patients were unable to tolerate the MFNS dose, or its use was prohibited due to a specific regulatory requirement, patients could reduce the dose to 2 actuations of MFNS in each nostril once daily (200 μg per day total).[68] 

The following treatments were permitted as rescue therapies throughout both studies:[71,72] 

- Nasal lavage with saline and/or systemic antibiotics (≤2 weeks in case of acute infection) 

- Short course SCS (≤2 weeks prednisone or prednisolone) 

- Sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps 

Other permitted concomitant therapies included short term antibiotics (<2 weeks), short and long-acting beta agonists, long-acting muscarinic antagonists, methylxanthines, INCS and systemic antihistamines, as well as leukotriene antagonists/modifiers and allergen immunotherapy if started prior to screening.[71,72] 

## **2.3.5 Outcomes** 

The co-primary endpoints in SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were the change in bilateral endoscopic NPS (range 0 to 8) and NC score (range 0 to 3) from baseline at Week 24.[68] In Japan, the change in sinus opacification (LMK-CT score) was included as a third co-primary outcome, whereas it was a key secondary outcome in the other trial countries.[68] Two of the key secondary endpoints in both trials, which assessed HRQoL and one of the most burdensome symptoms in patients with CRSwNP, were changes from baseline at Week 24 in SNOT-22 score and in daily symptoms of decreased/loss of smell, respectively.[68] 

Additionally, two key secondary endpoints (proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment with SCS or sinonasal surgery and change from baseline in lung function in patients with

## **2.3.6 Baseline characteristics** 

A total of 276 patients were randomised in the SINUS-24 study (n=143 in dupilumab arm; n=133 in placebo arm) and 448 patients in the SINUS-52 study (n=150 in Arm A [dupilumab Q2W]; n=145 in Arm B [dupilumab Q2W to Q4W]; n=153 in placebo arm).[68] 

In SINUS-24, 263 patients completed study treatment during the randomised 24-week treatment period; 12 (4.3%) patients discontinued treatment prior to Week 24 and 13 (4.7%) patients had discontinued from the study at Week 48.[68] One patient randomised to dupilumab 300 mg Q2W was not treated.[68] The majority of patients completed the 24-week treatment period (placebo: n=130 [97.7%]; dupilumab: n=141 [98.6%]), as well as the entire study period including post-treatment follow up (placebo: n=124 [93.2%]; dupilumab: n=138 [96.5%]).[68] 

In SINUS-52, 419 patients completed the first 24 weeks of study treatment (dupilumab: n=285 [96.6%]; placebo: n=133 [86.9%]); 29 patients (6.5%) among the full study population discontinued treatment during the 24-week period.[68] Only 49 patients (10.9%) discontinued study treatment prior to Week 52, with the majority of patients completing study assessments over the 52-week period (Arm A: n=146 [97.3%]; Arm B: n=142 [97.9%]; placebo arm: n=140 [91.5%]).[68]

<!-- page 49 -->

In both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, baseline and demographic factors were balanced between treatment arms and were consistent with a population with severe CRSwNP, based on the ubiquity of chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms, bilateral obstructive polyps and extensive sinus involvement (Table 17).[68] 

The mean patient age was 52 years (range: 42, 61) and the majority of the patients were male (60%).[71] The studies met their prespecified enrolment goal of 50% patients with comorbid asthma and/or NSAID-ERD and 50% with prior sinonasal surgery.[68] History of sinonasal surgery and SCS use was comparable among the treatment groups.[68] The mean time since first diagnosis of CRSwNP in the overall study population was 11.0 years (SD: 9.45).[68] Most patients (63%) had previous surgery for nasal polyps with the number of surgeries ranging from 1 to 11.[68,71,72] In the two years prior to randomisation, 74% of patients received SCS at least once. The mean number of days of SCS use was 14.4 days (range: 1 to 135) in SINUS-24 and 45.5 days (range: 1 to 732) in SINUS-52.[71,72] 

There were 577 (80%) patients with a medical history of ≥1 type 2 inflammation-mediated condition, including 428 (59%) patients with a history of asthma.[68,71,72] The most frequently reported comorbidity other than asthma was allergic rhinitis (SINUS-24: 52.5%; SINUS-52: 60.7%) seasonal or perennial, followed by allergic conjunctivitis (SINUS-24: 10.1%; SINUS52: 12.1%) and food allergy (SINUS-24: 10.1%; SINUS-52: 8.9%) which were comparable between treatment groups.[71,72] 

In the population with comorbid asthma:[71,72]

   - Most patients (88.8%) were on asthma medication in the prior year, with most (76.7%) using both ICS and long-acting beta agonists 

   - At baseline, asthma was uncontrolled in some patients as reflected by median 6-item Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ-6) score of 1.67 

## • In SINUS-52: 

- The mean time since asthma diagnosis was 17.7 years (range: 0.2 to 74.6) and the mean baseline percent predicted FEV1 was 83.4% (range: 52 to 188.3)

## _**2.4 Statistical analysis and definition of study groups in the relevant clinical effectiveness evidence**_ 

## **2.4.1 Study population** 

In the SINUS-24 study, 276 patients were randomised 1:1 to the two treatment groups (dupilumab Q2W: 143; placebo: 133).[68] All 276 randomised patients were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population (used for all primary and secondary efficacy endpoints) and 275 randomised patients (dupilumab Q2W: 143; placebo: 132) were included in the safety population (defined as all patients randomly assigned to study intervention who received at least one dose of study drug).[68,71] 

In the SINUS-52 study, 448 patients were randomised 1:1 to the two treatment groups (dupilumab Q2W: 150; dupilumab Q2W to Q4W: 145; placebo: 153).[68] All 448 randomised patients were included in the ITT population (used for all primary and secondary efficacy endpoints) and 447 randomised patients (dupilumab Q2W: 149; dupilumab Q2W to Q4W: 148; placebo: 150) were included in the safety population (defined as all patients randomly assigned to study intervention who received at least one dose of study drug).[68,72]

## _**2.4.2.2 Sensitivity and subgroup efficacy analyses**_ 

Supportive and sensitivity analyses (e.g., mixed-effect model with repeated measures [MMRM], pattern mixture model with copy increment from placebo, tipping point analysis, as-observed analysis, MMRM approach for NC as binary response data) were conducted on the co-primary outcomes.[71,72] For all sensitivity analyses (except for the ‘as-observed’ analysis), data collected post-surgery or post-SCS were set to ‘missing’ for patients who underwent surgery for nasal polyps or received SCS for any reason.[68] Note that the ‘as-observed’ analysis included data post-SCS for any reason and/or treatment discontinuation but excluded data post-surgery for nasal polyps.[71,72] 

Pre-specified subgroup analyses of the co-primary outcomes were conducted by age, gender, region, territory, race, ethnicity, baseline weight, baseline body mass index (BMI), prior surgery for nasal polyps, asthma comorbidity and/or NSAID-ERD, and SCS use in the Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 54 of 171 



<!-- page 57 -->

prior two years.[71,72] An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model incorporating subgroup-bytreatment interactions was built to test the interaction between treatment and subgroup factor.[71,72] 

## _**2.4.2.3 Pre-specified pooled analyses**_ 

Two prespecified pooled analyses of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 data (proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment [SCS or sinonasal surgery] and FEV1 at Week 24) were included in the statistical hierarchy (Figure 11):[68] 

- For FEV1, data from all dupilumab arms and placebo arms at Week 24 were pooled. 

- For the proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment, data from SINUS-24 were pooled at Week 24, and data from SINUS-52 were pooled at Week 52 for dupilumab Arm A and the placebo arm, and at Week 24 for dupilumab Arm B. 

The change from baseline in FEV1 was analysed using the same hybrid method of worst observation carried forward (WOCF) and multiple imputation (MI) methods as for the coprimary and key secondary outcomes, followed by an ANCOVA model, with an additional covariate of the study indicator in the ANCOVA model.[68] 

The proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment was analysed using the Cox proportional hazards model and the Kaplan Meier method.[68] The Cox model used the event as the dependent variable and the study indicator, treatment group, asthma or NSAID-ERD strata, previous surgery strata and study region as covariates.[68]

## _**2.5 Critical appraisal of the relevant clinical effectiveness**_ 

## _**evidence**_ 

Where available, the primary source of clinical effectiveness evidence was study results published in a peer-reviewed journal; clinical study reports (CSRs) were used as additional data sources as needed. The quality of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, which are highquality studies (double-blinded RCTs with generally balanced patient demographics and characteristics) that are pertinent to the decision problem, was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool 2.0,[89] in line with recommendations from NICE and good practice guidelines. Overall, the risk of bias was considered low for both trials (Table 20). A detailed quality assessment of all the included RCTs is provided in Appendix D.

## _**2.6 Clinical effectiveness results of the relevant studies**_ 

Results from the pooled analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 (including the prespecified pooled analysis for three of the key secondary endpoints) and from selected post-hoc 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 59 of 171 



<!-- page 62 -->

analyses of the trials are presented in this section. Individual trial results for SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are presented in Appendix N. 

The co-primary endpoints were successfully met in both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, and in the pooled ITT population.[68,90] Dupilumab demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in NPS and NS score between baseline and Week 24 compared to placebo.[68,90] 

Please note the thresholds for meaningful changes in scores for objective and patientreported treatment outcomes are not well defined in CRswNP.[71,72] Based on a post-hoc pooled analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 data which used an anchor-based method, the thresholds for clinically meaningful within-patient change were estimated to be 1 point for NC, 1 point for NPS, 5 points for LMK-CT, 3 points for TSS, 8 points for UPSIT and 1 point for LoS.[91] For SNOT-22 total and ACQ-6 scores, the validated MCID defined by the developer is 8.9 points for the SNOT-22 total score and 0.5 points for ACQ-6.[71] The definition of ‘clinically meaningful’ improvements in efficacy in this section, along with the relevant values for each outcome, are presented in Appendix M. 

## **2.6.1 Pooled analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 primary and key secondary endpoints** 

SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 primary and key secondary endpoints were successfully met in the pooled ITT population; results are summarised in Table 21.[90] 

Patients treated with dupilumab demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the co-primary endpoints of NPS and NC score at Week 24 compared with the placebo arm (Figure 12, Figure 13, Table 21), including:[90] 

- Change in NPS from baseline to Week 24: least square (LS) mean difference: −1.91 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −2.14, −1.68), p<0.0001. 

- Change in patient-reported NC score from baseline to Week 24: LS mean difference: −0.88 (95% CI: −1.00, −0.76), p<0.0001.

## **2.6.2 Prespecified pooled analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52** 

The key secondary outcomes in the prespecified pooled analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS52 were successfully met.[68] Dupilumab resulted in a 76% lower proportion of patients who required SCS or sinonasal surgery (73.9% lower for SCS and 82.6% for sinonasal surgery, individually; Table 23) during the treatment period and demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in FEV1 and ACQ-6 in patients with comorbid asthma between baseline and Week 24, compared to placebo.[68] 

Pre-planned pooled analyses of data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were conducted for three outcomes:[68] 

- The proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment (SCS or sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps) 

- The change from baseline at Week 24 in FEV1 in the subset of patients with comorbid asthma 

- The change from baseline at Week 24 in ACQ-6 score in the subset of patients with comorbid asthma 

Data used in the pre-planned pooled analyses are summarised in Table 22.

In the pre-specified pooled analysis, the proportion of patients who required SCS or sinonasal surgery during the treatment period was 76% lower with dupilumab (42 patients) compared with placebo (97 patients; hazard ratio [HR]: 0.243; 95% CI: 0.169, 0.351; p<0.0001; Figure 14, Table 23); specifically:[68] 

- The proportion of patients who required SCS decreased by 73.9% with dupilumab vs. placebo (HR: 0.26; 95% CI: 0.18, 0.38; p<0.0001). 

- The proportion of patients who required surgery decreased by 82.6% with dupilumab vs. placebo (HR: 0.17; 95% CI: 0.07, 0.46; p=0.0005). 

The difference in the proportion of patients who required SCS or sinonasal surgery was evident by Week 8 and continued to become greater in magnitude throughout the treatment period (up to Week 24 for SINUS-24 and Arm B of SINUS-52, and up to Week 52 for Arm A of SINUS-52).[68] Overall, 9.6% of patients receiving dupilumab and 33.9% of patients receiving placebo required rescue treatment over the treatment period.[68]

## **2.6.3 Post-hoc analyses of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52** 

Results of post-hoc analyses of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials are summarised in Table 25. 

Post-hoc analyses of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials demonstrated the efficacy of dupilumab across various CRSwNP outcomes, including reduction of SCS use and sinonasal surgery, improvements in objective disease measures and improvements in patient-reported symptoms and disease-specific HRQoL.[7,11,35,43,65,73,74,76-81,83-86] Improvements with dupilumab were observed across various subgroups of patients including patients with type 2 inflammatory signature, comorbid asthma, comorbid NSAID-ERD, eosinophilic CRSwNP, smell impairment or history of sinus surgery.[7,11,35,43,65,73,76-85] 

The treatment effects with dupilumab, which had a rapid onset and were maintained through Week 52, resulted in statistically significant, clinically meaningful improvements in patientreported symptom outcomes and objective measures:[74,78,81,83] 

- In terms of **olfactory outcomes** , dupilumab produced rapid (as early as Day 3 for LoS) and sustained improvements regardless of prior sinonasal surgery, SCS use or comorbid asthma and/or NSAID-ERD.[43] 

- Dupilumab reduced **anosmia** in patients with smell impairment, and 11.5% of patients even achieved **normosmia** .[85] 

- In a patient population with smell impairment and almost complete sinus opacification, dupilumab significantly reduced **sinus opacification** , a reduction which was correlated with improvements in the **sense of smell** .[86] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 66 of 171 



<!-- page 69 -->

- Dupilumab reduced the need for **SCS use** by 73.9% and **sinonasal surgeries** by 82.6% in patients with CRSwNP even in those with a history of SCS use and/or sinonasal surgery.[79] 

- **Loss of smell/taste** and **nasal obstruction-related symptoms** were of high importance to patients in the SINUS trials, and dupilumab demonstrated significant improvement in these symptoms.[7] 

- Dupilumab increased the number of patients able to achieve mild or no symptoms of nasal congestion, LoS or rhinorrhoea over a month, with 50% of patients who reported a **symptom-free month** and 38.3% who reported a mild-to-no symptom month after 52 weeks of treatment with dupilumab.[73] 

- In terms of HRQoL, patients in the SINUS trials had worse HRQoL compared with the general population, and dupilumab significantly improved **general health status** and all components of **disease-specific HRQoL** including sleep, sense of smell and fatigue.[65,77] 

- Dupilumab reduced the incidence of **infections** , specifically the adverse event (AE) categories ‘infections and infestations’ and ‘upper respiratory infections.’[75] 

Most patients in the SINUS trials (64.3-95.3% of the pooled population depending on the definition used) displayed type 2 inflammatory signature, and dupilumab was effective across type 2 inflammatory signatures definitions.[11] Most patients in the SINUS trials (63.4% of the pooled population) had a history of sinus surgery, and dupilumab was effective regardless of the number of prior surgeries and time since last surgery.[84] Similarly, most patients in the SINUS trials (83.3% of the pooled population) displayed eosinophilic disease, and dupilumab was effective regardless of eosinophilic status.[80] In patients with comorbid asthma who represented almost 60% of the SINUS trials pooled population and had more severe CRSwNP disease compared with those without comorbid asthma:[35,76,82] 

- Dupilumab significantly improved upper and lower airway outcomes irrespective of relevant baseline asthma characteristics and comorbid NSAID-ERD 

- Dupilumab significantly improved asthma outcomes and reduced SCS use irrespective of asthma exacerbations history and prior SCS use 

- Dupilumab significantly improved HRQoL outcomes.

## _**2.9 AROMA registry study**_ 

## **2.9.1 Methodology** 

AROMA was a study designed to characterise patients who receive dupilumab for CRSwNP in a real-world setting and the long-term effectiveness of dupilumab in these patients.[87] 

AROMA was a global, prospective, observational, multicentre, open-label, single-arm, realworld registry study assessing the safety and effectiveness of dupilumab by evaluating objective measures and PROs in adult patients with CRSwNP.[87] 

AROMA included a screening period (1 day to 12 weeks long) followed by an assessment period (≤36 months long) which started from completion of the baseline visit and corresponded to the initiation of treatment with dupilumab.[87] Patients who discontinued from the study before the end of study visit at Month 36 were asked to complete an early termination visit.[87] The timing of visits and the allowed missed visits and unscheduled visits were intended to reflect real-world clinical practice, while allowing adequate analysis and interpretation of the data collected.[87] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 79 of 171 



<!-- page 82 -->

Eligible patients enrolled into AROMA comprised adults who initiated dupilumab for CRSwNP according to country-specific prescribing information as part of their routine care, following prescription by their physician.[87] Key inclusion and exclusion criteria for AROMA are presented in Table 26. 

## **Table 26. Inclusion and exclusion criteria for AROMA** 

- **Inclusion criteria** • ≥18 years of age at dupilumab initiation 

- Newly initiating dupilumab for the treatment of CRSwNP according to country-specific prescribing information 

- Willing and able to comply with clinic visits and study-related procedures 

- **Exclusion criteria** 

- <18 years of age at dupilumab initiation 

- Contraindication to dupilumab according to country-specific prescribing information 

- Previous treatment with dupilumab for any condition 

- Any condition that may interfere with the patient’s ability to participate in the study as per the investigator’s opinion (e.g., short life expectancy, substance abuse, severe cognitive impairment, other medical/social/ personal conditions and circumstances) 

- • Participation in an ongoing interventional or observational study that might influence AROMA’s registry study assessment as per the treating physician’s opinion

US = United States Source: Regeneron Pharmaceuticals data on file, AROMA Registry Study Protocol.[87] 

There were no protocol requirements regarding treatment with dupilumab or other agents during the study.[87] Patients were allowed to receive drugs as necessary for the treatment of CRSwNP and/or comorbid conditions.[87] Treatments other than dupilumab administered during the study (screening and/or assessment periods), including medications started before, during and after treatment with dupilumab, were considered concomitant medications or procedures.[87] Temporary or permanent discontinuation of dupilumab and/or any other treatment were permitted based on physician’s decision.[87] Patients could stay enrolled in the study irrespective of their CRSwNP treatment(s).[87] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] ©Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved Page 80 of 171 



<!-- page 83 -->

The co-primary endpoints in AROMA were the descriptive summary of symptoms/HRQoL and their change over time, and the descriptive summary of patients and disease characteristics for CRSwNP and type 2 comorbidities.[87] Several efficacy outcomes evaluated in AROMA had also been evaluated in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials including NC score, LMK-CT, decreased/loss of smell, SNOT-22, TSS, UPSIT, PNIF, ACQ-6 and FEV1.[87] Among these outcomes, LMK-CT, PNIF and FEV1 were not required per the protocol and were assessed at the treating physician’s discretion.[87] The time frames for assessing the outcomes were as follows:[87] 

- LMK-CT, SNOT-22, PNIF and FEV1 were assessed every three months up to Month 24 and then every six months from Months 24 to 36 

- NC score, decreased/loss of smell and TSS were assessed every three months up to Month 6 and then every six months from Months 6 to 36 

- UPSIT and ACQ-6 were assessed every six months throughout the study period. 

The sample size was selected empirically as no statistical analysis was conducted.[87] Considering an estimated study discontinuation rate of approximately 15% to 20% per year, a sample size of approximately 1,000 patients was decided.[87] Patients who prematurely withdrew from the study could be replaced, if needed, to ensure an adequate number of evaluable patients.[87] The population definitions used in AROMA are presented in Table 28; the registry evaluation analysis set (REAS) population was used for all analyses.[87]

## **2.9.3 Effectiveness and safety results** 

In AROMA, patients demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in SNOT-22 score at 6 months, with a mean change from baseline of −25.0 points (SD: 21.13).[92] Improvements were maintained at 12 months and 24 months, with mean changes from baseline of −27.3 points (SD: 22.61) and −18.0 points (SD: 16.63), respectively (Table 30).[92] 

A total of 7 (1.0%) patients required sinonasal surgery in the first six months of the study.[92] No patients required sinonasal surgery over the period from six months to 24 months.[92] A total of 72 (10.4%) patients required treatment with SCS in the first six months of the study.[92] Among these patients who required SCS in the first six months, the need for SCS decreased thereafter (Table 30):[92] 

- 47 (6.8%)  patients required SCS both in the first six months and between 6 and 12 months. 

- 27 (3.9%) patients required SCS both in the first six months, between 6 and 12 months, and between 12 and 24 months.

## _**2.10 Meta-analysis**_ 

Pooled efficacy results from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are presented in Section 2.6.3 and Section 2.6.2. The SLR did not identify any additional relevant phase 3 studies assessing the efficacy of dupilumab in patients with CRSwNP. Therefore, no additional meta-analyses were conducted. The economic analysis is based on a within-trial comparison with ECM. 

## _**2.11 Indirect and mixed treatment comparisons**_ 

There are currently no NICE-recommended targeted systemic treatments for patients with previously treated uncontrolled CRSwNP. As none of the comparators identified in the clinical SLR for the treatment of patients with previously treated uncontrolled CRSwNP are recommended in England, no indirect or mixed-treatment comparisons with other systemic therapies were conducted. 

## _**2.12 Adverse reactions**_ 

The safety profile of dupilumab has been established in an extensive clinical development programme involving 15,834 participants (as of 28 March 2024) included in the safety population and 12,250 exposed to dupilumab of various ages and in multiple indications (AD, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, allergy, asthma, bullous pemphigoid, chronic pruritus of unknown origin, COPD, eosinophilic gastritis, eosinophilic oesophagitis, PN, rhinosinusitis, ulcerative colitis and urticaria).[93] The cumulative exposure to dupilumab parenteral formulations is estimated to be 1.9 million patient years[93] and to date. over 1 million patients have been treated with dupilumab for licenced indications worldwide.[94] Favourable long-term safety and tolerability of dupilumab have been demonstrated based on five-year safety data, contributing to a well-characterised benefit-risk profile.[17,18] Furthermore, according to the latest Periodic Benefit-Risk Evaluation Report based on the evaluation of the cumulative safety data, the benefit-risk balance of dupilumab across all indications remains positive in the currently approved conditions of use.[93] 

## **2.12.1 Pooled safety analysis of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52** 

A pooled safety evaluation was conducted using data up to Week 24 from the safety populations of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 populations.[68] Safety results from the individual SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials are presented in Appendix F. A total of 722 randomised patients from both studies were exposed to either dupilumab 300 mg Q2W (n=440) or placebo (n=282) and included in the pooled safety analysis set.[68] Most patients in the

<!-- page 89 -->

dupilumab and placebo groups completed 24 weeks of treatment (96.6% and 90.8%, respectively) and both groups had a median duration of treatment of 168 days.[95] 

During the 24-week treatment period, patients treated with dupilumab vs. placebo had a lower incidence of any TEAE (69.3% vs 73.8%), severe TEAE (3.9% vs 6.4%), serious TEAE (3.4% vs 5.7%) and TEAE leading to permanent discontinuation (2.5% vs 5.3%) (Table 32).[68] No injection site reactions resulted in treatment discontinuation and all injection site reactions in the dupilumab group were classified as resolving or resolved despite treatment continuation.[95]
