## _**2.14 Interpretation of clinical effectiveness and safety evidence**_ 

The challenges in achieving optimal CRSwNP disease control for many patients are driven by the lack of NICE-recommended systemic treatments for patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP experiencing recurrence after sinonasal surgery, and, beyond dupilumab, the absence of systemic treatments targeting type 2 inflammation via the IL-4/IL-13 signalling pathway. 

In patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP and a history of sinonasal surgery, treatment options include SCS therapy and revision surgery, which are associated with limited clinically meaningful benefit and AEs/complications.[1,10,14,55,59] Given that the majority of patients do not experience sufficient treatment efficacy from subsequent revision surgeries, there is a significant clinical unmet need for alternative therapies. Patients and clinicians require alternative, efficacious and well-tolerated treatment solutions to address type 2 inflammation, reduce the burden of LoS and sinonasal congestion/obstruction, and improve HRQoL, with specific focus on sleep and mental health.[7,12] 

Data used to support the efficacy and safety of dupilumab in CRSwNP for this submission were taken directly from the randomised, double blind, Phase 3 SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials which represent the most robust available evidence to address the decision problem. SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 had similar study designs but differed in the timing of some of their secondary endpoints and locations.[68,71,72] Safety results and efficacy results for two of the key secondary efficacy endpoints (proportion of patients requiring rescue treatment [SCS or sinonasal surgery] and FEV1 at Week 24) from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were pooled as part of a prespecified protocol to increase the statistical power of these efficacy and safety analyses.[68] 

Results from both the pooled analysis and individual pivotal phase 3 studies demonstrated the efficacy and tolerability of dupilumab vs. placebo in improving the symptoms of CRSwNP.[68] Statistical significance was achieved for the co-primary endpoints in both individual studies, as measured by change in NPS and change in patient-reported NC from baseline to Week 24.[68] Furthermore, the proportion of patients with improvement in both NPS (defined as a decrease from baseline ≥1 point) and NC (defined as a decrease from baseline ≥0.5 points) was higher with dupilumab vs. placebo at Week 24 (p<0.0001 in both studies).[68] 

Key secondary endpoints were also met across both studies.[68] In SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, patients treated with dupilumab showed statistically significant and clinically meaningful 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 94 -->

improvements in each hierarchically tested secondary endpoint compared with patients in the placebo arm, who showed no or minimal improvement.[68] Treatment with dupilumab significantly improved symptoms compared with placebo, as measured by the LMK-CT score, TSS, UPSIT score and LoS score from baseline to Week 24 in both studies, and NPS and NC score from baseline to Week 52 in SINUS-52.[68] In addition, dupilumab provided significantly greater improvement in HRQoL compared with placebo, as measured by the SNOT-22 score from baseline to Week 24 in both studies and Week 52 in SINUS-52, in a trial population which had worse HRQoL compared with the general population at baseline.[65,68] 

Similarly, key secondary endpoints that were assessed in the prespecified pooled analyses were met.[68] The proportion of patients who required SCS or sinonasal surgery during the treatment period was 76% lower with dupilumab compared with placebo (HR: 0.243; p<0.0001).[68] Patients with comorbid asthma receiving dupilumab had statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in FEV1 and ACQ-6 compared with placebo.[68] 

In SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, the onset of symptom improvement in patients treated with dupilumab was rapid (by Week 2 for UPSIT, Week 4 for TSS and self-reported LoS and as early as Week 4 for SNOT-22) and continuous, with improvement reported through Week 24.[68] Furthermore, in SINUS-52, patients receiving dupilumab continued to experience improvement in clinical outcomes and symptoms through Week 52, beyond what was observed at Week 24.[68] Therefore, it is likely that in the longer term, the efficacy benefits of dupilumab in CRSwNP will continue beyond Week 52. Real-world data in patients treated with dupilumab for CRSwNP from the AROMA registry study supports this hypothesis, with improvements in SNOT-22 score maintained over 24 months.[92] 

Treatment with dupilumab was well tolerated in patients with CRSwNP in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 studies.[68] In the pooled safety analysis, 69.3% of patients on dupilumab vs. 73.8% on placebo experienced at least one TEAE, of which the majority were mild or moderate in intensity.[68] Only 2.5% of patients in the dupilumab group discontinued treatment due to TEAEs compared to 5.3% of patients in the placebo group and no new safety signals were identified.[68] Data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are generally consistent with existing safety data in patients with asthma, AD, COPD and PN. Therefore, it can be concluded that dupilumab has favourable long-term safety and tolerability and is associated with mostly mild or moderate TEAEs, a low rate of treatment discontinuation and a low rate of serious TEAEs.[68] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 95 -->

A combined total of 724 patients (n=440 received dupilumab) were randomised in SINUS-24 and SINUS-52.[68] This number of participants was considered sufficient to demonstrate the benefit of dupilumab in patients with CRSwNP given the existing safety database in patients with AD, asthma, COPD and PN ; the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 studies were accepted by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) as sufficient evidence for approval of dupilumab in patients with CRSwNP. Overall, the efficacy and safety of dupilumab in CRSwNP has been demonstrated in SINUS24 and SINUS-52 and is further supported by clinical trial outcomes in several other approved indications. 

Subgroup analyses have demonstrated that dupilumab is efficacious regardless of comorbid conditions (asthma, NSAID-ERD) or history of sinonasal surgery.[68] In addition, post-hoc analyses have demonstrated the efficacy of dupilumab across various CRSwNP outcomes, including reduction of SCS use and sinonasal surgery, improvements in objective disease measures and improvements in patient-reported symptoms and disease-specific HRQoL.[7,11,35,43,65,73,74,76-81,83-86] Improvements with dupilumab were observed across various subgroups of patients including patients with type 2 inflammatory signature, comorbid asthma, comorbid NSAID-ERD, eosinophilic CRSwNP, smell impairment and history of sinus surgery.[7,11,35,43,65,73,76-85] Dupilumab significantly improved general health status and all components of disease-specific HRQoL including sleep and mental health.[7,12,65,77] 

In conclusion, dupilumab provides sustained, clinically meaningful and statistically significant improvements in CRSwNP signs and symptoms, as well as HRQoL, while having a manageable safety profile.[11] Dupilumab has an acceptable risk-benefit profile in patients with CRSwNP who are uncontrolled on SCS therapy after sinonasal surgery.[11] Dupilumab can represent a significant step change in the treatment trajectory of patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP, providing clinically and humanistically meaningful benefits to a burdened patient population with limited available treatment options.

## **3 Economic analysis** 

## _**Model Overview**_ 

- A cost-effectiveness analysis was conducted to evaluate dupilumab plus ECM in comparison to ECM alone, for the treatment of adults with uncontrolled CRSwNP for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control. from the perspective of the English NHS. 

- Following a systematic review of the literature, a cost-utility model structure was chosen consisting of a 1-year decision tree followed by a Markov model with an annual cycle duration. The decision tree, directly modelling the trial period, addresses short-term treatment decisions and initial response to treatment. The Markov component addresses long-term treatment response, potential need for nasal polyp surgery, the post-operative period and the possibility of revision surgery. 

   - _Population:_ Adults with uncontrolled disease following one (or more) surgeries. This reflects a subgroup of the full licensed indication for dupilumab in CRSwNP, as described in the scope and decision problem. 

   - _Trial model inputs_ : The pre-specified pooled SINUS-24 & -52 phase 3 trials provides the most robust clinical efficacy and safety data for dupilumab. 

   - _Real world evidence_ : Where appropriate other sources of evidence to inform discontinuation, HCRU and the societal perspective are included. 

- Utility data were derived using a published mapping algorithm from the SNOT-22 data collected directly during the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. These values were tested in extensive sensitivity analyses using the observed EQ-5D data. 

- Resource utilisation and unit costs were based on published data[13,97] and NHS Reference Costs 2022/2023.[98] Estimated unit costs for SCS and antibiotics were based on the drug price from the eMIT National Database, and daily dosage derived from 2016 UK Commissioning Guide for CRS.[99,100] 

- A combined efficacy response criterion was included at Week 24 in the model to determine the proportion of patients continuing treatment with dupilumab plus ECM. This was developed in consultation with clinicians and defined as: 

   - Change from baseline in SNOT-22 ≥8.9 _and_ NPS ≥1. 

   - Efficacy response was derived from analysis of pooled SINUS-24 & -52 data. 

   - The rate of sustained response at Week 52 was modelled using data from Week 24 responders in SINUS-52. 

## _**Results of the cost effectiveness modelling**_ 

- The base case generated a probabilistic incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of £24,491 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained (Deterministic: £24,383). 

- Base case results were driven by utility values for the controlled and uncontrolled health states and the proportion of responders (dupilumab and ECM) at Week 52. 

- Choice of utility was examined in sensitivity analyses, (Mapped vs. Regression or observed change from baseline) and was found to be the biggest driver in sensitivity analsyis. 

- Scenario analysis for alternative populations indicated modest differences in costeffectiveness between the modelled subgroups.

## **Conclusions** 

- Dupilumab is a clinically- and cost-effective use of NHS resources in adults with uncontrolled CRSwNP for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control. 

- Adding dupilumab to ECM is a cost-effective approach to addressing significant unmet need and burden among people with CRSwNP, alleviating symptoms and lowering the requirement for revision surgeries. 

- Dupilumab has the potential to relieve pressure on the healthcare system through a reduction in in-patient wait times, the need for sinus surgery and primary care visits. 

## _**3.1 Published cost-effectiveness studies**_ 

An SLR was conducted to identify published economic evaluations and cost-effectiveness studies of treatments for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP (Appendix G). The SLR was conducted on the 6 June 2019 and limited to articles published after 1 January 1999. An update to this SLR was performed on 4 September 2024, limiting to articles published after 1 March 2019. No geographical or language restrictions were applied in the searches. 

In the original SLR (June 2019), a total of 868 unique records were identified from electronic database sources and were eligible for screening, including 660 unique records via Embase, 151 via MEDLINE and 57 records via the Cochrane Library. Internet searches, performed between 25 and 26 June 2019, yielded a total of 53 abstracts deemed relevant and eligible for detailed screening, whilst hand searching the bibliographies of 3 SLRs and 6 economic evaluations of treatments identified an additional 49 unique and relevant references. Therefore, a total of 970 articles were screened. 

In the updated SLR (September 2024), an additional 1,049 unique records were identified from electronic database sources and were eligible for screening, including 935 unique records via Embase, 54 via MEDLINE, 59 via the Cochrane library, and one via the International Network of Agencies for Health Technology Assessment (INHATA). Internet searches, conducted between 15 August and 25 September 2024, yielded 17 unique abstracts considered eligible for detailed screening. Hand searching the bibliographies of 8 SLRs and one HTA submission identified 12 unique and relevant references. Therefore, a total of 1,078 articles were screened. The combined total of unique reports for screening from the original and updated SLR was 2,048. 

Considering the original and updated SLR, exclusion of reports based on title/abstract screening resulted in a total of 95 unique reports for systematic review (Appendix G), six of which were not selected for data extraction. In total, there were 19 economic evaluations of

Models used in the 19 economic evaluations identified through SLR (Table 35 and Appendix G) were either decision trees, Markov structures, or a combination of both. In alignment with the economic evaluations identified, and with previous NICE appraisals of biologics for other type 2 inflammatory conditions, we have chosen a decision tree followed by a Markov model structure for this submission. This model structure is the most appropriate option to capture the benefits of dupilumab as an add-on to ECM for the treatment of adults with uncontrolled CRSwNP for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control. 

It is important for the economic model to fully capture the costs and health outcomes associated with the life-long management of people uncontrolled CRSwNP. The model chosen for this submission is based on that published by De Corso et al., 2022, which was developed by Sanofi to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of dupilumab as a treatment for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP.[104] For the purposes of this submission, modifications to some model inputs have been made in order for the model to reflect the specific patient population for which dupilumab reimbursement is sought. Refinement of the model has also been achieved through the inclusion of utilities values which we consider to be more appropriate compared with those used in the model published by De Corso et al., 2022.[104]

## **3.1.1 Key considerations for the CEM** 

People with CRSwNP require lifelong treatment due to the persistent, relapsing nature of the condition. Therefore, the economic model captures both short- and long-term costs and outcomes associated with the management of CRSwNP. 

## **Costs and burden of disease associated with CRSwNP** : 

- _Definition of Control:_ The EUFOREA/EPOS guideline defines controlled CRSwNP as minimal or no symptoms (e.g., nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, facial pain/pressure, loss of smell) that do not significantly impact daily activities or quality of life, and where no urgent surgical intervention is required.[1,6] 

- _Assessment of Control:_ Main criteria include patient-reported symptom scores (e.g., SNOT-22), endoscopic evaluation of nasal polyp size, and imaging assessments such as CT-scans (though the latter may not be feasible in routine practice). See Section 1.2.1.2 for a definition of efficacy response criteria. 

- _Challenges to Maintain Long-term Control:_ Variability in patient response, treatment adherence, and the chronic, relapse-prone nature of CRSwNP make long-term management complex. Patients who fail to maintain control risk symptom worsening, additional treatments, and possible surgical intervention. 

- _Healthcare Resource Use:_ Because CRSwNP requires ongoing medical management (e.g., intranasal corticosteroids, oral steroids, or biologics), the cumulative costs over a patient’s lifetime can be substantial. Frequent specialist visits, diagnostic tests, and potential comorbidity treatments (e.g., for asthma) further add to the economic burden. 

## **Costs and burden of surgery** : 

- _ESS:_ Sinus surgery is often indicated for uncontrolled or refractory CRSwNP. While it can offer symptomatic relief, recurrence of nasal polyps is common, limiting longterm effectiveness.[16] 

- _Risks and Costs:_ ESS involves significant procedural and post-operative expenses, including pre-operative assessment, anaesthesia, potential complications (e.g., bleeding, infection, anaesthesia-related complications), and future revision surgeries.[97] 

- _Burden on the NHS:_ Long wait times (up to three years in some regions of England) reflect both the high demand for sinus surgery and systemic resource constraints, highlighting the need for effective non-surgical treatments.[31] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved

In the UK, dupilumab is indicated as add-on maintenance treatment for adults with severe CRSwNP or for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control.[17] To fully capture the burden of uncontrolled CRSwNP as well as the clinical benefits of dupilumab in this population, the model structure considers the key relationships summarised in Table 36. 

**Table 36. Key considerations of the cost-effectiveness model for dupilumab as a treatment for people with CRSwNP** 

|**Parameters**|**Rationale**|
|---|---|

|**Number of previous**<br>**surgeries**|Sinus surgery is a key factor in the economic burden of CRSwNP. Evidence<br>exists to show that prior surgery (cumulative number) is associated with the<br>probability and frequency of future surgery.|
|**Treatment effect is**<br>**limited to trial duration**<br>**of 52 weeks**|The SINUS-24 trial duration was 24 weeks, and the SINUS-52 trial duration was<br>52 weeks. Therefore, from the clinical trial data it is not clear whether the benefits<br>of dupilumab can be maintained beyond 52 weeks. However, the AROMA study<br>has provided real world evidence of continued benefit (Section2.9.3). The model<br>needs to be flexible to allow testing of different assumptions around the long-term<br>benefit of dupilumab and allow for incorporating long-term efficacy outcomes.|

Based on the considerations listed above and the rationale provided in Table 36 we have developed a cohort Markov model structure with a decision tree component representing the first year (trial period), which accurately captures key aspects of the disease and treatment practices while reflecting the key trial endpoints and treatment effect of dupilumab. Our approach was endorsed at an advisory board held by Sanofi in June 2024 (Appendix R),[31] followed by consultancy meetings led in November 2024 with nine British clinicians (4 English) with expertise in CRSwNP and one health economist (Appendix R).[12] 

## **3.1.2 Patient population** 

Dupilumab is licensed in the UK for adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with SCS and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control.[17,18] After consulting with clinicians and people with CRSwNP, it is clear that the optimal place in therapy for dupilumab is after treatment failure with current standard of care (Appendix R).[12] This includes surgery, which for some people can be a good and lasting option (Appendix R).[12] However, people with more aggressive disease can experience rapid recurrence and for these patients, revision surgery(ies) does not provide long term satisfactory outcomes.[8,31] Therefore the base case population focuses on people with uncontrolled disease following one (or more) surgeries. This is a subgroup of the licensed indication.[17,18] We do recognise that not all people with CRSwNP are eligible for surgery and that patients with comorbid type-2 conditions usually have worse symptoms and could benefit from biologics.[10] Therefore, in addition to the base case population we also provide two scenarios in line with the scope, which consider people with any prior type-2 medical history: 

- Patients with type 2 medical history 

- Patient with prior surgery AND any prior type-2 medical history 

Patient characteristics in the model were based on those of the pooled SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials.[68] 

## **3.1.3 Cost-effectiveness model structure** 

The CEM was developed in Microsoft Excel[®] using a cohort Markov model structure with a decision tree component representing the first year (trial period). 

The model structure begins with a 1-year decision tree followed by a Markov model with an annual cycle duration. The decision tree, which directly models the trial period, addresses short-term treatment decisions and initial response to treatment, while the Markov component addresses long-term treatment response, potential need for NP surgery (including revision surgery) and the post-operative period. A similar structure (i.e., a short- 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 103 -->

term decision tree and Markov model for long time effect) has been used to model the cost effectiveness of dupilumab in the treatment of atopic dermatitis[69,106] , prurigo nodularis[107] asthma[60] and CRSwNP[108] , and for the use of biologics in the treatment of psoriasis.[109] 

In the decision tree (Figure 17) people with inadequately controlled CRSwNP can be treated with either dupilumab plus established clinical management (DUP + ECM) or ECM alone. Treatment response is determined at two different assessment points: 

- First assessment (Week 24): 

   - Responders remain in the decision tree until the second assessment (Week 52). 

   - Dupilumab non-responders discontinue dupilumab and enter the Markov model in either the inadequately controlled disease health state, or, if they receive surgery, the post-operative controlled health state. 

   - ECM non-responders can enter the Markov model in either the inadequately controlled disease health state or the post-operative controlled health state. 

   - One-off costs and utilities associated with surgery are applied when people first arrive in the post-operative controlled health state. 

- Second assessment (Week 52): 

   - Responders enter the controlled health state of the Markov model. 

   - Dupilumab non-responders discontinue dupilumab and enter the inadequately controlled or post-operative controlled health state of the Markov Model. 

   - ECM non-responders can enter the Markov model in either the inadequately controlled disease health state, or the post-operative controlled health state. 

**Figure 17. Decision tree structure**

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 104 -->

In the Markov model (Figure 18), people remain in the controlled disease health state until discontinuation for reasons such as loss of response, AEs or patient/physician preference. After discontinuation, people enter the inadequately controlled disease health state – a temporary state in which people can stay for only 1 year. This health state is included to model the gradual loss of quality of life before returning to the fully uncontrolled health state where baseline utility is applied. Utilities for the inadequately controlled disease health state are based on Week 52 utility weights from people in the placebo arms of the SINUS trials who did not respond at Weeks 24 and 52. 

Following 1 year in the inadequately controlled health state, people can either: 

- Move to the uncontrolled health state (where baseline utility is applied). 

- Receive surgery and move to the post-operative controlled health state, where they remain until the disease becomes uncontrolled again. The model permits multiple surgeries. 

People who are ineligible for surgery transition to the uncontrolled health state and stay there for the remaining time horizon. All health states may transition to the death health state.

The base case analysis takes the UK NHS perspective. A societal perspective is also provided in sensitivity analysis to account for productivity loss and out of pocket expenses. The base-case analysis uses a lifetime horizon (49 years), starting with treatment initiation.

<!-- page 105 -->

Alternative shorter time horizons (i.e., 5 years, 10 years and 20 years) are explored in scenario analyses. 

The cost-year for the analysis was 2024. Costs quoted for other cost-years are inflated to 2024 costs using annual inflation rates from Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2023 from the Personal Social Services Research Unit (PSSRU) and Consumer Price Inflation (CPI) annual rates from Office for National Statistics.[110,111] 

In the base-case analysis, costs and outcomes are discounted at the same rate according to the reference case: 3.5% for both costs and outcomes. Alternative discounting rates of 3% and 5% were explored in the sensitivity analyses. 

Half cycle correction is applied in the Markov portion of the model. 

## **3.1.4 Intervention technology and comparators** 

The model is designed to compare the use of dupilumab plus ECM, with ECM alone in England. ECM treatments in England include nasal irrigation with saline solution, INCS and SCS.[1] The model did not evaluate the cost impact of INCS because the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials were not designed to show a difference in INCS use between the 2 treatment arms and so costs were assumed to be the same in both arms. This is likely to be a conservative approach.[68] 

Short courses of SCSs or antibiotics can also be considered to manage moderate-to-severe CRSwNP, according to guidance published by EUFOREA and EPOS (Section 1.2.2.1).[1,10] The same guidelines describe surgical intervention (endoscope sinonasal surgery, ESS) for the treatment of people with CRSwNP whose disease is uncontrolled by ECM, with revision ESS recommended for people with recurrent disease (Section 1.2.2.1).[10] 

Although ESS is a key element in the treatment pathway[1,10] and is considered in the modelling as an event which drives patients between health states, it is not considered as the main comparator in its own right, but rather as a component of ECM. Note that the majority of people treated with dupilumab in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials had received at least 1 surgery prior to enrolment (92% and 74%, respectively).[68] As outlined in Section 1.2.2.3, dupilumab is positioned for use following 1 surgery and ESS is considered a subsequent treatment for a proportion of patients. SCS and antibiotic use were considered in the calculations of ECM treatment for all patients. 

Other biologics with regulatory approval for the treatment of patients with CRSwNP (omalizumab and mepolizumab) are not currently reimbursed in the UK and so are not valid 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 106 -->

comparators or components of ECM. These have not been included as comparators in the model.[62,63] A third biologic, benralizumab has been evaluated in clinical trials for CRSwNP but is currently not approved for use in the UK and therefore also not included in the model.[112]

## _**3.2.2.1 Efficacy response criteria and rates**_ 

Efficacy response criteria define which patients continue treatment with dupilumab plus ECM. In the model, the base-case response criterion is defined as improvement (reduction) from baseline ≥ 8.9 in SNOT-22 and improvement from baseline ≥ 1 point in NPS. For SNOT-22, the MCID to detect the meaningful change by a patient has been defined as ≥8.9 points and used as an anchor to determine the clinically meaningful score change for NPS as ≥1 point.[91,113] 

This combined efficacy response criterion was tested with clinicians at an Advisory Board held on 26 June 2024[31] and consultancy meetings on 13 November 2024 (Appendix R).[12] Clinicians told us that SNOT-22 is highly applicable and routinely used as a patient-reported outcome measure alongside their preferred objective measurement assessment of NPS to provide a meaningful response to treatment. They emphasised this combined approach resonates with clinical practice. 

Assessment of nasal polyp size alone using the objective NPS measure does not necessarily provide an all-round indicator of response because loss of smell has a significant impact on patients. Similarly, SNOT-22 improvement alone which is a subjective measure, does not necessarily encompass all the elements necessary to assess disease control. Taken together the combined efficacy response criteria were deemed to be a suitable efficacy response measure by the clinicians we have spoked to. Furthermore, they supported the response criteria at the level of an improvement in SNOT-22 and NPS where a change was greater than the minimally clinically important difference in each measure (≥8.9 in SNOT-22 and improvement from baseline ≥1 for NPS). 

_Week-24 efficacy response_ : The response data available for people with inadequately controlled CRSwNP **AND** at least one prior surgery at Week 24 were derived from pooled analyses of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. 

_Week-52 efficacy response_ : Rate of sustained response at Week 52 was modelled using data from Week 24 responders in the SINUS-52 trial. The results for the ITT and base case

## _**3.2.2.3 Transition probabilities for people in the inadequately controlled disease health state.**_ 

In the decision tree portion of the model which reflects the clinical trial, XXXXXX of dupilumab patients and XXXXXX of patients in the ECM arm receive surgery up to week 24. From week 24 to 52, XXXXXX and XXXXXX respectively receive surgery. 

The inadequately controlled health state in the Markov model is a temporary state. People can stay in this health state for 1 cycle only and then either move to the uncontrolled health state or, if they receive surgery, to the post-operative controlled health state. 

In the base case, the percentage of people who are ineligible for surgery was based on data from the pooled analyses of SINUS-24/52 (23.7%; Sanofi data on file, 2019a) In the Markov model people ineligible for surgery move to the uncontrolled health state and remain in that state until death. Among the 76.3% of people who are eligible for surgery, 15.1% (11.5% of all patients in the health state) receive surgery in the following year and transition to the post-operative controlled health state every year.[16] The remaining 64.8% of surgery-eligible patients (total of 88.5%) move to the uncontrolled health state [Figure 19]). 

No age limit for surgery was applied, although the model offers the option to increase the ineligibility to surgery with age (linear or polynomial increase). This is tested in sensitivity analysis. If age is a factor in decision making, we have assumed that ineligibility due to age is accounted for in the overall ineligible for surgery rate. ## _**3.2.2.6 Mortality**_ 

In itself, CRSwNP is not expected to increase mortality and so in the base case, only allcause mortality by age and sex was included for patients with no asthma comorbidity. UK life tables were used to populate the all-cause mortality.[114] Conversely there is an increased risk of mortality with severe asthma and so a relative risk of increased mortality due to comorbid asthma is applied in the base case. The relative risk used is 1.36 which was taken from a meta-analysis of asthma studies that examined the relationship between asthma and allcause mortality. This is tested in sensitivity analysis.[115] 

## _**3.3 Measurement and valuation of health effects**_

An SLR with a cut-off date of 6 June 2019 was conducted and limited to reports published after 1 January 1999. This SLR was updated on 4 September 2024 to capture additional reports published since 1 March 2019 (Section 3.1) and included studies reporting health utility values and HRQoL measures in patients with severe CRSwNP (Appendix H). - For the base case we have used the published mapping algorithm by Crump et al. to estimate utility weights from the SNOT-22 disease specific instrument.[119]

## _**3.3.3.2 Base case: Derivation of utility weights from SNOT-22**_ 

CRSwNP is a disease which primarily affects olfactory function with wide ranging and significant impact on quality of life. Patients report that loss of smell (anosmia) and sleep disturbance both due to nasal obstruction are the most troubling symptoms. 

EQ-5D-5L was collected during the SINUS studies and whilst it does show differences in severity of disease across the duration of the studies, the high utility values observed suggest that it may not fully capture the burden of disease and differentiate well between levels of response. For example, the utility score derived for patients in the controlled health state (responders) as they enter the MARKOV model at 52 weeks is 0.917 (pooled SINUS 24 and 52 data. Regression ‘Model 1’; 3L cross walked to 5L using Hernandez Alva; Section 3.3.3.5). This is much higher than the utility experienced by people of equivalent age in the UK general population (0.834 population norm for persons aged 53 years old)[121] and so lacks face validity. Testimony from patients at a round table held by SINUS UK in January 2025 (Appendix S). highlighted that CRSwNP causes issues with breathing, speaking, hearing, socialising and overall confidence. Poor sleep caused by breathing difficulties leads to fatigue, reduced productivity, work problems and relationship stresses. They said that at its worst, CRSwNP leaves them in a “ _desperate state”_ and feeling like they “ _can’t carry on_ ” living like that. The EQ-5D utility observed in the studies used to describe uncontrolled disease in the model is assumed to be pooled study baseline (0.782). For example, this is equivalent to utilities reported in well-controlled diabetes[122] or stable coronary disease[123] and is not commensurate with the real world lived experience described by patients with CRSwNP. 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 118 -->

EQ-5D HUV is a generic instrument which does not include items specifically related to anosmia and sleep, the key domains of HRQoL impact for patients, and this may be why scores from the dupilumab studies are higher than might be expected. 

However, at baseline the EQ-5D VAS score from the pooled SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 studies is very much lower (Mean (SD) baseline EQ-VAS = 65.4 (20.4)) than population norm, which is 82.0 (Section 2.6.3).[65] This score at baseline is lower than those of other chronic conditions including rheumatoid arthritis, type-2 diabetes, and asthma (Global Initiative for Asthma steps 1–3 and 4–5).[124] The preference-based measure of utility using the EQ-5D HUV is not the same as the VAS but it is noteworthy that there is more correspondence between population norm utility and the VAS score for this age group (0.857 vs. 82.0) than in the baseline values for patients in the dupilumab studies (0.782 vs. 65.4). Other studies have shown that although the VAS is not used to measure HUV, it may possibly reflect a broader underlying construct of general health compared to the EQ-5D HUV in CRS and other conditions, since it likely reflects dimensions of health (such as sleep disturbance) that are not included in the calculation of EQ-5D HUV.[125] The comparison of the VAS score and the HUV at baseline may indicate poor performance of the EQ-5D HUV in this context. 

Analysis of the correlation between disease specific measures and EQ-5D from the pooled SINUS data at baseline and change from baseline also suggests that EQ-5D does not perform well. The Spearman correlation coefficients for the relationship between Decreased/loss of sense of smell score, UPSIT smell test score, Nasal polyposis score, Nasal congestion/obstruction score and Lund-Mackay score at baseline and change to week 24 are provided in Table 46 below.

All the correlation coefficients are between 0.3 and -0.3 indicating poor correlation for these objective and subjective measures. 

Overall, the observations above suggest that EQ-5D HUV is unlikely to fully capture the burden of CRSwNP or sufficiently describe changes to that burden and so may not be reflective of either the disease impact on patients or the potential benefit of treatments. 

The 22-item Sinonasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22) is the most widely used and generally preferred CRS-specific patient reported measure to record quality of life. This assesses 22 symptoms with 6 levels of severity from 0 (no problem) to 5 (maximum problem). The SNOT-22 reflects CRS-specific impairment that patients feel across multiple domains, which include nasal symptoms, sensory deprivation, sleep quality/disturbance, craniofacial discomfort, emotional disturbance, and functional impairment. 

Analysis of the SNOT-22 data from the SINUS clinical trials suggests that dupilumab treatment was associated with significant improvements in all SNOT-22 items vs. placebo, with the two domains most important to patients (decreased sense of smell/taste and nasal symptoms/blockage) showing the greatest improvement (Section 2.6.2) for the SNOT-22 data for the base case population).[125] It is therefore reasonable to consider that the disease specific SNOT-22 instrument is a more appropriate measure of quality-of-life impact on patients than EQ-5D, and we consider that mapping between the two instruments provides suitable utility values for use within the economic model. 

The mapping to derive utilities from SNOT-22 is summarised below in Section 3.3.3.3 and in detail in Appendix O. The results for the application of the Crump mapping algorithm ‘Crump Models 1 - 3’ to the SINUS data are shown in Table 48 for the base case population and responder definition (patients with prior surgery and responder definition of SNOT-22 change from baseline [cfb] ≥8.9 AND NPS cfb ≥1). All of the results for ‘Models 2 and 3’ are provided in Appendix O including the population scenarios. 

## _**3.3.3.3 Mapping SNOT-22 to EQ-5D**_ 

A systematic review conducted by the Health Economics Research Centre (HERC) identified mapping algorithms in various disease areas (including but not limited to chronic rhinosinusitis) between 2013 and January 2023.[126] The database identified Crump et al., 2017[119] as the only relevant publication in the target population. We carried out a targeted 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 120 -->

review to supplement the research conducted by Dakin et al. 2023,[127] with the aim of capturing any additional relevant published information since January 2023 (Appendix Q). 

The targeted review included any publications with chronic rhinosinusitis and was not restricted by intervention. Health related quality of life outcomes were included in the search strategy. Additionally, economic studies in the target population were also reviewed to ensure a wide search of published literature. The targeted review was carried out in PubMed and all results were restricted by date of publication between January 01, 2023 to January 17, 2025 (Appendix Q). 

A total of 351 unique HRQoL publications, and 19 economic studies were identified. The titles and abstracts were screened to identify mapping algorithms or models for mapping SNOT-22 on the EQ5D scale. No further studies beyond Crump et al. 2017[119] were identified in the HERC database of mapping studies[128] were found. 

A detailed discussion of the mapping using the results from Crump et al., 2017[119] carried out for the purposes of this submission is provided in Appendix O. 

Crump presents three regression models developed using SNOT-22 and EQ-5D-3L data collected in 2012 from adult CRS patients in Vancouver entered into the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority registry. Patients enrolled in the registry were awaiting bilateral endoscopic surgery and so are likely to be representative of the population considered in this submission. A side-by-side comparison of baseline characteristics between the Crump cohort and the SINUS studies is provided in Appendix O as are the model regression coefficients along with their p-values. ‘Model 1’ includes only the SNOT-22 global score as a covariate whereas ‘Models 2 and 3’ include all 22 of the items from SNOT-22 (weighted equally). In addition, ‘Model 3’ includes Age and Gender. 

The analysis included the pooled data from the two Phase 3 studies SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, encompassing visits where both SNOT-22 and EQ-5D-5L were assessed. After excluding missing data, the final dataset for mapping consisted of 3,011 observations. 

- Notably, missing data occurred only when all items of the SNOT-22 or all dimensions of the EQ-5D-5L were absent, and no imputation was performed when scoring SNOT-22 total or EQ-5D-5L utility using tariffs. 

- The distribution of SNOT-22 and EQ-5D-5L measures was highly similar between the two studies, and their relationship remained stable over time. As a result, data from both studies and all visits were pooled for analysis.

‘Crump models 2 & 3’ provide higher estimates for utility values than ‘Crump model 1’. However, inspection of the coefficients for models ‘2 and 3’ suggests that including the individual level terms in the models may not be an optimal approach. This because some of the individual level items have positive coefficients. (See Table 2, Appendix O for a full list of the regression coefficients). 

Consider the case where the worst value possible (“Problem as bad as it can be”) is recorded for the SNOT22 items with a positive coefficient, and 0 (“No problem at all”) for the other items.  In this case a utility value larger than 1.0 is predicted (We have estimated this at 1.2144). 

In the extreme case a patient with the characteristics above would have a utility score higher than the patient provided as an example in the published paper (No problem at all for the 22 items: utility=0.8390). 

We contacted the authors of the study to discuss the scenario above but did not receive an answer. 

This may explain the higher values estimated for ‘Crump models 2 and 3’. Therefore, we have chosen ‘Crump Model 1’ for our base case which uses the SNOT-22 total score and avoids the issue of the individual positive regression coefficients above. We also conducted a post-hoc analysis to measure the level of correlation between the SNOT-22-derived utilities and the EQ-5D-5L utilities from SINUS clinical trials at baseline and Week 24. 

The Spearman correlation coefficients were higher for ‘Model 1’ which gave us more confidence in our selection of it for the base case analysis (Appendix O). The utilities derived from the other models were also tested in sensitivity analysis (see Section 3.10.3). 

## _**3.3.3.5 EQ-5D from the studies. Utility Weight Estimation Based on a Regression Model**_ 

The mapped EQ-5D data derived from the disease specific SNOT-22 instrument, is the more appropriate utility source for use in this evaluation for the reasons discussed above. However, we also provide the EQ-5D data collected in the clinical trials for comparison in sensitivity analysis.  Linear regression analysis was performed to estimate utility weights for use in the model using EQ-5D-5L data from the studies converted to EQ-5D-3L, using the UK crosswalk tariffs. This is summarised below. More detail is provided in Appendix P along with details for the alternative subgroups tested in scenario analysis.

## _**3.3.3.7 Utility adjustments according to age**_ 

As patients age in the model, adjustments are made using the multiplicative or additive method. In the multiplicative method, general population utility weights from Ara and Brazier (2011) are used to estimate the relative decline over time.[121] In the additive method, a linear trendline to the Ara and Brazier (2011) data is fit to estimate how much utility is lost with each year of age gained. In the base-case analysis, utility weights are adjusted over time using the multiplicative method. 

## _**3.3.3.8 Disutility associated with surgery**_ 

In the immediate postoperative period following endoscopic sinus surgery for CRSwNP, patients typically experience a temporary decline in health-related quality of life due to several factors.[12,26] Nasal congestion, drainage, and pain are common, and some individuals may require nasal packing that exacerbates discomfort. These symptoms often interfere with sleep, daily activities, and social interactions, leading to a short-term reduction in overall well-being. However, this period of reduced quality of life is generally limited to the first one to three weeks after surgery and tends to improve as healing progresses and nasal function is restored. 

Direct evidence from the clinical studies is not available to support this and so we have used published data from Scangas et al. (2017) applied a short-term postoperative disutility of 0.15 over a two-week period in their cost-utility analysis of endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis (with and without nasal polyposis).[130] This value reflects the temporary decrease in patients’ health-related quality of life due to postoperative pain, congestion, and 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 128 -->

general recovery. This level of disutility is consistent with prior cost-effectiveness research in chronic rhinosinusitis, which frequently applies short-term disutilities ranging from -0.10 to - 0.20 for one to three weeks post-surgery.[130] By incorporating this commonly accepted shortterm decrement, the economic model captures both the immediate morbidity of the surgery and the longer-term utility gains (via the post-operative controlled HS utility). It is assumed that acute disutility associated with sinus surgery lasts for 2 weeks, while no chronic impact (i.e., longer than 2 weeks) of surgery on utility is included. 

## _**3.3.3.9 Health-related quality of life in the post-operative controlled health**_ 

## _**state**_ 

In the longer term, utility gain from surgery is expected whilst in the post-operative health state. Once again evidence from the SINUS studies is not available and so we have identified two alternative sources. In the base case, utility gain from surgery of 0.051 taken from Soler et al. 2011 is applied to the inadequately controlled and uncontrolled disease health states from which surgery patients originated.[118] An alternative value based on EQ-5D was taken from Remenschneider et al. 2015 estimated to be 0.08; this was tested in sensitivity analysis.[117] Of the two sources, Soler was considered the most appropriate because it is estimated using SF-6, which is deemed more appropriate to capture the burden of disease for conditions such as CRSwNP. 

## _**3.3.3.10 Disutility associated with adverse reactions**_ 

The list of adverse events (AEs) considered in the model was derived from Bachert et al. (2019) which is the published pooled analysis for the SINUS studies.[68] Events occurring with a rate more than 5% were chosen.  Annual incidences were estimated from pooled analyses of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 (Sanofi data on file, 2019a), based on the number of treatmentemergent AEs (TEAEs) per 100 patient-years during the entire treatment-emergent AE period. These events are costed in the model (Section 3.4.6) but while each AE could in principle have an associated disutility and duration, we do not apply any separate disutility for these TEAEs in our base-case analysis. This decision reflects both the limited and predominantly mild nature of the TEAEs observed in the dupilumab studies and the assumption that any minor impact on quality of life is already captured by the EQ-5D utility measurements in each health state. Consequently, no additional disutility is modelled for TEAEs in either treatment arm.

## _**3.4 Cost and healthcare resource use identification, measurement and valuation**_ 

Resource utilisation rates and unit costs most appropriate to this submission were identified through a systematic review of the literature to identify published and unpublished studies, an advisory board conducted in June 2024 and several consultancy meetings conducted in November 2024 to validate British clinicians’ perceptions on HCRU among people with severe CRSwNP. 

## **3.4.1 Resource identification, measurement and valuation studies.** 

An SLR with a cut-off date of 6 June 2019 was conducted and limited to reports published after 1 January 1999. This SLR was updated on 4 September 2024 to capture additional reports published since 1 March 2019 (Section 3.1). Studies included those with cost and resource use data related to the management of people with severe CRSwNP (Appendix I). Of the 95 unique reports included in the SLR, 55 were unique studies of costs and resource use (Appendix I). Among the 55 unique studies, 33 reported resource use, 31 reported direct costs, 11 reported indirect costs, and 1 reported productivity. Most studies were conducted in the US (n=31), with other study countries including Spain (n=5), England (n=4), China (n=3), Finland (n=3), France (n=2), US and Canada (n=2), Canada (n=1), the Netherlands (n=1), Japan (n=1), Sweden (n=1). There was one multinational study. 

## **3.4.2 Advisory board and consultancy meetings to evaluate UK clinical perceptions of HCRU** 

A UK HTA advisory board was held on the 26[th] of June 2024 with six clinicians and one health economist with a geographical spread across the UK. A further series of consultancies (with some overlap between attendees) focused on England alone which included a panel of four rhinology experts and one respiratory expert were held in November 2024. Several of these experts have published on HCRU for CRSwNP in the English setting.[9,16] These experts advised on the current UK treatment pathway for patients with severe CRSwNP, and other aspects of the disease and its burden on patients for the purposes of this assessment (Appendix Q). 

The experts were presented with the estimates shown in Table 53 below derived from Davies 2022[13] to stimulate discussion about the likely levels of HCRU for patients in the controlled and uncontrolled disease health states. In this publication, CRSwNP-related events were collected for 2 separate groups of patients:

## _**3.4.2.1 GP visits**_ 

The experts agreed that patients whose disease is controlled are unlikely to visit the GP for CRSwNP and the number of visits could be set to zero. 

For patients who would be regarded as ‘uncontrolled’ there was less agreement between the advisory board and the subsequent consultancies. The experts consulted during the consultancies agreed that the suggested six GP visits reflect English clinical practice. This is because patients revisit the GP repeatedly while on the surgery waiting list due to recurrent acute exacerbations, repeated infections, stopping and restarting of medications such as INCS and antibiotics, and for management of other symptoms such as loss of sleep. Experts at the advisory board felt that patients would visit the GP more than six times. 

## _**3.4.2.2 Outpatient consultant attendance**_ 

The advisory board experts agreed that around 1.7 visits per year to see a specialist is reasonable for patients who are uncontrolled. A specialist might see the patients and then put them on a list for surgery, so the advisors felt that two specialist visits is realistic for the modelling. 

The experts consulted in the individual consultancies suggested that a patient would have two to three visits to the ENT service before sinus surgery (which characterised the patient as uncontrolled). Typically, at the first ENT appointment, a patient will restart their topical treatments (if necessary). If surgery is still required, the patient is then booked for a CT scan and will be seen back in the clinic after the scan. If the patient is unsure about surgery, they may return for a third appointment through patient-initiated follow-up. If the patient was 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 131 -->

originally seen by a general ENT specialist, they may have a further appointment with them before being referred to the rhinology clinic. 

The clinicians also advised that patients who are doing well (controlled disease) are often discharged from specialist care and attendance in clinic is generally low for these patients. However, they can return through the patient-initiated follow-up pathway if their disease becomes less well controlled. An estimate of ~1 visit is not unreasonable. 

The experts were asked about their expectations for HCRU amongst patients who might be well controlled on a biologic. One of the experts with significant experience of dupilumab commented that a well-controlled patient may only need to see a specialist nurse once a year. 

## _**3.4.2.3 Accident and emergency attendance and hospitalisation**_ 

The experts did not comment on these parameters and did not include them in the patient pathway described. It is also clear from the published literature that these services are not routinely used by CRSwNP patients and very low HCRU is recorded against them.[9,13]

## **3.4.4 Intervention and comparator costs** 

## _**3.4.4.1 Drug unit and administration costs**_ 

_**3.4.4.1.1 Dupilumab unit costs**_ Treatment acquisition costs are calculated based on the package price costs and the drug quantity required according to expected treatment schedules. Treatment schedules are based on the SmPCs for each individual treatment. The dosing of dupilumab is 300 mg given every other week by subcutaneous injection. The annual cost for dupilumab at list price is £16,500 PPPY. According to the confidential simple patient access scheme (approved by NHS England and Improvement and the Patient Access Scheme Liaison Unit in 2021) there is a XXXXXX discount off the list price of dupilumab corresponding to XXXXXX PPPY, or XXXXXX per pack of two 300 mg syringes or pens. In the model, the unit cost per dose is multiplied by the treatment frequency (26 doses required PPPY as per the MHRA licence) to estimate the cycle-specific drug costs. (Table 55). In the model, different drug-acquisition costs can be entered for the first year alone, the second year alone, and for subsequent years, which enables the model to estimate cost-effectiveness under various patient-access schemes or rebate scenarios. 

In the model, dupilumab is assumed to be self-administered following instruction from a nurse. No training is assumed for the administration of ECM. The model also allows users to define the percentage split between self-administration and administration by a nurse for subsequent doses. No nurse administration is assumed in the base case in line with other assessments for dupilumab (TA534, TA751).[60,69] This is varied to 95% in sensitivity analysis. The unit cost for subcutaneous administration training used in the model is £65.86 taken from the Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2023 for Hospital-based nurses - Band 6: Cost per working hour with qualification costs; inflated to 2024 (Table 55)

## _**3.4.5.2 Surgery costs (first year post operative controlled health state)**_ 

Table 54 in Section 3.4.3 provides the estimates for HCRU rates used in the model. We noted that during the year in which a surgery takes place (the first year post operative controlled health state), resource use is treated in a different way from simply multiplying HRCU estimates by an appropriate tariff. An explanation of the treatment of the costs for this health state is provided below. 

Costs for the year (cycle) in which the surgery event take place were taken from Clarke 2022.[97] This was an observational retrospective study examining cost of healthcare of patients receiving CRS surgery and represents a comprehensive assessment of surgery costs. Linked electronic healthcare records from the Clinical Practice Research Data link, Hospital Episode Statistics and the ONS databases were used covering the period 1997– 2016. 62685 patients were identified as definitely having CRS and 13,462 received CRSrelated surgery and were included in the analysis. 

To capture the costs directly associated with the surgery event to align with the annual model cycle length, we have used the reported mean inpatient and outpatient costs for the

## **3.4.6 Adverse reaction unit costs and resource use** 

The model calculates an aggregated cost of AE management for each treatment. Since the AEs included in the model are not severe, the unit costs are assumed to be the cost incurred for one GP visit. Costs are sourced from 2022/23 PSSRU based on a 10 minute consultation.[132]

## **3.4.7 Miscellaneous unit costs and resource use** 

## _**3.4.7.1 Asthma**_ 

The most common Type-2 comorbidity for people with CRSwNP is asthma (Section 1.2.1.4). Dupilumab has been shown to demonstrate efficacy in several type 2 inflammatory diseases including CRSwNP and asthma by blocking the shared receptor component for IL-4 and IL-13 (Sections 1.2.2.3 and 2.8). In this way dupilumab improves upper and lower airway outcome measures in patients with severe CRSwNP and comorbid asthma. Dupilumab is licenced of the treatment of both CRSwNP and asthma and asthma outcomes were also collected in the SINUS CRSwNP studies. For example in the pooled SINUS studies, overall the asthma control questionnaire (ACQ-6) score at week 24 revealed a clinically significant improvement that exceeded the MCID of 0.5 points (LS mean difference vs placebo [95% CI] of −0.82 [−0.98 to −0.67]; nominal _P_ < .001).[35] 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 139 -->

In the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials 59.6% and 58.3% respectively of subjects had comorbid asthma at baseline. 24.4% of patients had severe co-morbid asthma in the pooled population defined as GINA step 4-5 at baseline. 

At the end of the study period the population of patients with asthma had differential outcomes being distributed between controlled, partially controlled, and uncontrolled asthma according to the asthma control questionnaire (ACQ-6) score administered at week 24 (Table 63). Annual costs have been assigned to these levels of according to Willson et al. 2014, (See Technical appendix, Tables 7 to 9 from the supplementary materials to the publication); assuming that the average resource use of well-controlled (referred to as “controlled” in the source) and partly controlled patients in Willson et al. would be equivalent to the average resource use observed in controlled patients in the model.[133] 

**Table 63. Distribution of asthma control at study end[*] and associated costs from Wilson[133]** 

|**Control level***|**DUP+ECM, %**|**ECM, %**|**Cost by control status, £**|
|---|---|---|---|
|Controlled asthma|76.0|15.4|960|
|Partially controlled asthma|10.0|19.4|1,795|
|Uncontrolled asthma|14.0|63.9|2,629|



DUP = dupilumab; ECM = established clinical management *According to asthma control questionnaire (ACQ-6) score at Week 24. Source: Sanofi data on file, 2019b (pooled trial data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52). 

Given the importance of asthma in this patient population and the differential impact on asthma outcomes between ECM and the dupilumab treated patients we have included asthma related costs in the model. The proportion of patients with severe asthma is multiplied by the distribution of asthma severity level at the end of the study by treatment arm and the cost for each category. These costs are applied at each model cycle. 

Real world evidence exists to support the assumption that differential asthma outcomes would be improved in the longer term and persist in the real world. In a prospective follow-up study (January 2021 to May 2022) amongst 166 patients with CRSwNP treated with dupilumab for at least 6 months, changes in ACT scores for those patients with asthma (n = 99) were recorded.[134] The ACT scores after dupilumab treatment were significantly higher than before dupilumab treatment increasing from 16.923 to >22 (p<0.001).Similarly, in the study by Gal et al., 17% of patients reported completely uncontrolled asthma at baseline compared to 0% at 12 months (p<0.01).[129]

## _**3.6 Uncertainty**_ 

Challenges associated with modelling the course of severe CRSwNP and the long-term impact of treatment with dupilumab have the potential to create uncertainty in model outputs. Specifically, uncertainty in the model may result from: 

- Issues in capturing the burden of CRSwNP with EQ-5D data 

- A lack of consensus on the definition of treatment response in people with severe CRSwNP 

- Insufficient published evidence on post-operative disease recurrence and revision surgeries 

- Insufficient published evidence on HCRU based on the UK population 

- Insufficient published evidence on the long-term impact of SCS overuse in the UK (costs and disutility associated) 

- Insufficient published evidence on the impact of comorbid asthma 

- The variability of surgery long term outcomes, with differences in the magnitude of response after surgery 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 143 -->

There is also uncertainty around the extrapolation of trial data beyond the follow-up period. Dupilumab is the first biologic used to treat moderate-to-severe CRSwNP and so, as is typical for newly approved agents targeting chronic conditions, long-term treatment effect data are limited. Sensitivity and scenario analyses evaluate the uncertainty surrounding the consequent use of external data and assumptions in long-term predictions (Section 3.10).

## _**3.10 Exploring uncertainty**_ 

## **3.10.1 Probabilistic sensitivity analysis** 

A probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA) has been conducted to assess the parametric uncertainty associated with the base case model results. ## _**3.11 Subgroups including comorbid asthma and NSAID-ERD**_ 

The NICE scope suggests that an important consideration is the impact of asthma, which is a type-2 comorbidity in CRSwNP. We believe that these patients are best described as having the NSAID-ERD. 

NSAID-ERD, is characterised by 3 main features: 

1. Asthma: This is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that causes breathing difficulties 

2. Nasal polyps: These are non-cancerous growths in the lining of the nasal passage or sinuses, leading to congestion and sinus issues 

3. Aspirin sensitivity: individuals have adverse reactions to aspirin and other NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen and naproxen 

In the clinical studies all patients with the asthma comorbidity fell into this category. 

It is likely be the case that these patients even without prior surgery, are at higher unmet medical need. The subgroups of interest are therefore: **a)** Patients with prior type 2 medical history including asthma/NSAID-ERD (i.e., no prior surgery) and **b)** Patients with prior surgery and with prior type 2 medical history including asthma/NSAID-ERD. These scenarios are explored in Sections 3.11.1 and 3.11.2. 

## **3.11.1 Patients with prior type 2 medical history including asthma/NSAID-ERD**

## _**3.12 Benefits not captured in the QALY calculation**_ 

_**Holistic impact of dupilumab on symptoms:**_ The model is designed to capture a multitude of benefits, such as quality of life, severity, reductions in surgery, including associated shortterm disutility. However, several benefits are likely to remain uncaptured in the QALY. In particular, we discussed the limitations of the EQ-5D instrument in Section 3.3.3.2 and showed how the mapping from SNOT-22 is the better choice. 

1. **Symptom Relief** : EQ-5D is a generic instrument which does not include items specifically related to anosmia and sleep, the key domains of HRQoL. For example, enhanced sleep quality due to reduced nasal obstruction can have a profound impact on overall health and well-being, which might not be fully represented in the QALY. Our Mapping to SNOT22 seeks to address this and those data should be considered in the base case. 

One of the patient-reported endpoints captured in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, in addition to the SNOT-22 outcome, is the E-RS: CRSwNP instrument. SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 showed that dupilumab was associated with greater reductions in E-RS: CRSwNP total score than ECM alone, indicating improvements in the severity of respiratory symptoms in patients receiving dupilumab. However, there is no mapping algorithm available to convert E-RS: CRSwNP scores to EQ-5D. Therefore, this benefit may not have been fully captured by the model in the same way as the SNOT-22 outcomes, which can be mapped to EQ-5D. 

2. **Mental Health** : Similarly, the psychological impact of CRSwNP, including anxiety and depression due to chronic discomfort and social embarrassment, might not be adequately reflected in QALY calculations. 

3. **Productivity** : Improvements in productivity at work due to better management of symptoms are not captured in the QALY calculation in the base case. 

4. **Reduced Healthcare Utilization** : Decreased need for medications, doctor visits, and surgeries can lead to cost savings which are factored into the calculations but more generally the reduced burden on healthcare capacity is not directly captured by QALY. This has been described to us by a senior consultant ENT surgeon who told us:

## _**3.13 Validation**_ 

## **3.13.1 Validation of cost-effectiveness analysis** 

A technical model validation was conducted to evaluate the validity of the model programming and sources used to derive input parameters in the model adaptation. The technical validation examines the extent to which mathematical calculations in the model are performed correctly and evaluates their consistency with the model’s specifications. The following steps were performed to ensure the model’s technical validity: 

1. Extreme-value testing: Each model parameter was set to extremely low and high values to identify any inconsistencies in model behaviour or unexpected results. 

2. Technical review (internal): The model programming was reviewed by a senior modeller who was not part of the project team. The technical review process included using different model settings to ensure that they yielded expected calculations. The validator also checked the links between worksheets to ensure that the correct cells were referenced. In addition, mathematical formulae, and the sequence of calculations for each parameter and the model engine were checked. 

3. Technical review (external): Further technical review of the final model was conducted by a third-party agency who provided additional technical expertise. Some minor issues were identified and rectified with very minimal impact on the ICER. 

4. Input verification: Values for all parameters were reviewed against source documents, and the inconsistencies were corrected. 

Following the validation process, errors identified by the validator were corrected, and the revised model was rechecked by the internal validator. 

An additional validation of the model structure and inputs was also performed as part of the advisory board and consultancies held in June and November 2024 with experienced UK clinical experts (including respiratory physicians and experts in respiratory epidemiology and respiratory medicine) and a health economist (Appendix R). 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 162 -->

In addition to the technical validation of the formulae to ensure correctness, the costeffectiveness model was also subject to external validation, by comparing the model structure and outcomes to published cost-effectiveness models. The most appropriate model comparison is with the model published by De Corso et al. (2022).[104] This is because the structure is similar and the comparison is for Dupilumab as an add-on to BSC vs. BSC, which included: nasal irrigation with saline solution and inhaled corticosteroids; oral corticosteroids and at least one surgery. The authors found incremental costs of € 22,283 and incremental QALs of 1.02 resulting in an ICER of € 21,817 per QALY. The model is from the Italian perspective however these results are close to the outcomes reported for our submission. 

## _**3.14 Interpretation and conclusions of economic evidence**_ 

Our cost-effectiveness analysis demonstrates that dupilumab represents good value for the NHS as a treatment for patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP who have had one or more surgeries. 

At the patient access scheme price, add-on treatment with dupilumab results in higher QALYs (XXXXXX) compared with ECM alone but is more expensive (£XXXXXX) due to the higher acquisition cost of dupilumab. Dupilumab + ECM generates a probabilistic ICER/QALY of £24,491 which is within the commonly accepted WTP threshold of £30,000/QALY. The base case ICER was most sensitive to the source for utility calculations. 

## **3.14.1 Strengths of the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

The SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials were large robust, duplicate studies which provided strong evidence of a significant treatment effect for dupilumab as add-on to maximal inhaled therapy in patients with inadequately controlled CRSwNP. A key feature of the studies was the close representation of current clinical practice in CRSwNP as defined by various clinical guidelines. To make best use of the clinical data in the economic model, we have used the pooled subgroup data for patients with prior surgery from SINUS 24 and 52 data for our analyses. 

Our model was designed based on careful consideration of the existing published models and the clinical characteristics and treatment pathway of patients with inadequately controlled CRSwNP as explained to us by clinical experts. This ensured that key aspects of the disease and English treatment practices are captured.

## **3.14.2 Limitations of the cost-effectiveness analysis** 

## _**3.14.2.1 Treatment effect is limited to trial duration of 52 weeks**_ 

The follow-up period of the SINUS-24 trial extends to 48 weeks, and there was no follow-up period after the 52 weeks of the SINUS-52 trial, therefore whether the benefit of dupilumab can be maintained over the long run is uncertain. However, a phase 4 global registry of dupilumab (AROMA) is currently ongoing, with a follow-up period of 3 years. The model has been developed to assess how those clinical benefits observed within the 52-week trial period can potentially transfer into meaningful economic value over an extended time horizon. 

## **3.14.3 Generalisability to clinical practice in England** 

The base case population reflects the anticipated place in therapy for dupilumab in England and is driven by the epidemiology for England (Section 1.2.1), the clinical evidence presented (Section 2.6), and English real-world evidence where appropriate (Section 2.9.3). The patient population in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials included in the economic analysis is generalisable to the patient population expected to be treated with dupilumab in English clinical practice and the study comparator of established clinical management makes a within-trial comparison for the economic assessment the most appropriate analysis. 

The cost-effectiveness analysis shows that, in addition to treatment effect, long-term discontinuation rates and surgery rates are model drivers. These factors may significantly vary in local clinical practice, especially considering the extremely long wait time for sinonasal surgery after the pandemic. 

The model structure and approaches for the current analysis are designed to not only closely reflect the clinical outcomes observed in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, but also provide maximum flexibility to use external data where applicable. This allows the generalisability to clinical practice to be assessed in cases where real world data may differ substantially from the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. Despite the challenges and limitations of developing a model that addresses the challenges associated with replicating the complex natural history of CRSwNP, the submitted model sufficiently describes the disease to enable the value of dupilumab from both the healthcare and societal perspectives to be assessed, based on the available evidence and data. 

## **3.14.4 Conclusion** 

The burden of CRSwNP is considerable; medically, socially and economically. For patients whose disease continues to progress, unfortunately the ultimate outcome for patients 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved 




<!-- page 164 -->

inadequately controlled CRSwNP despite systemic steroid or surgery us is to cycle through revision surgeries and overuse of steroids, with impacts on mental health and quality of life. There is no curative treatment for CRSwNP, which is a medical condition led by type-2 inflammation, and not a surgical condition, and none of the biologics developed in this indication are currently reimbursed in the UK. A proportion of severe CRSwNP patients continue to experience debilitating symptoms and poor HRQoL despite maximal available therapy (SCS & surgery which we have characterised as Established Clinical Management). These patients are at high risk of disease recurrence a long-term loss of QoL, as exemplified in the patient quote below: 

_‘At 14, I was diagnosed with one of the most aggressive cases of nasal polyps my doctor had ever seen, leading to six surgeries and a myriad of treatments with steroids and various antibiotics over the course of ten years. Despite these efforts, I suffered constant inflammation, congestion, pressure headaches, migraines, and the loss of smell and taste.’_ 

The sequalae of CRSwNP are driven by underlying chronic inflammation, and type 2 inflammation specifically is associated with a poorer prognosis. Type 2 inflammation (defined by blood EOS ≥300 cells/µL) can be targeted with dupilumab, and in two phase III studies, SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, dupilumab has been proven to be effective at statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the co-primary endpoints of NPS and NC score at Week 24 compared to placebo. Improvements were observed at week 8 for NPS and week 4 for NC score. In SINUS-52, these results were maintained for a year. Rapid onset of symptom improvement and HRQoL were observed by week 2 for UPSIT, week 4 for TSS, self-reports LoS and SNOT-22. Specifically for SNOT-22 items, the greatest treatment effect relates to improvements in sense of smell/taste and nasal blockage. 

There are currently over 1 million patients treated with dupilumab worldwide establishing a strong benefit-risk profile for dupilumab, validated by many clinical trials and further supported by real-world safety data across multiple indications.[93] No new safety signals have been identified in patients with CRSwNP. Dupilumab addresses the high unmet need for a targeted, systemic biologic treatment for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP following one (or more) surgeries. 

The economic cost of CRSwNP is large, both societally and in terms of medical management (which includes surgery). Our health economic modelling has shown that dupilumab is a cost-effective treatment for uncontrolled CRSwNP with Type 2 inflammation as an add-on to ECM from the NHS perspective. In our base case, we have estimated that 

Company evidence submission for dupilumab for treating chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] © Sanofi (2025). All rights reserved

the probabilistic ICER is £24,491 which is below the commonly accepted WTP threshold of £30,000. The ICER results were consistent when tested against a range of key model inputs and assumptions with very few incremental ICERs rising above £30,000/QALY in extreme scenarios. 

Dupilumab is the first biologic which has demonstrated significant benefits both in terms of clinical signs and symptoms but also in QoL improvements and is a significant step-change in the effective treatment of uncontrolled CRSwNP with Type 2 inflammation. Dupilumab will provide meaningful benefits to a burdened patient population and has the potential to relieve pressure on the healthcare system through a reduction in in-patient wait times, the need for sinus surgery and burden in primary care. 

A patient enrolled in the UK Compassionate Use Scheme told us: 

_“Within three days of my first dose, I could breathe more clearly than I had in over a decade, and by the end of the first week, all symptoms vanished. Four years later, I remain symptom-free, my sense of taste and smell fully restored, and I no longer need steroids…. Dupixent has truly been life-changing, succeeding where everything else had failed.”_
