## **Summary of Information for Patients (SIP):** 

## **The pharmaceutical company perspective** 

## **What is the SIP?** 

The Summary of Information for Patients (SIP) is written by the company who is seeking approval from NICE for their treatment to be sold to the National Health Service (NHS) for use in England. It is a plain English summary of their submission written for patients participating in the evaluation. It is not independently checked, although members of the public involvement team at NICE will have read it to double-check for marketing and promotional content before it is sent to you. 

The **Summary of Information for Patients** template has been adapted for use at NICE from the Health Technology Assessment International – Patient & Citizens Involvement Group (HTAi PCIG). Information about the development is available in an open-access IJTAHC journal article. 

## **SECTION 1: Submission summary** 

**1a) Name of the medicine** (generic and brand name): 

**Generic name:** Dupilumab 

**Brand name:** DUPIXENT[®] 

**1b) Population this treatment will be used by.** Please outline the main patient population that is being appraised by NICE: 

Adults with uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) following one (or more) surgeries. 

Note that dupilumab treatment is not indicated for all people with CRSwNP, only those fulfilling the specific criteria described below. 

**1c) Authorisation:** Please provide marketing authorisation information, date of approval and link to the regulatory agency approval. If the marketing authorisation is pending, please state this, and reference the section of the company submission with the anticipated dates for approval. 

Dupilumab was authorised as an add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids (SCS) and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control by the United Kingdom (UK) regulator, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), on 01 January 2021.(1, 2) 

In the UK, dupilumab has also been authorised by the MHRA for the following indications:(1, 2) 

2 



<!-- page 176 -->

## **Atopic dermatitis (eczema)** 

Adults and adolescents: Dupixent is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in adults and adolescents 12 years and older who are candidates for systemic therapy. 

Children 6 months to 11 years of age: Dupixent is indicated for the treatment of severe atopic dermatitis in children 6 months to 11 years old who are candidates for systemic therapy. 

## **Asthma** 

Adults and adolescents: Dupixent is indicated in adults and adolescents 12 years and older as add-on maintenance treatment for severe asthma with Type 2 inflammation characterised by raised blood eosinophils and/or raised fraction of exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), who are inadequately controlled with high dose inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) plus another medicinal product for maintenance treatment. 

Children 6 to 11 years of age: Dupixent is indicated in children 6 to 11 years old as add-on maintenance treatment for severe asthma with Type 2 inflammation characterised by raised blood eosinophils and/or raised FeNO, who are inadequately controlled with medium to high dose ICS plus another medicinal product for maintenance treatment. 

## **Prurigo Nodularis (PN)** 

Dupixent is indicated for the treatment of adults with moderate to severe PN, who are candidates for systemic therapy. 

## **Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE)** 

Dupixent is indicated for the treatment of eosinophilic oesophagitis in adults and adolescents 12 years and older, weighing at least 40 kg, who are inadequately controlled by, are intolerant to, or who are not candidates for conventional medicinal therapy. 

## **Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)** 

Dupixent is indicated in adults as add-on maintenance treatment for uncontrolled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) characterised by raised blood eosinophils on a combination of an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA), and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA), or on a combination of a LABA and a LAMA if ICS is not appropriate.

## **SECTION 2: Current landscape** 

## **2a) The condition – clinical presentation and impact** 

Please provide a few sentences to describe the condition that is being assessed by NICE and the number of people who are currently living with this condition in England. 

Please outline in general terms how the condition affects the quality of life of patients and their families/caregivers. Please highlight any mortality/morbidity data relating to the condition if available. If the company is making a case for the impact of the treatment on carers this should be clearly stated and explained. 

## **What is CRSwNP?** 

CRSwNP is a long-term condition affecting the spaces inside the nose and head (sinuses).(3, 4) In people with CRSwNP, the sinuses become inflamed and their lining becomes swollen, forming soft growths inside the nose called nasal polyps.(4, 5) CRSwNP interferes with the way mucus normally drains and may cause troublesome symptoms, including loss of smell and taste, blocked nose (nasal congestion/obstruction), difficulties breathing, runny nose (rhinorrhoea), facial pain/pressure, fatigue, trouble sleeping, infections, hearing issues and mucus running down the throat (post nasal drip).(6-9) These symptoms, especially blocked/runny nose and sleep disturbances, have a significant negative impact on the patients by preventing them from carrying out their daily activities as normal.(9-12) 

## **What causes CRSwNP?** 

CRSwNP is caused by type 2 inflammation.(4, 6, 13, 14) This inflammation increases immune cells in the sinuses and nasal cavity, leading to tissue damage, excess mucus, and nasal polyp formation.(4, 6) It can also lead to chronic upper airway infections.(4, 6) 

## **How many people are living with CRSwNP in England?** 

In 2026 (anticipated first full year of patient access to dupilumab for CRSwNP), it is expected that 225,991 adults will be living with CRSwNP in England.(15, 16) Of these, approximately 29,232 will have uncontrolled disease after one (or more) surgeries and are expected to be eligible for treatment with dupilumab.(15, 17) 

## **What is the impact of CRSwNP on a person’s quality of life?** 

The impact of CRSwNP on a person’s quality of life is understood to be comparable to that associated with other serious chronic diseases, such as migraine and epilepsy.(18) CRSwNP affects several aspects of people’s life, including sleep, mood and daily activities.(10-12) Sinonasal congestion and/or obstruction, loss of smell and taste and difficulties sleeping are the symptoms with the biggest impact on the quality of life of people with severe CRSwNP.(7, 11, 12) The disease also has a negative impact on people’s mental health, and people with CRSwNP are at greater risk of conditions such as anxiety and depression.(19) 

5 



<!-- page 179 -->

For example, a study of 445 people with CRSwNP carried out across Europe, found that people with CRSwNP had worse general health, mental health, vitality, and physical, emotional and social functioning compared with the general population of a similar age.(10) Similarly, one patient with CRSwNP interviewed in the UK said that CRSwNP _‘can be a bit depressing because it's relentless. There's no escape from it. It gets you down, combine that with tiredness and it does get a bit depressing after a while.’_ (9) 

CRSwNP also affects the ability to work. A survey in the Netherlands found that people with CRSwNP reported a mean of 10.6 missed days of work per year, and 34.9% of people reported reduced effectiveness when at work.(20) 

As CRSwNP is caused by type 2 inflammation, people with CRSwNP often have other existing clinical conditions caused by type 2 inflammation, such as asthma, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug-exacerbated respiratory disease (NSAID-ERD) and inhalant allergy.(15, 19, 21-25) A study with data from five clinical trials (1,748 participants in total) reported that 56.0% to 71.0% of people with CRSwNP have comorbid asthma.(26) 

Sanofi interviewed 11 people living with CRSwNP in the UK in 2024 to understand their experience of the condition.(9) Participants reported feelings of anxiety and embarrassment from having a blocked but runny nose, which impact hugely on every aspect of their life.(9) People interviewed explained that the constant need to blow their nose and changes in their voice were causing them to avoid social situations and public speaking.(9) One patient said _‘I lost confidence in social situations. I started to avoid some social situations because I felt like I sounded strange when I spoke.’_ (9) 

These interviews with people with CRSwNP also found that loss of smell and taste had an important negative impact on the people’s quality of life: ‘ _The hardest thing is the no smell and no taste. You adjust to it, and you live with it, but that's the thing I miss most, smelling and tasting food.’_ (9) 

## **What is the economic cost of CRSwNP to patients and the NHS?** 

CRSwNP is associated with high indirect costs, causing patients to both take time off work and to be less productive at work, as well as considerable costs to themselves and to the NHS.(4, 20, 23, 27) Surgery is the main driver of medical costs among people with CRSwNP who undergo sinus surgery (see Sections 2c for additional information about treatments).(23) In a study of 101,054 people with CRSwNP who underwent sinus surgery in England, the total cost of sinus surgery from 2010 to 2020 was £174 million, of which £66.7 million was due to revision surgeries.(23) 

## **2b) Diagnosis of the condition (in relation to the medicine being evaluated)** 

Please briefly explain how the condition is currently diagnosed and how this impacts patients. Are there any additional diagnostic tests required with the new treatment? 

The clinician will initially assess symptoms and history. They will ask if the person experiences persistent nasal blockage (obstruction/congestion), runny nose (rhinorrhoea), facial pain/pressure and/or reduction/loss of smell.(4) 

To confirm if a person has CRSwNP, the clinician will ask them to undergo imaging tests, including a nasal endoscopy and/or computed tomography (CT) scan.(4) During an endoscopy, a small camera is passed through the nose to look at the nasal cavity and sinuses.(28) A CT scan provides detailed pictures of the inside of the nose and 

6 



<!-- page 180 -->

sinuses.(29) If endoscopy shows that the person has nasal polyps and/or the CT scan shows changes to the lining of the sinuses/nasal cavity, the clinician may diagnose CRSwNP.(4) 

For people with a confirmed CRSwNP diagnosis, dupilumab is only indicated for those fulfilling specific additional criteria as outlined in the licence.(1, 2) The licence states that:(1, 2) 

_‘Dupilumab is licenced in the UK as an add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids (SCS) and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control.’_ 

Disease control is defined via a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), where the severity of symptoms is ranked from 0 (best) to 10 (worst).(4) Partially or uncontrolled CRSwNP corresponds to symptoms of blocked nose, runny nose, facial pain/pressure, reduced smell and sleep disturbance of severity >5, in addition to nasal endoscopy findings and the need for rescue medication (surgery and/or steroid tablets [SCS]).(4) 

## **2c) Current treatment options** 

The purpose of this section is to set the scene on how the condition is currently managed: 

- What is the treatment pathway for this condition and where in this pathway the medicine is likely to be used? Please use diagrams to accompany text where possible. Please give emphasis to the specific setting and condition being considered by NICE in this review. For example, by referencing current treatment guidelines. It may be relevant to show the treatments people may have before and after the treatment under consideration in this SIP. 

- • Please also consider: 

   - if there are multiple treatment options, and data suggest that some are more commonly used than others in the setting and condition being considered in this SIP, please report these data. 

   - are there any drug–drug interactions and/or contraindications that commonly cause challenges for patient populations? If so, please explain what these are. 

Guidance on the management of CRSwNP in England is based on recommendations from the European Rhinologic Society in the European Position Paper on Rhinosinusitis and Nasal Polyps (EPOS) 2020,(30) and supported by recommendations from the British Rhinological Society (BRS) and European Forum for Research and Education in Allergy and Airway Disease (EUFOREA).(4, 11, 31, 32) 

The EPOS 2020 guideline recommendations are presented in Similarly, BRS experts recommend biologics to be considered for people with CRSwNP based on disease severity, impact on quality of life, need for steroids, number of prior surgeries and comorbidities.(31) 

Figure 1. The treatment pathway for CRSwNP includes multiple steps and steroid nasal sprays (INCS) are recommended at each one.(32) 

• As a first step, patients are generally prescribed saline rinses and steroid nasal spray.(32) 

7 



<!-- page 181 -->

- If symptoms do not improve after 6 to 12 weeks of treatment with saline rinses and steroid nasal spray, short-term treatment (defined as less than 3 weeks) with steroid tablets (SCS) may be considered for relieving acute increase in symptom severity.(32, 33) 

- Surgery (endoscopic sinonasal surgery [ESS]) is recommended for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP whose symptoms do not improve after 6 to 12 weeks of treatment with saline rinse and steroid tablets.(4) 

- For people with no improvement at 6 to 12 weeks following treatment with saline rinse, steroids and surgery, and who have evidence of type 2 inflammation, EPOS recommend either revision surgery, or a treatment with a biologic (medicine derived from living organisms [e.g., proteins, cells, or tissues]).(4) 

Specifically, EPOS and EUFOREA guidance recommend biologic therapy to be offered to people with uncontrolled CRSwNP who have received one surgery (or are ineligible for surgery) and meet at least 3 of the following 5 criteria:(11, 32) 

- Evidence of type 2 inflammation 

- Need for or contraindication to steroid tablets 

- Significantly impaired quality of life 

- Significant loss of smell 

- Comorbid asthma. 

Similarly, BRS experts recommend biologics to be considered for people with CRSwNP based on disease severity, impact on quality of life, need for steroids, number of prior surgeries and comorbidities.(31)

CRS = chronic rhinosinusitis; CRSwNP = chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps; EPOS = European Position; ESS = endoscopic sinonasal surgery; INCS = intranasal corticosteroid; NERD = NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease; NSAID = non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug; SCS = systemic corticosteroid Sources: Generated based on current clinical guidance in Fokkens et al., 2020(4) and Hellings et al., 2024(32) 

**However, there are currently no biologic therapies licensed for the treatment of people with CRSwNP in England and available to patients through the NHS.** Currently established treatments for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP include steroid nasal sprays with saline rinses, steroid tablets (for acute increase in symptom severity) 

8 



<!-- page 182 -->

and surgery (for people whose symptoms do not improve despite treatment with saline rinse and steroids).(4, 32) 

The established treatments for people with CRSwNP have several limitations, including limited clinical benefit that is temporary.(34) Additionally, there are risks of severe adverse events (AEs) and complications: 

- AEs associated with steroid tablets use include osteoporosis (weakened bones), hypertension, pneumonia, heart failure, heart attack, cataracts and glaucoma.(32, 35) 

- Complications associated with surgery include bleeding during surgery, post-surgery infection, haemorrhage and orbital/intracranial complications.(34, 36) For people requiring revision surgery, the risk of complications increases with each subsequent surgery.(15, 37) 

- Surgery may not be appropriate for all people with CRSwNP and is contraindicated in those with severe uncontrolled asthma due to the risks associated with anaesthesia.(32) 

NHS waiting lists for sinonasal surgery (50% of which are revision surgeries) range from 6 months to up to 3 years following specialist referral, and represent another important limitation of surgery.(34) Waiting lists negatively impact people with uncontrolled CRSwNP who, as a result of persistent type 2 inflammation, experience significant and detrimental worsening of their disease and prolonged use of steroid tablets, therefore establishing suboptimal steroids stewardship principles.(34) Steroids stewardship aims to limit the use of steroids to reduce the risk of AEs.(34) 

## **2d) Patient-based evidence (PBE) about living with the condition** 

## **Context:** 

- **Patient-based evidence (PBE)** is when patients input into scientific research, specifically to provide experiences of their symptoms, needs, perceptions, quality of life issues or experiences of the medicine they are currently taking. PBE might also include carer burden and outputs from patient preference studies, when conducted in order to show what matters most to patients and carers and where their greatest needs are. Such research can inform the selection of patient-relevant endpoints in clinical trials. 

In this section, please provide a summary of any PBE that has been collected or published to demonstrate what is understood about **patient needs and disease experiences** . Please include the methods used for collecting this evidence. Any such evidence included in the SIP should be formally referenced wherever possible and references included. 

Sanofi UK interviewed 11 people living with CRSwNP in the UK in 2024 to understand their experience with the disease.(9) All the people interviewed had uncontrolled disease and had undergone at least one surgery for nasal polyps.(9) The interviews reinforced that CRSwNP is a condition characterised by despair for the patient.(9) 

People with CRSwNP reported that blocked nose, trouble sleeping and loss of smell and taste hugely impacts every aspect of their life.(9) Patients change their lifestyle and avoid social situations due to the constant need to blow their nose and changes in their voice, which make them embarrassed and anxious.(9) Several people mentioned that their blocked nose would sometimes cause them panic attacks at night.(9) One patient said _‘I was almost having panic attacks at night because of drifting off to sleep and instinctively trying to breathe through my nose and remembering that I couldn’t.’_ (9) Because of sleep 

9 



<!-- page 183 -->

disturbances, people with CRSwNP also feel tired and are unable to continue with their normal daily activities, including work.(9) 

People reported that CRSwNP was also a problem for their family:(9) 

- _‘It doesn't just affect me. It affects my family as well.’_ 

- _‘My wife and I have not been in the same bedroom for a good number of years now because of the snoring.’_ 

During the interviews, people described CRSwNP as relentless with no durable escape possible;(9) they find that the available treatments (steroids and surgery) only provide benefits for a few months at a time.(9) People with CRSwNP feel stuck in a circle of repeated surgeries and periods of steroid treatment, where little can be done to improve their quality of life.(9) Surgery was a very negative experience for some people and they would like another effective treatment option to be available.(9) People with CRSwNP said:(9) 

- _‘My body went into shock over it_ [surgery] _. I mean, the pain was horrific. It was just the most horrific experience’._ 

- _‘I just wish there was an alternative to surgery. If anything, I'd rather not have surgery again, to be honest with you.’_ 

## **SECTION 3: The treatment** 

## **3a) How does the new treatment work? What are the important features of this treatment?** 

Please outline as clearly as possible important details that you consider relevant to patients relating to the mechanism of action and how the medicine interacts with the body 

Where possible, please describe how you feel the medicine is innovative or novel, and how this might be important to patients and their communities. 

If there are relevant documents which have been produced to support your regulatory submission such as a Summary of Product Characteristics or patient information leaflet, please provide a link to these. 

As described in Section 2a, CRSwNP is caused by long-term inflammation known as type 2 inflammation.(4, 6, 13, 14) A study in the UK involving 33,107 people with CRSwNP found that those needing multiple surgeries for nasal polyps had high levels of certain immune cells called eosinophils, which are linked to type 2 inflammation.(15) 

## **Dupilumab** 

Dupilumab is a special type of medicine called a monoclonal antibody.(1, 2) It works by blocking 2 proteins, interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13, which are involved in type 2 inflammation.(1, 2) By blocking these proteins, dupilumab reduces type 2 inflammation and prevents damage to the sinuses and nasal cavity.(1, 2) 

Dupilumab is a unique treatment for CRSwNP because it specifically targets IL-4 and IL-13, which play a major role in type 2 inflammation.(1, 2) This makes it particularly effective for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP who have not responded well to steroids and/or surgery. Other treatments for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, such as mepolizumab and omalizumab, target different proteins (IL-5 and immunoglobulin E 

10 



<!-- page 184 -->

[IgE], respectively) that are also involved in type 2 inflammation but play smaller roles compared to IL-4 and IL-13.(38-40) 

## **Safety and Monitoring** 

One of the advantages of dupilumab is that it can be prescribed without needing routine monitoring beyond what is normally done for people with CRSwNP.

## **3c) Administration and dosing** 

How and where is the treatment given or taken? Please include the dose, how often the treatment should be given/taken, and how long the treatment should be given/taken for. 

How will this administration method or dosing potentially affect patients and caregivers? How does this differ to existing treatments? 

Dupilumab is intended to be prescribed at all UK specialised centres. These centres currently prescribe dupilumab for conditions like severe asthma and moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (eczema). 

The recommended dose of dupilumab for adults with CRSwNP is 300 mg given every other week (once every 2 weeks).(1, 2) Dupilumab can be self-administered or administered by a carer or healthcare professional.(1, 2) It is administered by 

subcutaneous injection (into the layer of fatty tissue immediately under the skin) in the thigh or abdomen, except for 5 cm around the navel (belly button), using a single-use prefilled syringe or pen.(1, 2) If the injection is being administered by somebody else, the upper arm can also be used.(1, 2) 

Current treatments for people with CRSwNP are nasal sprays (saline rinses, steroids) or tablets (steroids) to be taken daily, so one of the advantages of dupilumab is that it is not given every day but only once every 2 weeks.(1, 2)

## **3d) Current clinical trials** 

Please provide a list of completed or ongoing clinical trials for the treatment. Please provide a brief top-level summary for each trial, such as title/name, location, population, patient group size, comparators, key inclusion and exclusion criteria and completion dates etc. Please provide references to further information about the trials or publications from the trials. 

The clinical efficacy and safety of dupilumab for the treatment of CRSwNP has been studied in two phase 3 randomised clinical trials, LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 (i.e., SINUS-24; NCT02912468) and LIBERTY NP SINUS-52 (i.e., SINUS-52; NCT02898454). 

People enrolled in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials were adults with severe CRSwNP (signs of nasal polyps on nasal endoscopy that persisted despite prior treatment with SCS in the past 2 years [and/or had a contraindication/intolerance to SCS] and/or prior surgery for nasal polyps), who had:(41) 

- Evidence of medium or large size polyps in each nasal cavity on nasal endoscopy 

- Ongoing symptoms of blocked nose (nasal congestion/obstruction), and either decreased/loss of smell or runny nose (rhinorrhoea). 

SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 primarily looked at how adding dupilumab to background therapy with INCS reduced people’s nasal polyps size and nasal blockage over 24 weeks, compared to the nasal polyps size and nasal blockage of people who had been randomly allocated to receive placebo in addition to background therapy.(41) 

Both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were phase 3, placebo-controlled, double blind, randomised trials.(41) Double blinding means that both the people enrolled in the trial and the healthcare professionals involved do not know which people have been randomised to receive either dupilumab or placebo.(42) The placebo acts as a basis for comparing the effect of the medicine being studied, which is otherwise known as a control.(42) 

There were differences between the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, including study duration (24 weeks in SINUS-24 and 52 weeks in SINUS-52) and the number of dupilumab treatment groups (one group in SINUS-24 and two groups in SINUS-52 with a different dosing to SINUS-24 in one of the groups).(41) 

- **SINUS-24(41, 43)** – Completed in July 2018 

   - The SINUS-24 trial lasted for 24 weeks. 

   - The trial was conducted in 79 sites across 13 countries worldwide, including the UK. SINUS-24 enrolled 19 people from 6 sites in the UK. 

   - A total of 276 people with CRSwNP were enrolled and randomised to receive dupilumab (143 people) or placebo (133 people), with continued background therapy with INCS. 

12 



<!-- page 186 -->

- **SINUS-52(41, 43)** – Completed in November 2018 

   - The SINUS-52 trial lasted for 52 weeks. 

   - The trial was conducted in 119 sites across 14 countries worldwide. 

   - A total of 448 people with CRSwNP were enrolled and randomised to receive dupilumab (once every 2 weeks: 150 people; once every 4 weeks: 145 people) or placebo (153 people), with continued background therapy with INCS. 

## **3e) Efficacy** 

Efficacy is the measure of how well a treatment works in treating a specific condition. 

In this section, please summarise all data that demonstrate how effective the treatment is compared with current treatments at treating the condition outlined in section 2a. 

- Are any of the outcomes more important to patients than others and why? 

- Are there any limitations to the data which may affect how to interpret the results? 

Please do not include academic or commercial in confidence information but where necessary reference the section of the company submission where this can be found. 

In both the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, the primary endpoints (the main things that the trials were designed to measure) were nasal polyps size and nasal blockage.(41) Treatment with dupilumab significantly reduced the size of nasal polyps and nasal blockage compared to placebo in the trial participants.(41) These statistically significant improvements were measured in terms of Nasal Polyp Score (NPS) and Nasal Congestion (NC) score,(41) as follows:(43, 44) 

- The NPS, which is based on the sum of the right and left nostril scores (total score from 0 to 8, with a score from 0 to 4 per nostril and higher values indicating larger polyps), was determined by physicians from video recordings of nasal endoscopy. 

- • The NC score was recorded every morning by the participants based on symptom severity over the past 24 hours, from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severe symptoms). 

In both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, NPS and NC score rapidly improved starting from 4 weeks and improved continuously throughout 24 weeks (Figure 2).(41) In SINUS-52, significant improvements in NPS and NC score were maintained at 52 weeks in participants treated with dupilumab once every 2 weeks compared to placebo.(41) 

13 



<!-- page 187 -->

**Figure 2. Change from baseline over time in nasal polyp score (NPS) and nasal congestion/ obstruction (NC) score in the pooled population of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52** 

**==> picture [441 x 153] intentionally omitted <==**

NC = nasal congestion/obstruction; NPS = nasal polyp score; Q2W = once every two weeks Sources: Sanofi. Data on File, Summary of Clinical Efficacy.(45) 

As planned before the start of the trials, data collected in both SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 were combined for the testing of certain endpoints.(41) This was called the “pooled 

analysis” and people in the dupilumab arms of both trials were combined into one group, and people in the placebo arms of both trials were combined into another group.(41) In this pooled analysis, dupilumab reduced the proportion of participants who required rescue treatment with SCS or sinonasal surgery during the trials by 76% compared to placebo (73.9% for SCS and 82.6% for sinonasal surgery, individually), which was a statistically significant difference.(41) 

In people with comorbid asthma, dupilumab led to greater lung function improvements (as measured by forced expiratory volume in 1 second [FEV1] and Asthma Control Questionnaire 6 [ACQ-6]) compared to placebo at 24 weeks.(41) The FEV1 is a spirometry test, which measures the volume of air that can be breathed out in the first second of forced exhalation.(43, 44) At 24 weeks, dupilumab improved FEV1 by 0.21 L compared to placebo.(41) The ACQ-6 is a questionnaire assessing the most common asthma symptoms on a 7-point scale (0 = no impairment to 6 = maximum impairment), with the ACQ-6 score being the mean of the scores for all 6 symptoms.(43, 44) The ACQ-6 was completed weekly by participants.(43, 44) At 24 weeks, dupilumab improved the ACQ-6 score by 0.82 point compared to placebo.(41) 

This shows that dupilumab has an impact on nasal polyps, nasal blockage and disease control (reduced need for SCS and/or sinonasal surgery) in people with uncontrolled CRSwNP, as well as lung function in those with uncontrolled CRSwNP and comorbid asthma.(41)

## **Quality of life** 

In the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, researchers measured the participants’ quality of life using a survey called the 22-item Sinonasal Outcomes Test (SNOT-22).(43, 44) This survey has 22 questions, each scored from 0 (no problem) to 5 (worst problem).(43, 44) The highest possible score is 110, indicating the worst quality of life.(43, 44) To show a meaningful improvement, a treatment needs to reduce the score by at least 8.9 point (the “minimum clinically important difference”).(43, 44) In both trials, participants filled out this survey every 2 weeks.(41, 43, 44) 

- SINUS-24 trial: dupilumab improved quality of life early (from 8 weeks) and continued to do so up to 24 weeks compared to placebo. At 24 weeks, dupilumab reduced the SNOT-22 total score by 21.12 points compared to placebo. 

- SINUS-52 trial: dupilumab also showed early (from 4 weeks) and sustained quality of life benefit at 24 weeks compared to placebo. At 24 weeks, the SNOT-22 total score was 17.36 points lower for dupilumab compared to placebo.(41) These benefits lasted up to 1 year, with a 20.96-point improvement at 1 year. 

When combining results from both trials (“pooled analysis”), more people on dupilumab saw a meaningful improvement in their quality of life compared to those on placebo.(46) At 24 weeks, 75.1% of people on dupilumab had an improvement of 8.9 points or more in SNOT-22 total score, compared to 43.4% of people on placebo.(46) 

Researchers also used another survey called the EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D) VAS, where participants rated their health from 0 (worst) to 100 (best).(43, 44) A meaningful 

improvement in the EQ-5D VAS is 8 points or more.(43, 44, 46) At 24 weeks, 46.8% of people on dupilumab saw this improvement compared to 25.9% of people on placebo.(46) While participants had lower health scores compared to the general population at the start of the trials, those on dupilumab reached health scores similar to the general population at 24 weeks.(46) 

## **Sleep** 

The SNOT-22 survey includes questions about sleep, such as “difficulty falling asleep,” “wake up at night,” “lack of a good night’s sleep,” and “wake up tired.”(43, 44, 47) During the trials, participants rated their sleep every 2 weeks from 0 (no problem) to 5 (worst problem).(43, 44, 47) 

Dupilumab improved sleep early (from 8 weeks) and continued to do so up to 52 weeks compared to placebo.(47) The sleep score improved by 0.97 points at 24 weeks in SINUS-24 compared to placebo and continued to improve through 52 weeks in the SINUS-52 trial (by 0.93 points compared to placebo).(47) 

## **Loss of smell** 

In both trials, participants rated their sense of smell daily using the Loss of sense of Smell (LoS) scale, from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severe symptoms).(43, 44) Based on data from the trials, it was estimated that a meaningful improvement in the LoS is 1 point or more.(48) In both trials, dupilumab led to early (from 4 weeks) and sustained meaningful improvements in the sense of smell at 24 weeks compared to placebo.(41) The LoS score 

15 



<!-- page 189 -->

improved by 1.12 points in SINUS-24 and 0.98 points in SINUS-52 compared to placebo.(41) 

## **Patient preference** 

In a survey of 75 people with CRSwNP who had undergone at least one surgery and were receiving dupilumab, 91.5% of patients preferred taking dupilumab over having another surgery.(49) Similarly, a patient currently treated with dupilumab for CRSwNP through the Compassionate Use Scheme in the UK, reported a preference for dupilumab over the treatments previously received:(50) 

_‘Within three days of my first dose, I could breathe more clearly than I had in over a decade, and by the end of the first week, all symptoms vanished. Four years later, I remain symptom-free, my sense of taste and smell fully restored. […] Dupixent has truly been life-changing, succeeding where everything else had failed.’_ 

## **3g) Safety of the medicine and side effects** 

When NICE appraises a treatment, it will pay close attention to the balance of the benefits of the treatment in relation to its potential risks and any side effects. Therefore, please outline the main side effects (as opposed to a complete list) of this treatment and include details of a benefit/risk assessment where possible. This will support patient reviewers to consider the potential overall benefits and side effects that the medicine can offer. 

Based on available data, please outline the most common side effects, how frequently they happen compared with standard treatment, how they could potentially be managed and how many people had treatment adjustments or stopped treatment. Where it will add value or context for patient readers, please include references to the Summary of Product Characteristics from regulatory agencies etc. 

Dupilumab is an established treatment for multiple diseases and has been used in England since 2018. Over 1 million people have been treated with dupilumab across multiple licenced indications worldwide.(51) 

In SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, dupilumab demonstrated a favourable risk/benefit ratio and tolerability profile in adults with severe CRSwNP (uncontrolled despite prior treatment with SCS and/or prior sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps).(41) 

Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) are safety events recorded in clinical trials that arise during the course of treatment. They may or may not be associated with, or caused by, the treatment (i.e., either dupilumab add-on to background therapy, or placebo add-on to background therapy). 

Data from the pooled analysis showed that:(41, 52) 

- The proportion of participants with TEAEs was lower with dupilumab (69.3%) compared to placebo (73.8%). 

- The most common TEAEs in the dupilumab group were common cold (nasopharyngitis) (12.5%), headache (7.3%) and redness (erythema) at the injectionsite (6.4%). 

- The most common TEAEs in the placebo group were common cold (nasopharyngitis) (14.5%), worsening of nasal polyps (11.7%) and headache (8.5%). 

16 



<!-- page 190 -->

- Treatment-emergent serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported in 3.9% of participants in the dupilumab group and 6.4% of participants in the placebo group. 

- 2.5% of participants receiving dupilumab had to stop treatment due to a TEAE, compared to 5.3% of participants receiving placebo. 

As dupilumab is already approved and used for several other conditions (e.g., atopic dermatitis, asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps), its safety profile is well understood and has been established in several other randomised clinical trials including over 15,000 participants.(53) 

## **3h) Summary of key benefits of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key benefits of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. 

- Please include benefits related to the mode of action, effectiveness, safety and mode of administration. 

There are currently no therapies targeting type 2 inflammation that are recommended and reimbursed for people with severe CRSwNP in England. Dupilumab has an established safety profile and is the first therapy for uncontrolled CRSwNP that specifically targets IL-4 and IL-13 in the inflammatory pathway, thereby reducing type 2 inflammation and the resulting damage to the sinuses and nasal cavity.(1, 2, 41) 

In SINUS-24 and SINUS-52, people treated with dupilumab had reduced nasal polyp size, nasal blockage, loss of smell and need for SCS and/or surgery, less severe symptoms and better quality of life compared to those receiving placebo (see Sections 3d to 3g for additional information about the clinical efficacy and safety outcomes).(41) Dupilumab also demonstrated a favourable safety and tolerability profile, in people with severe CRSwNP and other diseases.(53) In a real-world study of people receiving dupilumab as prescribed by their doctor for the treatment of CRSwNP, the safety and quality of life benefit of dupilumab lasted for 2 years.(54, 55) 

The proportion of patients who needed rescue treatment with SCS and/or sinonasal surgery during the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials was reduced with dupilumab, which has the potential to reduce the burden of managing the long-term condition encountered by people with severe CRSwNP in attending multiple appointments for monitoring and for revision surgeries.(34, 41) 

Improvements in symptoms and quality of life, especially reduction/loss of smell and sleep, may allow people with uncontrolled CRSwNP to improve their overall wellbeing and to avoid any loss of income due to their disease.(20, 41, 47) 

People can self-administer dupilumab (or have a caregiver help with administration) through a simple injection every other week.(1, 2) No additional tests or monitoring beyond those already recommended for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP are required.

## **3i) Summary of key disadvantages of treatment for patients** 

Issues to consider in your response: 

- Please outline what you feel are the key disadvantages of the treatment for patients, caregivers and their communities when compared with current treatments. Which disadvantages are most important to patients and carers? 

- Please include disadvantages related to the mode of action, effectiveness, side effects and mode of administration 

- What is the impact of any disadvantages highlighted compared with current treatments 

People with CRSwNP may need to travel to their nearest secondary care centre for their first consultation with a specialist to access dupilumab add-on therapy, which may be a challenge for some people (see Section 3l). Dupilumab is self-administered via subcutaneous injection into the thigh or abdomen, except for 5 cm around the navel (belly button), using a single-use pre-filled syringe or pen.(1, 2) Administration via injection may be unpleasant to people who experience a fear of needles or prefer other modes of administration, such as oral pills or inhalation. 

## **3j) Value and economic considerations** 

## **Introduction for patients:** 

Health services want to get the most value from their budget and therefore need to decide whether a new treatment provides good value compared with other treatments. To do this they consider the costs of treating patients and how patients’ health will improve, from feeling better and/or living longer, compared with the treatments already in use. The drug manufacturer provides this information, often presented using a health economic model. 

In completing your input to the NICE appraisal process for the medicine, you may wish to reflect on: 

- The extent to which you agree/disagree with the value arguments presented below (e.g., whether you feel these are the relevant health outcomes, addressing the unmet needs and issues faced by patients; were any improvements that would be important to you missed out, not tested or not proven?) 

- If you feel the benefits or side effects of the medicine, including how and when it is given or taken, would have positive or negative financial implications for patients or their families (e.g., travel costs, time-off work)? 

- How the condition, taking the new treatment compared with current treatments affects your quality of life. 

Sanofi has submitted a health economic model for evaluation by NICE. The following sections describe how the model was structured and how it attempts to reflect the progression of CRSwNP over time. The goal of the economic modelling is to quantify the differences in outcomes and costs between using dupilumab or established clinical management (ECM). These differences are combined and used by NICE to determine whether dupilumab is cost-effective or not. 

## **How the model reflects the condition** 

The model starts with a close description of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials by using a “decision tree”, in which people with CRSwNP are allocated to dupilumab plus 

18 



<!-- page 192 -->

ECM or ECM alone. This is a common way of modelling a clinical trial period. At the end of the decision tree, outcomes for the people taking dupilumab are assessed and, if they do not experience a significant improvement of their symptoms (assessed via the NPS [an endoscopic score to measure nasal polyp size] and the SNOT-22 score [a survey to measure quality of life]), their treatment is stopped in the model and they revert back to what they were taking before. This rule is put in place in the model to reflect what may happen in reality to ensure that the NHS does not continue to spend money and resources on treating people who would not benefit. 

After the decision tree, people then move to the longer-term part of the model that uses the clinical trial results to predict the difference between what would happen if people were treated with dupilumab plus ECM compared to what would happen if they only received ECM. During this part of the model, the impact of dupilumab treatment on the need for sinonasal surgery is considered as well as how treatment influences disease control and quality of life over time. 

## **Modelling how much a treatment extends life** 

As people with CRSwNP do not experience an increase in mortality compared to the general population. There is no evidence to suggest that treatment with dupilumab in people with CRSwNP extends life. 

## **Modelling how much a treatment improves quality of life** 

People with less controlled CRSwNP have worse quality of life. Quality of life was measured during the clinical trials using the SNOT-22 (as described in Section 3f), and SNOT-22 data are used in the model to assess differences in outcomes for people treated with dupilumab + ECM and those treated with ECM only. To do this, the model assigns different quality of life outcomes to each level of disease control (controlled on medication, inadequately controlled, post-operative controlled or uncontrolled disease). 

The clinical trials showed that CRSwNP remains controlled for longer whilst taking dupilumab, and so people treated with dupilumab experience better quality of life in the model than people treated with ECM alone. This difference is used to show the benefit of dupilumab over ECM. 

## **Modelling how the costs of treatment differ with dupilumab** 

The model also compares the cost of treating people with dupilumab plus ECM to ECM alone. It calculates the differences in the cost of the medicines and the cost of NHS services used for the management of CRSwNP, such as general practitioner (GP) appointments or hospital stays. 

As would be expected, dupilumab plus ECM is more expensive than ECM alone, as people are receiving two treatments rather than one. However, the cost of CRSwNP on patients and the NHS is substantial (Section 2a), and dupilumab has the potential to reduce these costs by preventing many of the events that occur due to uncontrolled symptoms/disease, revision surgeries and poor quality of life. This is because treatment with dupilumab leads to: 

- Reduced symptoms and better quality of life (Section 3f).(41, 47) This could enable people with uncontrolled CRSwNP to avoid any loss of income if they would have 

19 



<!-- page 193 -->

   - otherwise needed to reduce their working hours or to stop working due to their disease.(9) 

- Significantly improved disease control and quality of life, as measured by the NPS and SNOT-22 scores (Section 3e).(41) People with controlled CRSwNP have fewer GP visits, outpatient visits and hospital admissions, and use their rescue medication less (e.g., steroid tablets and surgery). By improving symptoms and reducing nasal polyp size, dupilumab has the potential to reduce the burden of CRSwNP on the NHS, as well as the associated costs. 

- Significantly improved lung function in people with uncontrolled CRSwNP and comorbid asthma, which has the potential to reduce the burden of asthma on the NHS, as well as the associated costs.(41) 

- Sanofi UK heard from a group of UK clinicians with experience in treating CRSwNP. The clinicians confirmed that dupilumab could reduce the number of times people with uncontrolled CRSwNP have to undergo revision nasal polyp surgery in comparison to the current situation where there is no reimbursed targeted treatment for people with severe CRSwNP in the UK.(34) 

- The reduced frequency of revision nasal polyp surgery for people living with uncontrolled CRSwNP that dupilumab treatment represents would reduce the burden for both the person living with CRSwNP (taking time away from work, educational or social activities for pre-surgery appointments, surgery and post-surgery recovery); and also reduce the burden on the healthcare system, freeing up capacity (note that waiting lists are currently up to 3 years) by reducing the number of people requiring nasal polyp surgery.(34) 

Dupilumab is self-administered every other week (once every 2 weeks) via a pre-filled syringe or pen, and has a favourable risk/benefit ratio.(1, 2) No tests are required to prescribe dupilumab beyond what is required for routine CRSwNP diagnosis and monitoring. 

## **Uncertainty** 

Challenges associated with modelling the course of severe CRSwNP and the long-term impact of treatment with dupilumab have the potential to create uncertainty in model outputs. Specifically, these challenges include: 

- Insufficient published evidence on post-operative disease recurrence and revision surgeries 

- Insufficient published evidence on the utilisation of healthcare resources based on the UK population 

- Insufficient published evidence on the long-term impact of steroids overuse in the UK 

- The variability of long-term outcomes following surgery. 

20 



<!-- page 194 -->

## **Additional factors** 

Some health benefits of dupilumab could not be considered in the health economic model. These additional health benefits of dupilumab include: 

- Reducing the pressure on NHS resources during cold weather months by reducing symptoms and the need for revision surgeries in people with CRSwNP, who are especially vulnerable during such time periods 

- Reducing the severity of respiratory symptoms in people with CRSwNP 

- Reducing the environmental impact of CRSwNP by reducing the number of doctor visits, hospitalisations and revision surgeries that people with CRSwNP need. 

## **3k) Innovation** 

NICE considers how innovative a new treatment is when making its recommendations. 

If the company considers the new treatment to be innovative please explain how it represents a ‘step change’ in treatment and/ or effectiveness compared with current treatments. Are there any QALY benefits that have not been captured in the economic model that also need to be considered (see Section 3f) 

As the first and only licensed therapy which targets the underlying IL-4/IL-13 signalling pathway that is involved in type 2 inflammation in CRSwNP,(1, 2) dupilumab has demonstrated improvements in clinical outcomes and quality of life compared to INCS alone for people with severe CRSwNP (uncontrolled despite prior treatment with SCS and/or prior sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps).(41) 

Other biologics licensed for the treatment of CRSwNP work in a different way to dupilumab and are not currently available to patients through the NHS. The treatments used routinely for people with severe CRSwNP, including steroid nasal sprays, steroid tablets and surgery, are not designed for CRSwNP specifically, are associated with significant safety concerns, and/or provide only temporary and limited clinical benefit.(15, 32, 34, 36, 37, 56) 

The pivotal SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 clinical trials have shown that the use of dupilumab as an add-on to background therapy with INCS addresses the current unmet need for a targeted, effective and well-tolerated treatment that can address type 2 inflammation, reduce the burden of loss of smell and sinonasal blockage (congestion/obstruction), and improve quality of life in people with uncontrolled CRSwNP.(41) 

Dupilumab provides people with CRSwNP and clinicians with a treatment option that has demonstrated efficacy and a well-established and favourable safety profile.(41) Please see Sections 3d to 3g for additional information about the clinical efficacy and safety outcomes.(41)

## **3l) Equalities** 

Are there any potential equality issues that should be taken into account when considering this condition and this treatment? Please explain if you think any groups of people with this condition are particularly disadvantaged. 

Equality legislation includes people of a particular age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation or people with any other shared characteristics 

More information on how NICE deals with equalities issues can be found in the NICE equality scheme 

Find more general information about the Equality Act and equalities issues here 

The current lack of licenced, reimbursed, effective and targeted treatments with favourable safety profiles places people with uncontrolled CRSwNP at a significant disadvantage compared to people with other forms of chronic type 2 inflammatory conditions, such as asthma and PN, for whom targeted biologic therapies are already reimbursed.(1, 2, 57, 58) Thus, a NICE recommendation for dupilumab in uncontrolled CRSwNP would have a positive impact on people with uncontrolled CRSwNP. 

Additionally, depending on where they live, people with uncontrolled CRSwNP are currently expected to be on a waiting list for nasal polyp surgery for 6 months to up to 3 years, and about half of these people are waiting for revision surgery.(34) Based on the evidence presented here, adding dupilumab to the treatment options for uncontrolled CRSwNP is expected to reduce the number of people who require revision surgery, freeing up capacity and potentially reducing NHS wait times.(34)

## **4b) Glossary of terms** 

**Adverse event/Side effect:** An unexpected medical problem that arises during treatment with a drug or other therapy. Adverse events may be mild, moderate, or severe. 

**Clinical trial:** A type of research study that tests how well new medical approaches work in people. These studies test new methods of screening, prevention, diagnosis or treatment of a disease. Also called clinical study. 

**EMA (European Medicines Agency):** The regulatory body that evaluates, approves and supervises medicines throughout the European Union. Similar to the MHRA for the UK. 

**Endoscopic sinonasal surgery (ESS):** A type of operation used to treat problems in the nose and sinuses. A thin, flexible tube with a camera and light on the end (called an endoscope) is used to see inside the nose and sinuses, so a doctor can remove blockages and fix issues to help people breathe better and reduce sinus problems. 

**Healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU):** Refers to the use of healthcare services, such as treatments, GP visits, outpatient hospital visits, hospitalisations, emergency room admissions etc. 

23 



<!-- page 197 -->

**HTA (Health Technology Assessment) bodies:** Bodies that make recommendations regarding the financing and reimbursing of new medicines and medical products based on the added value (efficacy, safety, medical resources saving) of a therapy compared to existing ones. 

**Interleukin:** A type of chemical signal produced by white blood cells which regulate the response of the immune system. 

**Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS):** Medications administered as a spray into the nose, which deliver a small dose of steroids directly to the nasal passages. They help to reduce inflammation and swelling. 

**MHRA (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency):** The regulatory body that regulates medicines, medical devices and blood components for transfusion in the UK. Similar to the EMA for Europe. 

**Nasal congestion/obstruction (NC) score:** Score measuring the severity of nasal blockage based on a person’s own assessment of their daily symptoms of nasal blockage. 

**Nasal Polyp Score (NPS):** Score assessing the severity of nasal polys given by doctors depending on the size and number of polyps seen in a person’s nose during examination. 

**Pooled analysis:** Analysis combining data from several different trials (the data are all “pooled” together). 

**Primary endpoint:** The outcome measured to answer the key question in a clinical trial. 

**Quality of life:** The overall enjoyment of life. Many clinical trials assess it to measure aspects of an individual’s sense of wellbeing and ability to carry out activities of daily living. 

**Recombinant human monoclonal antibody:** Identical antibody produced from a single type of immune cells using genetic engineering techniques in a laboratory that can precisely target and neutralize harmful agents in the body and help the immune system fight diseases. 

**Secondary endpoint:** An outcome measured to answer an additional question of interest in a clinical trial. 

**SNOT-22 (22-item Sinonasal Outcomes Test):** Questionnaire used by doctors to measure how much sinus and nasal problems are affecting a person's life. 

**Systemic corticosteroids (SCS):** Medications usually in the form of pills or injections, which work by mimicking hormones that your body naturally produces (steroids) to fight inflammation. They affect the entire body, not just one specific area. 

**Type 2 inflammation:** An overactive immune response in which Type 2 immune cells (e.g., eosinophils) are activated even though there is no infection or allergen. As a result, the immune cells end up damaging the body itself and causing inflammation.

**A7. Priority question [updated]: The EAG notes that two of the subgroups proposed by NICE (patients who have asthma and patients who have NSAID-ERD) have been combined in the company submission. Please provide the results of subgroup analyses for each outcome (bilateral NPS, NC, TSS, SNOT-22 score, daily symptoms of decreased/loss of smell and UPSIT score) for the following subgroups:** 

**a) Patients who have no comorbidities;** 

**b) Patients who have asthma (who do not also have NSAID-ERD); and** 

**c) Patients who have NSAID-ERD.** 

**Please provide this information for the pooled ITT population and the subgroup who had prior surgery for nasal polyps. Please also implement these subgroups as a scenario in the economic model (for the prior surgery patients only).** 

As requested, Sanofi have conducted additional analyses in the requested subgroups of: 

- Patients with comorbid asthma; 

- Patients with prior NSAID-ERD; 

- Patients with any type-2 prior medical history. 

Clarification questions 26 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 228 -->

Internal 

All in the pooled ITT population AND in the population of patients having had at least one prior sinus surgery. These subgroups (baseline characteristics, NPS, SNOT-22 and utility scores) have been added as a user-selectable population in the CEM [Worksheet ‘Settings’; Cell F17/ SubgroupDropDown]. Please find details of the SINUS-24/52 post-hoc reports used to inform this at the end of this response document (after section C). 

Sanofi have not conducted a subgroup analysis for the population of patients who have asthma (and specifically who do not also have NSAID-ERD) as the presentation of NSAIDERD includes asthma within its characteristics and, therefore, removing NSAID-ERD patients from the asthma subgroup would introduce a degree bias to the results and is also not in line with the clinical experts opinion or the recognised guidelines for the treatment of CRSwNP. Sanofi have also not conducted a subgroup analysis for the requested subgroup of ‘patients who have no comorbidities’, as this subgroup was not requested as part of the NICE scope. Moreover, this is not a subgroup the company wishes to pursue reimbursement in and is not in line with the clinical expert’s opinion gathered both during the advisory board in June 2024 and the consultancy meetings in November 2024, or the recognised guidelines (such as EUFOREA/EPOS 2020). CRSwNP is driven by type 2 inflammation, which plays a pivotal role in the manifestation of several other inflammatory conditions such as, asthma, NSAID-ERD and AD and therefore, it is clinically not appropriate to investigate results in a subgroup specifically without any of these concomitant pathologies. Furthermore, the number of people with no type-2 comorbidity in SINUS-24/52 was very limited, and would have introduce significant uncertainty especially when calculating the long term response in the Markov model (based on responders throughout, which would be a very small number in the ECM arm).

## **Section B: Clarification on cost-effectiveness data**

## _**Model structure**_ 

**B1. The EAG notes that a one-year cycle length is not in line with the regularity of dupilumab administration and may not capture the timings of key clinical events. It is also not in line with how regularly response was assessed in the clinical trials. Please demonstrate that the one-year cycle length captures all relevant events and accounts for them appropriately or please adapt the model to use a shorter cycle length.** 

We acknowledge the EAG's concerns regarding the appropriateness of a one-year cycle length in our model, particularly in relation to the regularity of treatment administration and clinical event timing. Cycle length, in general, should reflect the frequency of key clinical events that influence patient outcomes. Below, we provide justification for the chosen cycle length: 

- **Disease progression and response assessments:** In the clinical trials, patient response was assessed at week 24 and week 52, which aligns with the annual cycle assumption. In line with the clinical trial, the first-year decision tree captures the shortterm treatment effect with a first efficacy assessment at week 24 followed by an adjustment based on trial outcomes at week 52. This is also in line with the timings of clinical assessment of CRSwNP response as per the guidelines.  EPOS 2020 guidelines endorsed European Forum for Research and Education in Allergy and Airway Diseases (EUFOREA) 2019 consensus on treatment response to biologic treatment in CRSwNP (EPOS, 2020; Fokkens et al., 2019). The EUFOREA states that treatment response should be evaluated after 16 weeks and after 1 year based on 5 criteria: nasal polyp size, need for SCSs, QOL, sense of smell and impact of comorbidities. Patients with no sufficient response in any of the criteria should discontinue treatment. Based on the investigation by Sanofi using the measures included in the SINUS trials, the best representation of the EPOS/EUFOREA response criteria is SNOT-22 CFB ≥ 8.9 and NPS CFB ≥ 1. 

For the Markov section of the model, a one-year time Horizon was preferred because responders at week 24 who continue to respond after week 52 and who enter the 

Clarification questions 57 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 259 -->

Internal 

Markov response states are not expected to experience significant change in their response status before one year if they remain on their current treatment. The same assumption is taken for the non-responders. 

- **Treatment modifications and adverse events:** Most clinically relevant changes, such as treatment discontinuation or disease progression, occur at a timescale that is consistent with a one-year cycle. Furthermore, even if dupilumab administration is twice a week, its stable long-term treatments effect suggests that no significant changes is expected within the 2 weeks’ timeframe. Therefore, we don’t expect the outcomes of the CEM to be different with a short cycle length. 

- **Consistency with prior health economic evaluations:** Other models for dupilumab submitted for evaluation by NICE have adopted a similar structure but incorporated various cycle lengths to account for different disease outcomes. In the Atopic Dermatitis (TA534) and COPD (ID6235) indications a one-year cycle length was used. For prurigo nodularis (TA955) 3 months was adopted and for Asthma (TA751) 4 weeks was chosen. The dosing schedule is Q2W for all these indications but alignment with the posology was considered less important than aligning with key model inputs, such as future risk of events and the efficacy response criteria. These have been discussed in the first part of this question. 

The use of the year cycle length in other models developed for CRsWNP is well established in the literature. For example, Yong 2023[7] and Scangas 2021[8] . 

- **Half-Cycle Correction Implementation:** To enhance the accuracy of the model and account for the fact that transitions can occur at any point within a cycle, we have implemented a half-cycle correction with the two Markov worksheets. This ensures that the model does not systematically overestimate, or underestimate patient time spent in each health state.

## **data in the CSR. However, the EAG is unclear on some of the numbers reported in Table 38 and the trial data it refers to:** 

## **a) Please clarify the exact difference between the ITT population and the base-case population?** 

Table 38 of the original CS compares response rates between the ITT population, and the company base case population. These response rates are determined based on the observed SINUS-24/52 pooled data, using the primary analysis method and the selected response criteria (in the company base case: according to the response criteria of SNOT 22 total score [8.9 points improvement] and NPS [1-point improvement]). Whilst this data was not provided along with the original CS, response analyses for all requested subgroups and requested criteria have been provided at the end of this document, after section C (all based on non-published post-hoc analyses of the pooled data of SINUS-24/52). 

The intention-to-treat (ITT) population of the pooled SINUS-24/52 trials is in line with the phase 3 studies recruitment criteria and the licensed indication: Adults with bilateral nasal polyps and symptoms of CRS despite intranasal corticosteroid therapy before randomisation and who had received systemic corticosteroids in the preceding 2 years (or had a medical contraindication or intolerance to systemic corticosteroids) or previous sinonasal surgery. This corresponds to **patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP despite prior treatment with SCS and/or surgery** .[9] 

As this ITT population comprises surgery-naïve patients, and following clinical experts’ opinion (advisory board in June 2024 and consultancy meetings in November 2024) the CS base case population is a slightly more restricted subgroup amongst the ITT population of the SINUS-24/52 trials: **patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP following one or more surgery** . Patients who are surgery-naïve (uncontrolled CRSwNP following SCS-use only) are therefore removed from the base case population. The clinical community supports the idea that recurrence of disease after surgery is an appropriate indicator for disease severity and future recurrence, and therefore this population is particularly relevant to be considered in this submission.[10] 

To cite the original CS, “after consulting with clinicians and people with CRSwNP, the optimal place in therapy for dupilumab is after treatment failure with current standard of care. This includes surgery, which for some people can be a good and lasting option.  However, people with more aggressive disease can experience rapid recurrence and for these patients, revision surgery does not provide long term satisfactory outcomes. Therefore, the 

Clarification questions 59 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 261 -->

base case population focuses on people with uncontrolled disease following one (or more) surgeries. This is a subgroup of the licensed indication”. 

## **b) Please clarify if the data reported under “base case population” and ‘Overall population: Response at Week 52’ is only patients who were in the SINUS-52 trial from the beginning and does not include patients in SINUS24?** 

In the CS and the CEM, response analysis at Week 52 in any subgroup population is only calculated amongst SINUS-52 patients who reached Week 52 (ECM Q2W or dupilumab 300mg Q2W) and does not include patients from SINUS-24, as these patients were not on IMP for 52 weeks. Patients from SINUS-24 are only included in the response analysis at Week 24 (pooled ECM Q2W or pooled dupilumab 300mg Q2W). 

**c) Please clarify why the patient numbers in the ‘Subpopulation: Responders at Week 24 - Response at Week 52’ category are so low as it is unclear from the data available to the EAG the reasons for patients not being included (e.g. discontinuation, lost to follow up?). Considering the long-term Markov model transition probabilities are based solely on these data, the EAG considers the small patient numbers introduce considerable uncertainty, particularly as the probability for moving from the controlled disease to the inadequately controlled disease health state for the ECM only arm is based on only * patients (* nonresponders).** 

The reason for ECM Week 52 responders’ numbers being low is due to the primary response analysis method used to inform the CEM. Indeed, during the SINUS-24/52 trial period, patients who were indicated for surgery for NP or received SCS for any reason were considered as non-responders for time points after using SCS or surgery. For patients who discontinue treatment without using SCS or surgery, data collected during the off-treatment period were used to determine the responder/non-responder status. Missing data at the visit of interest were considered as non-responders. 

Therefore, any patient assessed “non-responder”, according to the chosen response criteria, at one of the assessments of the trials (either Week 24 or Week 52) was included in the “non-responder” subgroup at Week 52. Non-responders at Week 52 include non-responders at Week 24 **OR** non-responder at Week 52. In addition to any patient who required rescue therapy during the 52-weeks treatment period. 

Clarification questions 60 of 231

To the contrary, Week 52 responders needed to be responders throughout the study, according to the defined response criteria, at both assessment points through to Week 52 and not having used any rescue therapy during the 52-weeks treatment period. Week-52 responders only include responders at Week 24 **AND** Week 52. 

This analysis method was chosen because the use of rescue therapy was one of the outcomes of SINUS-24/52, and one of the events assessed in the CEM (need for SCS and/or surgery). It could not be replaced with an “all observed” analysis as this would have introduced a bias in the CEM regarding the rate of rescue therapy per treatment arm.

## **a) Please clarify if the data used in the company’s base case analysis uses the ‘observed response method’ or the ‘primary response method’ and therefore censored patients receiving rescue therapy?** 

The data used in the company’s base case analysis uses the ‘primary response method’. This means that patients receiving rescue therapy (i.e. SCS and/or sinus surgery) during the 24-to-52 weeks treatment period are set as non-responders for all time points after the rescue therapy usage. It is important to note that the model includes both a controlled Health State and a specific post-op-controlled Health State. This implies that the controlled HS should only include responder patients who didn't undergo surgery and so the primary response method is the most appropriate for analysis. 

## **b) If the base case analysis did censor patients who required rescue therapy and classed them as non-responders, please clarify why this assumption was deemed appropriate, as this differs from the primary outcome of the SINUS 24 and 52 trials?** 

The base-case analysis is based on the ‘primary response method’. Therefore, patients who required rescue therapy (i.e. SCS and/or sinus surgery) were classed as non-responders. This approach differs from the one used in the SINUS trials, where the two primary endpoints (i.e. NPS and NC) were continuous changes from baseline and post-rescue data were imputed using the WOCF method. This choice reflects a more conservative approach, as applying WOCF to binary outcomes could have led to classifying some patients as responders despite having undergone rescue therapy. Furthermore, the model structure includes separate health states for controlled patients who received dupilumab without rescue therapy and those who underwent surgery so the primary response method is the most appropriate for analysis.

## _**Transition probabilities**_ 

**B7. Priority question: The EAG was unable to replicate both the 15.1% for the annual probability of surgery for eligible patients and the 42.8% probability of transitioning from post-op controlled to uncontrolled, based on data in Benson** _**et al.**_ **2023.** 

**a) The CS states that the 42.8% probability of losing control following surgery was based on “...mean time to third surgery for patients having had >2 surgeries during the follow-up period – adjusted to reflect average wait time for surgery in England”. Please clarify if this means that the company applied a separate adjustment for wait times that was not based on the data in Benson et al. 2023. If so, please provide a scenario analysis in which the annual transition probability is based solely on the data from Benson et al. without any additional adjustments.** 

A scenario analysis in which the annual transition probability is based solely on the data from Benson et al. 2022[11] without any additional adjustments has been provided. However, the company would like to clarify that loss of response or control after surgery for CRSwNP is distinct from the revision surgery rate, as patients do not necessarily access further surgery immediately after losing disease control. This is particularly relevant in the UK, where the average wait time for ESS is 2 to 3 years (as stated during the advisory board held in June Clarification questions Page 65 of 231 



<!-- page 267 -->

Internal 

2024 and the following HCP consultancy meetings held in November 2024), delaying surgical intervention even for those with recurrent or uncontrolled disease. Additionally, insights from clinician experts in our advisory board and HCP consultancy meetings indicated that within our base case population, approximately 40% to 50% of patients would lose control quickly after surgery, aligning with the rate used in our analysis. 

In addition, most studies investigating CRSwNP assess patients’ revision or recurrence rates regardless of disease severity, number of previous surgeries, or comorbidities such as asthma, which are known to increase the risk of disease recurrence and loss of response. Therefore, we expect the rate of loss of response post-surgery to be higher in our submission base case than in the general CRSwNP population as, according to the CEM structure in the CS base case, this rate apply to patients who have undergone their second (or more) surgery for CRSwNP (as patients need to have had a prior surgery to enter the CEM and they would have cycle once to the post-op-controlled state before being in a position to be applied that rate). 

Furthermore, the studies referenced below primarily evaluate disease control based on EUFOREA/EPOS guidelines, which, although relevant, are more restrictive than the criteria used in the CEM to assess response. As a result, the 40% rate used should be viewed as a conservative estimate, reinforcing its suitability in determining the expected yearly loss of response within our base case population. This highlights the importance of distinguishing between loss of control and surgical revision rates, as well as the need for optimised medical management in the interim period before further surgical intervention becomes accessible. 

**Additional references:** According to Bachert et al. (2021) “EUFOREA expert board meeting on uncontrolled severe CRSwNP and biologics: Definitions and management”, evaluating the efficacy of sinus surgery for CRSwNP is challenging due to variations in surgical techniques and differing opinions on the extent of surgery required.[12] Procedures range from minimally invasive approaches, such as balloon dilation aimed at opening sinus drainage pathways, to functional ESS focused on removing polyps and diseased mucosal tissue.[12] While experts agree that ESS should involve opening the ostiomeatal complex and addressing the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, some advocate for more extensive procedures, including creating large openings to all sinuses (e.g., modified Lothrop) or complete removal of sinus mucosa (reboot surgery).[12] This variability, coupled with differences in surgical quality, contributes to the low level of evidence regarding ESS efficacy. Most available data are retrospective or from limited prospective cohort studies with standardised approaches, often centred around single surgeons or institutions, limiting generalisability. For instance, the UK National Sinonasal Audit reported a 21% surgical Clarification questions Page 66 of 231 



<!-- page 268 -->

Internal 

revision rate over five years, while a meta-analysis by Loftus et al. found a revision rate of less than 20% in CRSwNP patients over an average follow-up of 7.4 years, with variations across regions and comorbidities. Given the challenges in conducting high-quality, prospective, multicentre randomised trials on sinus surgery efficacy, international registries may offer valuable real-life evidence. Post-operative management is crucial, as surgery often debulks polyps but does not prevent recurrence. 

Despite postoperative medical therapy, such as topical corticosteroids, recurrence rates remain high; a multicentre prospective cohort study, from DeConde et al. (2017), investigated the recurrence rates of nasal polyposis following ESS in patients with CRSwNP of 244 ESS patients reported a **38% polyp recurrence within 12 months** . These findings highlight the need for improved management strategies for nasal polyposis.[13] The study enrolled 363 CRSwNP patients who underwent ESS involving polypectomy.[13] Postoperative endoscopic evaluations were conducted on 244 participants (67%) over an average followup period of approximately 14.3 months.[13] The findings revealed that surgery combined with post-operative medical management significantly improved endoscopic scores at 6 months (p<0.001).[13] However, nasal polyposis recurred in 35% of patients at 6 months (68/197), 38% at 12 months (48/125), and 40% at 18 months (52/129).[13] Multivariate analysis identified prior ESS (odds ratio [OR]: 2.6; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.5-4.6; p=0.001) and greater preoperative polyposis severity (OR: 1.4; 95% CI: 1.1-1.8; p=0.016) as significant risk factors for recurrence.[13] These results underscore the commonality of polyp recurrence post-ESS and highlight the need for improved surgical and medical management strategies to enhance long-term outcomes. 

The study " Comparison of Long-Term Postoperative Outcomes of the Subtypes of Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps" analysed 202 patients undergoing endoscopic sinus surgery for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP).[14] The study compared eosinophilic (ECRSwNP) and non-eosinophilic (NECRSwNP) subtypes, evaluating preoperative clinical characteristics, blood eosinophil and IgE levels, and quality of life using the Sino-Nasal Outcome Test (SNOT-22).[14] Disease control was assessed according to the EUFOREA/EPOS 2020 guidelines.[14] One year after surgery, 23.4% of patients had uncontrolled disease, with a significantly higher rate in the eosinophilic group (39.5%) compared to the non-eosinophilic group (20.3%) (p = 0.035).[14] As dupilumab targets type 2 inflammation (eosinophilic type), this further reinforces the rate of approximately 40% of patients losing control according to the EPOS guidelines, 1 year after undergoing sinus surgery.[14]

For those undergoing revision surgery (second surgery or greater), the subsequent revision rate was 26.4% (p < 0.0001).[16] This suggests that patients requiring repeat revision surgeries are at a significantly higher risk of needing further surgical interventions.[16] Additionally, the study identified asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), and allergy as key risk factors associated with increased revision rates.[16]
