Since the CS and CEM base case population includes patients with at least one prior surgery and given that patients cycle through the ‘post-op controlled’ health state (HS) at least once before being in the position to be losing response and requiring another intervention, we identified that patients with at least two surgeries (N = 722) were relevant to calculate our transition probabilities. Specifically, patients with three or more surgeries (N = 122) would allow us to identify patients who already cycled once through the ‘post-op controlled’ HS and back. 

**==> picture [452 x 311] intentionally omitted <==**

We considered the mean time between the second and third surgery amongst these patients (875 days) and adjusted for the average 2-year wait time for surgery in the UK (two cycles of 365.25 days). This adjustment accounts for patients who became uncontrolled and remained on the surgical waitlist before receiving their next procedure. Additionally, since the cycle length in the CEM is one year, patients would require two cycles (i.e., two years) to transition back to the ‘post-op controlled’ HS following their third surgery. 

Thus, the annual transition probability from ‘post-op controlled’ to ‘uncontrolled’ HS was calculated as follows: 

- 𝑋 = 122 / 722 ÷ (875−(365.25 × 2) / 365.25) = 42.8%. 

Clarification questions 70 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 272 -->

Internal 

This estimate is consistent with previously published data on post-surgical loss of control rates in CRSwNP. DeConde et al. (2017) reported that 40% of patients experienced nasal polyp recurrence within 18 months post-ESS despite medical therapy. These findings also align with insights from our advisory board and HCP consultancy meetings, where experts estimated that 40% of the base case population would lose control quickly, reinforcing the clinical relevance of this assumption in the CEM model. 

Furthermore, the annual surgery rate (15.1%) was also based on patients with ≥2 surgeries during follow-up ion Benson et al. 2023 and was derived by calculating a simple annual probability—specifically, dividing the number of surgeries (52) by the total eligible population (344) after accounting for the average wait time in the UK. 

This denominator (344 patients eligible for revision surgery yearly) was obtained by dividing the 122 observed surgeries by the adjusted mean follow-up period (875 days minus 2-year wait = 145 days, or 0.3963 years), resulting in approximately 308 patients, and then adding 36 additional eligible patients (failed second surgery). 

The numerator (52 surgeries per year) was similarly calculated by dividing the 122 surgeries by the original mean follow-up duration (875 days, or approximately 2.3956 years; _Y_ = 122 / (875 / 365.25) = 52). Dividing this annualised event number by the total eligible population results in a simple annual probability of 15.1% included in the CEM. 

- _X2_ = 52 / 344 = 15.1% 

Conversely, using the log-based hazard approach, the calculation involves converting the observed probability (122/722 = 16.9%) into an instantaneous annual event rate by applying the formula: annual rate = -ln(1−probability)/mean time, yielding a slightly higher annual hazard rate of 16.5%.

- 15.1% * (1 – 23.7%) = 11.5%. 

Therefore, the annual transition probability to ‘post-op controlled’ is aligned between the CEM and the CS, and based on these two inputs (annual surgery rate and percentage of patients ineligible for surgery) which can both be varied in sensitivity analyses.

## **a) Please clarify if any ‘responder’ status analysis can be undertaken using the AROMA study to inform a more plausible scenario analysis and implement this in the model.** 

As NPS was not collected in the AROMA phase 4 registry[18] , we have carried out a responder analysis based on SNOT-22 alone (cfb >8.9; Table 15). This has been included in the CEM. [Worksheet ‘Clinical’; Cells AC43 to AD46] 

The calculation of discontinuation rates, including non-response and dropouts from AROMA, was conducted in three steps: 

- 1) First, the response rate among responders at previous visits was calculated at each visit. The analysis was performed in both the base case population and the ITT population. Since the objective was to best inform the model beyond SINUS trials and given the number of observations between month 12 and 30, the ITT population was used for the subsequent calculations. Moreover, the differences between the two populations appeared negligible. 

- 2) Then, non-response rates were calculated, and an exponential trendline was applied to the data. The resulting equation was then used to generate the discontinuation rates over three months during the first 5 years. As a next step, the discontinuation rates were annualized, considering the decrease in the size of the responder cohort every three months over the course of a year. 

- 3) Finally, the dropout rate was added to the discontinuation rates based on response.

demonstrated significant clinical improvements at most follow-up time points, with dupilumab showing particularly strong effects. The efficacy of biologics in real-world settings was found to be greater than that reported in phase 3 randomised controlled trials, and all biologics exhibited low discontinuation rates due to adverse events, 

Clarification questions 83 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 285 -->

Internal 

further supporting their sustained efficacy and favourable safety profiles. Collectively, these studies provide strong evidence that dupilumab and other biologics maintain their clinical benefits over extended treatment periods, with no signs of waning efficacy. 

Finally, in the study titled "The use of biologics in patients suffering from chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps—a 4-year real-life observation,"[24] Frankenberger et al. conducted a retrospective analysis of 191 patients with CRSwNP treated with biologics such as dupilumab, mepolizumab, or omalizumab over a period of up to four years. The study reported significant symptom improvements with few side effects, and no loss of efficacy or tolerability was noted during the 4-year period (“After four years of therapy, there was no evidence of symptom control deterioration following an initial good response or increased side effects after good tolerability.”). Patients reported high satisfaction compared to previous therapies, with overall improved quality of life. Notably, the need for revision surgery or oral steroid use during biologic therapy was rare. Some patients were able to prolong injection intervals or discontinue steroid nasal sprays. Biologic switching occurred infrequently due to side effects or inadequate response and was generally well tolerated. Many patients reported additional positive effects, such as improvements in asthma or allergy symptoms and reduced medication intake. These findings confirm the potency and tolerability of biologics for CRSwNP treatment, with sustained efficacy over four years (Frankenberger et al., 2024). 

Collectively, these studies provide strong evidence that dupilumab and other biologics maintain their clinical benefits over long-term treatment periods, with no signs of waning efficacy and reduced need for additional medical or surgical interventions.

## _**Mortality**_ 

**B13.  The company submission states that “...there is an increased risk of mortality with severe asthma and so a relative risk of increased mortality due to comorbid asthma is applied in the base case”. The EAG notes that the increased risk of mortality is applied to all patients with comorbid asthma (59.1%) and not just patients with severe asthma, which the CS reports as 24.4%. Please clarify why this assumption was made in the model.** 

The percentages of asthma patients differ between worksheets ‘Clinical’ and ‘Resource’ as they are referring to different subpopulations and are applied differently in the CEM: 

- In [Worksheet ‘Clinical’; cell J99/ Mortality_UncontrolledAsthma], the relative risk of mortality linked to asthma (any severity) versus general population is applied to all 

- Clarification questions Page 86 of 231 



<!-- page 288 -->

Internal 

asthma patients of the relevant subgroup (picked up in the ‘Baseline Characteristics’ Worksheet). 

- In [Worksheet ‘Resource’; Cell F205/ AsthmaPercentage_ResourceSheet] asthmarelated costs are only applied to severe asthma patients (GINA 4 or 5), to follow the referenced publication (picked up in the ‘Baseline Characteristics’ Worksheet), Willson et al. 2014.[25] 

The mention of “severe” asthma in the citation above was a typing error. The increased mortality calculate in the meta-analysis applies to all asthma patients versus general population, therefore should apply to all comorbid asthma patients in the model. This relative mortality risk has therefore been maintained in the CEM to all patients with comorbid asthma. In addition, further details have been added in the company’s response to question B14. 

B13a. The CS states that 24.4% of patients had comorbid severe asthma at baseline in the pooled population. On worksheet “Resource” it details the calculation used to derive this number ((126+32)/428*0.662 = 24.4%). Please clarify what data each of these numbers represents as the EAG was unable to verify them. In addition, please clarify the exact data used to calculate the proportions of patients with controlled, partially controlled and uncontrolled as it is unclear to the EAG if this is based on the ITT or base-case population. 

In the original CS, a detailed analysis of asthma in each subgroup by asthma severity level was not yet available. Therefore, the company had calculated the percentage of severe asthma patients (126 patients GINA 4 and 32 patients GINA 5) amongst the asthma population only (428 patients with comorbid asthma) and applied this factor to the asthma population of the base case. This value was hard-coded in the original CEM. The company has taken the opportunity to update baseline characteristics of all subgroups to include both asthma and severe asthma numbers from the relevant post-hoc analysis reports of SINUS24/52, now available in [Worksheet ‘Baseline Characteristics Data’; Lines 75-86]. 

B13b. The CS regularly refers to the source of data as “Sanofi data on file, 2019b (pooled trial data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52).”. Please provide any relevant documentation or reports that correspond with this source. 

All data used in the CEM and referred to “Sanofi data on file, 2019b (pooled trial data from SINUS-24 and SINUS-52)” is based on post-hoc analysis of the pooled SINUS-24/52 trials, non-published and run by the company global biostatistics team. ## **B14. The meta-analysis used to inform the relative risk for increased mortality for asthma patients was based on four studies, none of which were UK based and none were published recently. Please clarify if any more relevant and more recently published studies were searched for?** 

To comply with the EAG request, we have carried out an updated targeted literature review and selected a more recent meta-analysis by Zhang B et al. (2022),[26] which investigated the association between asthma and all-cause mortality. This study included 18 studies,[26] compared to the 4 studies utilized in Xu et al. (2017). Despite the increased number of studies, the results remained consistent, showing a statistically significant risk of increased all-cause mortality for asthma patients: 1.38 (95% CI: 1.07 – 1.77) in Zhang B et al. (2022)[26] vs. 1.36 (95% CI: 1.01 – 1.83) in Xu et al. (2017).[27] 

Zhang B et al. included a study conducted by Markowe et al. (1987) in England and Wales, which reported a relative risk of 1.64 (95% CI: 1.34 – 2.00). More recent studies, including He et al. (2021), Osvald et al. (2020), and Ng et al. (2020), reported relative risks of 1.38 (95% CI: 1.20 – 1.58), 1.46 (95% CI: 1.33 – 1.60), and 1.02 (95% CI: 0.60 – 1.73), respectively. It is important to note that the relative risk of 1.02 in Ng et al. (2020) was evaluated in childhood asthma, which may not align with the population of interest. To capture the full spectrum of patients with asthma, we recommend using the relative risk of 1.38 (95% CI: 1.07 – 1.77) from the meta-analysis by Zhang B et al. (2022). 

Additionally, data from Alt et al. (2017) indicated a significant difference in mortality risk between patients with CRSwNP versus CRSsNP (HR = 1.39, 95% CI: 1.09 – 1.77), highlighting the higher mortality risk for patients with CRSwNP.[28] 

The relative risk of mortality related to asthma (in comparison to general population mortality) has therefore been updated in the CEM to 1.38 in the CEM, [Worksheet ‘Clinical’; cell J99/ Mortality_UncontrolledAsthma]

**B17. Priority question: The Crump** _**et al**_ **. 2017 dataset used by the company to inform the mapping between SNOT-22 and EQ-5D uses patients exclusively awaiting ESS, therefore it is likely that there are few or no patients who would be categorised as responders. Therefore, please comment on the validity of using the Crump mapping algorithm to accurately quantify responders utility values.** 

As discussed in the CS (Section 3.3.3.3) a search of the HERC database of mapping studies and a targeted literature review which aimed to include any publications with chronic rhinosinusitis with information on mapping algorithms or models for mapping not restricted by intervention was carried out. These searches identified the study by Crump et al. from 2017 as the only published algorithm for mapping SNOT-22 onto EQ5D.[29] 

This study used data from CRS patients at the time they were enrolled onto the Canadian patient registry for elective surgery. However, patients were excluded if their surgery was considered emergent or cancer-related, or if their surgery was scheduled within 2 weeks of being enrolled on the waitlist. 

We recognise that these patients cannot be considered ‘responders’ under the definition used in our modelling and that this is therefore an imperfect dataset with incomplete overlap

There is no histogram of SNOT-22 total score published in the paper by Crump et al. but for illustrative purposes we have simulated this according to the published scores above. ## **What is the company's explanation for why other health-related quality of life studies appear to show higher utilities for patients?** 

In Section 3.3.3.2 of the CS we discussed the poor performance of the EQ-5D instrument in capturing the quality of life of patients with CRSwNP. We noted that EQ-5D is a generic instrument which does not include items specifically related to the key domains of HRQoL impact for these patients in particular for anosmia and sleep. 

In all the studies cited in question B21 the baseline EQ-5D was high (Tashman 2024: 0.820, Wahid: 0.797, Scangas 2017: 0.842 (regardless of asthma) and Scangas 2017a: 0.832 to 0.839) and close to or above EQ-5D population norms. 

The DeCorso study takes its evidence from the SINUS trials. In the CS we highlighted the poor correlation between several disease specific measures and EQ-5D from the pooled SINUS data at baseline. In all cases the correlation coefficients are between 0.3 and -0.3 indicating poor correlation for these objective and subjective measures and providing more evidence for the poor performance of EQ-5D in this disease area. 

The high mental, physical and emotional burden that CRSwNP places on patients cannot be ignored and this came across strongly in the patient testimonies at the SINUS UK roundtable held in January 2025, details of which are provided in Appendix S to the CS. 

The consistently high scores for EQ-5D, approaching population norm or above it, across the literature supports the assertion that EQ-5D cannot robustly capture the burden of CRSwNP (or sufficiently describe changes to that burden). This would very likely be common to any study in CRSwNP that uses this instrument and good reason to ensure disease specific measures are used in clinical trials that can be mapped to utility scores.

## **B23. In section 3.3.3.6 the directly observed EQ-5D used for sensitivity analysis is referenced. Please clarify is this EQ-5D-5L data or is this converted into EQ-5D-3L?** 

All utility values (HUVs) in the CS and the CEM are EQ-5D-3L, based on either: 

- Observed EQ-5D-5L in SINUS-24/52, converted into EQ-5D-3L using a crosswalk method (either Van Hout or Hernandez depending on scenarios). 

- Observed SNOT-22 in SINUS-24/52, mapped into EQ-5D-3L using Crump et al. 2017 models 1 to 3. 

Some titles in the CEM may have been misleading and have been updated appropriately. 

## **B24. What is the justification for using the week 24 response data to inform utility between week 13 and 24 but using an average of week 25-52 to inform utility in week 25-52? Why isn’t the same approach used for both periods?** 

In SINUS-24/52, EQ-5D utility values were collected at baseline, week 24, and week 52. To account for utility changes over time, the approach taken in the analysis was to apply baseline utility values from baseline to week 12, and week 24 utility values from week 13 to 

Clarification questions 99 of 231 

Page 



<!-- page 301 -->

Internal 

24. This method is mathematically equivalent to applying the average utility between baseline and week 24 over the entire 24-week period. Similarly, for the week 25 to 52 period, the average utility from week 25 to 52 was applied by responder status and by treatment arm. This is consistent in the approach (even if the calculation seems different). The key distinction is that this method allows differentiation by response status, which was not assessed before week 24, while ultimately leading to the same overall utility outcomes per treatment arm. 

## **B25. Please provide the justification for dupilumab non-responders who receive surgery having a higher utility than ECM non-responders who receive surgery?** 

Two key studies, Soler et al. (2011)[30] and Remenschneider et al. (2015)[31] , provide evidence of a one-off health utility value (HUV) gain following ESS in patients with CRS, including those with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). Soler et al. (2011) conducted a prospective, multicentre study evaluating SF-6D-derived health utility values in 110 CRS patients undergoing ESS. The study found a significant improvement in health-related quality of life, with a mean SF6D utility gain of +0.051 (0.099), p < 0.001, specifically in the nasal polyposis subgroup. Remenschneider et al. (2015) assessed EQ-5D utility values in 190 patients undergoing ESS for CRS, with preoperative, 3-month, and 12-month follow-up assessments. The study demonstrated a mean HUV increase from 0.81 (0.13) preoperatively to 0.89 (0.12) at 3 months, with stabilisation at 0.88 (0.10) at 1 year, resulting in a one-off utility gain of +0.080. 

Both studies confirm that ESS leads to a one-off quality of life improvement post-surgery, from the utility value before surgery. Therefore, this utility gain has been applied to the utility value of the patient’s health state of origin, reflecting the improvement from the pre-surgical condition. Furthermore, studies cited in questions B above show that response post-surgery is not well maintained, confirming the rationale for a one-off utility gain. As this is applied to the HS or origin of patients in the Markov model, there are four different utility values possible in that HS, all within close range. 

## **B26. Given NPS was not a statistically significant coefficient to include in the QoL regression analysis (as shown in table 41 of the company appendix) and it was not a component of the Crump model, please clarify why it was maintained as a definition for response?** 

The Crump et al. 2017[29] mapping exercise was based on patient-reported outcome data collected by the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority (VCH). This study was designed to understand the health of patients waiting for elective surgery, and prospectively collected Clarification questions Page 100 of 231 



<!-- page 302 -->

Internal 

PROs (including general health, pain, and depression status) on a longitudinal basis from community-dwelling patients waiting, receiving, and recovering from a range of elective surgeries. The NPS score was not collected in the dataset and the Crump mapping algorithm does not include it as a covariate. 

In our regression models (See also Q18 above) NPS did not emerge as a statistically significant covariate and has not been included in the model of choice.  However, our basecase response criterion is defined as improvement (reduction) from baseline ≥ 8.9 in SNOT22 and improvement from baseline ≥ 1 point in NPS. 

Whilst the NPS score does not feature in the calculation of utility it does not mean it is not a useful instrument for the assessment of response by clinicians. This was clear in the opinions of the experts we consulted at an advisory board who emphasised a combined approach resonates with clinical practice which seeks to determine the impact of treatment on patients’ quality of life and objectively assess nasal polyp size.

## **Single Technology Appraisal** 

## **Dupilumab for treating severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480]** 

## **Patient Organisation Submission** 

Thank you for agreeing to give us your organisation’s views on this technology and its possible use in the NHS.

## **Case Studies** 

A number of individuals provided us with personal accounts of how CRSwNP affects their daily lives. These case studies provide powerful, first-hand testimony. We spoke with one individual who is currently taking Dupilumab for CRSwNP who provided a case study.  These are included in full in the appendices. 

The combination of the survey, focus groups and individual case studies has helped to ensure that our submission is informed by a diverse range of experiences, highlighting the challenges faced by both patients and their families and reinforcing the need for better access to effective treatments.

_“CRSwNP has significantly impacted my life. Some people eat less due to the loss of enjoyment of food and drink, whilst some turn to more sugary or salty foods as they are still able to detect the basic tastes of sweet and salt.  The loss of enjoyment of eating and drinking affects social lives too, with those affected saying they eat out, or with family/friends, less, or stop altogether.  This in turn has another negative impact on people’s quality of life and mental health. _“Daily life is depressing and lacking colour in so many ways. It turned out there had been a small gas leak for several years which I hadn't identified.”_ **Bunged up, in pain, can’t breathe, can’t sleep** The inflammation in the nose and sinuses caused by CRSwNP causes breathing difficulties and facial pain, which leads to sleeping difficulties and ongoing fatigue as a result. Congestion can also occur in the ears, causing hearing difficulties. _“…I wake up every hour. I’m in constant pain and discomfort. I went through depression because I could no longer taste and smell. I get dizzy spells. I have to blow my nose 24/7. My hearing has reduced and I get ear pain.” “…when I have flare up and the steroids have become ineffective, it effects my hearing, which is by far the worst bit. I have diplacusis and this makes it almost unbearable to be around people and sounds. Even more unbearable when a sound is high pitched, coming from my young children.”_

**The mental health impact of CRSwNP** For those with severe and uncontrolled CRSwNP the quality of life impact is immense. Congestion and breathing difficulties result in poorer sleep and ongoing fatigue, loss of smell removes pleasure from many aspects of life whilst creating safety and hygiene worries, and for those for whom current treatments do not provide lasting relief from symptoms there is little hope for a return to normality. It’s perhaps not surprising, therefore, that many patients tell us the mental health impact of the disease is significant. _“I spent 10 years using SSRIs. I have been suicidal, depressed and emotionally and sexually limited. I’ve found I’m better off not socialising as the lack of any enjoyment has a dispiriting effect on me.” “I am tired all the time as struggle to sleep, feel like I am suffocating worse at night. Don’t enjoy food as can’t breathe when eating. Have no sense of taste or smell. My mental health is suffering. I’ve had enough of feeling like this. I can’t exercise as my asthma is exacerbated by the polyps.”_ **The impact on work and careers** Patients tell us that the condition significantly affects their careers, with some forced to leave jobs in food-related industries or unable to function effectively in roles that require clear communication or physical activity. _“I miss my job as a chef. I rely on memories of tastes and smells to create dishes – I no longer work because I have less sense of taste and no sense of smell.” “I find it very hard at work as I have to concentrate and I find this very difficult due to fatigue and constant blowing of nose…I regularly have sinus pain and often have to take time off_ ” **The impact on loved ones** It’s not only patients themselves whose quality of life is affected, but those around them too. Our survey results and conversations with patients have highlighted the knock-on impact on their partners and family members. _"It has an enormous effect on family and my husband in particular. We have taken to sleeping in separate rooms due to the volume of my snoring. This affects our relationship on lots of levels." "My partner has to deal with me being miserable and tired all the time. As a father, my child is growing up seeing the worst side of me.”_ We also heard from someone who is a carer for her sick husband who talked about how much more difficult this was made by her CRSwNP:

_I had to look after my daughter who had a terminal illness to a few years ago. Regardless what this condition has done to me I had to take care of her and now my husband. I'm currently signed off sick from work to do this as I couldn't manage work with my condition as well as look after my husband. Something had to give. Being a carer is hard enough without dealing with this condition on top of._ The comments provided here provide a snapshot of a condition that has a significant, deep and chronic impact on every aspect of people’s lives: family, work, social, pleasure, physical activity, mental health, safety.  Sleep deprivation, coupled with the relentless cycle of surgeries, medications, and symptom relapses, leaves sufferers feeling hopeless and exhausted. Many express frustration with the lack of effective treatments and the dismissive attitude of healthcare providers, leading to a sense of abandonment and despair. Another challenge for patients is that the impact of their condition is not well-captured by NICE’s preferred tool for assessing health-related quality of life, the EQ-5D. In our survey and focus group meetings we showed patients the EQ-5D and asked them whether they felt the EQ-5D adequately captures the impact that CRSwNP has on their quality of life.  Of those who answered the question: 61% said no 39% said yes The views provided by our survey respondents suggest that the EQ-5D does not adequately capture the reality of living with Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP). Many respondents express frustration that the questions are too general, focusing primarily on mobility and self-care, which are not the primary challenges faced by those with CRSwNP. Key issues raised include: **Lack of focus on smell and taste loss** : The form completely ignores smell loss and its profound impact on eating, drinking, safety and emotional well-being. **Failure to address mental health and emotional toll:** While anxiety and depression are mentioned, patients feel the grief, frustration, and social isolation caused by CRSwNP are not properly acknowledged. **Not enough consideration for daily challenges:** The impact on sleep, breathing difficulties, chronic congestion, personal hygiene concerns, and exhaustion is not covered in the assessment. **Too rigid and inflexible** : The tick-box format doesn’t allow for nuance, leaving patients unable to fully explain their struggles. **Not designed for CRSwNP** : Many feel the EQ-5D is more suited for mobility-related conditions and completely overlooks the myriad burdens of living with CRSwNP. 

Patient organisation submission Fifth Sense

Yet there are other Patient Reported Outcome Measures in use that do capture more of the nuances of CRSwNP.  The SNOT-22 was developed in 2006 and is now widely used as a robust means of capturing health-related quality of life of CRS (with and without nasal polyps). It covers symptom severity, the social and emotional impact, productivity, and sleep consequences of the disease. 

Considering patients’ views of the EQ-5D, as per our survey, the widespread use of the SNOT-22 in clinical trials (including in many of the trials for Dupixent/Dupilmuab) and its ability to capture a much more nuanced picture of the quality of life impact of CRSwNP, we request that NICE considers using data captured by SNOT-22 as a more detailed and accurate measure for assessing health-related quality of life in addition to the EQ-5D in health technology assessments of drugs to treat CRSwNP. 

As a final point in relation to the impact of CRSwNP, it is worth noting that just because mortality isn’t a factor in a disease doesn’t mean the quality of life impact of it is any less severe, especially if no relief can be found.  More than one respondent to our survey made reference to suicidal thoughts: 

_“I have seriously thought about suicide more than once, as I never get a day off from this illness.”_

_“My GP was not very understanding of my condition. And was not very sympathetic. My first ENT surgeon was also not very sympathetic and was very blunt in telling me I would never regain my sense of smell. I don’t feel there is much empathy form the medical profession towards sufferers of this condition.  I didn’t have better treatment with my second Consultant and I felt the second operation went well however I do feel that after care was not great. Advice on how to manage my condition and knowledge about Samters Triad was almost non-existent.”_ People also talked about long wait times and lack of follow-up.  Several respondents describe waiting years for an ENT appointment or surgery, with little to no follow-up care afterward. _“GP has referred me urgently to consultant but there is a 52 week waiting list. Previous operation was awful but helped for about 2 years. There seems to be nothing else I can do.” “The surgery has always been effective for a matter of weeks but then I lose my smell and taste again. Consultants never really follow up for any length of time.”_ Many people talked about being prescribed ineffective treatments (sometimes repeatedly) by GPs, or occasional prescriptions of oral steroids which do have a positive effect as long as they are taken, with symptoms returning once they are stopped. _“The sinus surgery is only effective to get rid of polyps it does not stop them growing back it does not stop the nasal drip or asthma you still get. There is no support once surgery done. Steroids and nasal sprays are prescribed but do not stop the polyps coming back.” "The only thing that has ever given me relief is prednisolone, but my GP refuses to prescribe it. I have to beg for a short course, even when I am desperate."_ Many respondents experience significant side effects from some CRSwNP treatments, particularly long-term steroid use and repeated surgeries. Oral corticosteroids (e.g. Prednisolone) provide temporary relief but come with serious health risks such as osteoporosis, weight gain, diabetes, mood swings, and digestive issues. Some feel trapped in a cycle of steroid dependency, as symptoms return once medication is stopped. Nasal sprays and rinses offer only partial relief, and some worry about their long-term effects on nasal health. Surgery can remove polyps, but they often regrow within months or years, leading to multiple procedures and complications like scar tissue, breathing difficulties, and hearing issues.

Currently we have nowhere to go but ongoing surgeries and steroid use.”_ The removal of the negative impact on long-term health associated with regular steroid use was an important factor for many of our survey participants: _“I think that using it could be a better/safer alternative to long term steroid use.” “At the moment, I am taking antihistamines, sprays for the sinuses, an inhaler, and decongestant drops when my sinuses are really blocked, which can't be good for me. But you just have to try and find something that helps alleviate the symptoms. It would be amazing to have an injection and not worry about all these pills and hopefully get some smell and taste back, even if it's only a little.”_ An important point to mention that was raised with us by clinicians and the patient who is taking Dupilumab for CRSwNP is that not all patients need to be given the dosage as per the licence in order to have respite from symptoms. _“Under the guidance of the consultant, I now do the injections every four weeks, and I’m hoping to increase it to every six weeks.”_ Finally, one participant in our survey neatly summarised the potential benefit of Dupilumab in the context of the myriad quality of life impacts of CRSwNP: _“To let me get on with my life like a normal person.”_

|**10. What do patients or carers**<br>**think are the disadvantages of**<br>**the technology?**|The person we spoke with who is taking Dupilumab for CRSwNP was unequivocal:<br>_“There are no disadvantages to taking this medication—only advantages.”_<br>Amongst our survey respondents, the main perceived disadvantages of Dupilumab are the potential side-effects, with some<br>people mentioning that they would not like having to inject themselves with the drug.<br>_“I am a bit worried about side effects including eye problems and self-injection sights/infection. I would not want to lose my_<br>_eyesight on top of everything else!!”_<br>_“Due to the asthma, I would be slightly more concerned about allergic reactions, plus I'm not keen on injections. ## **Equality** 

|**12. Are there any potential**<br>**equality issues that should be**<br>**taken into account when**<br>**considering this condition**<br>**and the technology?**|Patients with severe, uncontrolled CRSwNP face an inequality that we wish to raise as part of this appraisal.  Dupilumab<br>was approved to treat people with severe asthma with type 2 inflammation by NICE in December 2021. Moderate to severe<br>asthma is a co-morbidity of CRSwNP.  At present, those patients with CRSwNP who have severe asthma with type 2<br>inflammation and meet the criteria set out by NICE are able to be prescribed Dupilumab, which should then treat both<br>conditions. But patients with severe uncontrolled CRSwNP alone, or who have co-current mild to moderate asthma that<br>don’t meet the criteria, are unable to be prescribed the drug.<br>In our survey we asked patients living with both conditions how the quality of life impact of severe asthma compares to<br>CRSwNP.  41% of respondents say they have severe asthma with type 2 inflammation in addition to CRSwNP.  Of those:<br>9% said that the symptoms of CRSwNP have**less** **of an impact**on their quality of life compared to the symptoms of asthma<br>43% said that the symptoms of CRSwNP have**an equal** **impact**on their quality of life compared to the symptoms of asthma<br>48% said that the symptoms of CRSwNP have**a greater** **impact**on their quality of life compared to the symptoms of<br>asthma<br>To summarise this in the context of the rest of the responses to our survey:<br>•<br>Patients say that CRSwNP affects every aspect of their life<br>•<br>The majority say that the EQ-5D doesn’t adequately capture the impact on their life.<br>•<br>The majority of those living with both severe CRSwNP and severe asthma with type 2 inflammation feel that the<br>former has an equal or greater impact on their life than the latter, for which Dupilumab is approved|
|---|---|

## **Key messages** 

|**14. In up to 5 bullet points,**<br>**please summarise the key**<br>**messages of your**<br>**submission.**|•<br>CRSwNP can have a significant long-term impact on almost every facet of someone’s life, but this often goes<br>unrecognised by care providers.<br>•<br>The majority of patients we engaged with feel that the EQ-5D does not adequately capture the wide-ranging and<br>nuanced impact of severe CRSwNP. We request that NICE considers using data captured by SNOT-22 as a more<br>detailed and accurate measure for assessing health-related quality of life in addition to the EQ-5D in health technology<br>assessments of drugs to treat CRSwNP.<br>•<br>There is a clear unmet need amongst patients with more severe cases of CRSwNP (especially those for whom sinus<br>surgery does not provide long-term relief from symptoms or is not an option) for an effective, lasting treatment that<br>alleviates symptoms, restores quality of life and breaks the ongoing cycle of ineffective treatments, removing the mental<br>and physical health impact associated with these.<br>•<br>We believe there is a health inequality in relation to Dupilumab, where patients with severe CRSwNP who also have<br>severe asthma with type 2 inflammation are able to be prescribed the drug on the basis of their asthma, but patients<br>with severe CRSwNP alone, or less severe asthma, are currently unable to be prescribed it.<br>•<br>We would like to see Dupilumab to be available for NHS patients with more severe cases of CRSwNP for whom current<br>treatments don’t provide effective, lasting relief from symptoms.|
|---|---|

It is widely used to provide a standardised measure of health-related quality of life in clinical trials, economic evaluations and population health surveys. NICE use it as part of their technology appraisals of new medicines. It asks you how your health affects your daily life in five key areas: 

- Mobility (walking around) 

- Self-care (washing and dressing) 

- Usual activities (work, hobbies) 

- Pain/discomfort 

- Anxiety/depression

13. Do you have severe asthma with type 2 inflammation? Symptoms of severe asthma with Type 2 inflammation are similar to those of regular asthma, but they are more severe and persistent. These symptoms may include: 

- Frequent coughing, especially at night 

- Shortness of breath, even during mild activity or at rest 

- Wheezing that persists even with medication 

- Difficulty sleeping or sleep disturbances due to asthma symptoms 



<!-- page 463 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

- Increased use of quick-relief inhalers 

Asthma patients with excessive Type 2 inflammation may have one or more Type 2 inflammatory diseases of varying levels of severity, including Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) and Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), a chronic inflammatory condition that causes asthma, nasal polyps, and a reaction to aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)If you’re unsure whether you have severe asthma with type 2 inflammation, but you have the symptoms as outlined above, then please select ‘yes’.

## Case studies 

Case study 1 

## **Background** 

At 52 years old, I have endured over three decades of living with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP). My symptoms began at 16, and my first surgery was at 23. Since then, I have undergone 10 operations, yet my polyps always grow back within weeks. Despite everything, I have been told that surgery number 11 is inevitable unless I can access an alternative treatment. 

For years, my procedures were performed at my local hospital in the North West, but after my ninth surgery, they refused to operate again due to extensive scar tissue and high surgical risks. I had to travel to London for my tenth surgery, performed by a specialist. This came at a huge financial burden—I had to pay for train travel and two nights in a hotel because the surgery was scheduled early in the morning, and I needed to rest before returning home. The thought of enduring this financial and physical strain for every future surgery is exhausting. 

Repeated surgeries have also left me fearing for the structural integrity of my nose. I have spoken to another patient whose nose collapsed after multiple operations, and I worry I could be next. It feels like I’m playing a game of Jenga with my own face. 

Surgery only ever provides brief relief, and my current medications do little to control my symptoms. Nasal sprays and sinus treatments are ineffective, and even prednisolone—once my lifeline—has lost its effect. I still suffer from chronic migraines, facial pain, sinus pressure, and persistent mucus buildup. 

Despite my long medical history, I still have to beg my GP for prednisolone when my symptoms spiral out of control. Many doctors refuse to prescribe it due to concerns about long-term steroid use, yet they offer no alternative solutions. Instead, I am trapped in a merry-go-round of surgeries, antibiotics, and failed treatments, with no way forward. 



<!-- page 467 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

I have asked about biologic treatments like Dupilumab, but I am always told that it’s too expensive and reserved for patients with severe asthma or eczema. Meanwhile, patients in the USA and parts of Europe are already benefitting from it. I know biologics come with potential side effects, but the long-term effects of repeated steroid use and endless surgeries could be just as damaging—if not worse. I won’t know unless I am given the chance to try it. 

## **The impact on my daily life and relationships** 

My condition has profoundly affected my work, relationships, and quality of life: 

At work, my colleagues have learned to recognise that I always sound like I have a cold. I recently missed a fire alarm triggered by the smell of smoke—a stark reminder of how unsafe this condition can be. 

Hearing loss has become a growing problem. After my ninth surgery, I had grommets fitted in both ears, but my hearing still fluctuates unpredictably. Some days, I wake up unable to hear my colleagues or patients clearly, forcing me to repeatedly ask people to speak up, which is frustrating and embarrassing. 

Socially, my condition isolates me. I rarely go out for meals, even with family, because: 

- I constantly need tissues to clear my nose, which is embarrassing. 

- Food is tasteless, making eating feel like a chore. 

- I can’t smell anything, so I miss out on the simple pleasures of coffee, fresh bread, or even my own perfume. 

Even basic safety concerns add stress to my life. My husband checks all our food to ensure it hasn’t spoiled, because I wouldn’t be able to tell. He worries about what will happen when he isn’t here anymore—how will I know if there’s a gas leak, a fire, or if I’ve eaten something bad? 

## **Balancing my condition with being a full-time carer** 

My condition would be overwhelming enough on its own, but I am also a full-time carer. A few years ago, I looked after my terminally ill daughter, and now I care for my husband, who has stage 4 prostate cancer. 

Even on my worst days, when my sinus pain triggers a migraine, I can’t afford to rest—I have to push through. I was recently signed off work because I could no longer balance my condition with my caring responsibilities. Something had to give, and I had no choice but to prioritise my husband’s needs over my own health. 

Being a carer is already incredibly demanding, but dealing with CRSwNP on top of it is unbearable. The constant exhaustion, hearing loss, and sinus pain make every day a struggle. 



<!-- page 468 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

## **A desperate need for change** 

I urgently need access to alternative treatments like Dupilumab. The current system is failing patients like me, leaving us trapped in a cycle of ineffective surgeries and medications. Biologic treatments could finally stop my polyps from recurring, allowing me to: 

- Break free from the endless cycle of surgeries, steroids, and infections 

- Reduce my daily pain, fatigue, and hearing issues 

- Sleep better and function more easily as a carer 

- Possibly regain even a small amount of smell and taste—which would be lifechanging 

I know that biologic treatments aren’t perfect, but I am desperate to at least be given the chance to try. Until then, I am forced to endure a condition that takes more from me every year, with no real solutions in sight. 

## Case study 2 

## **Background** 

For more than 30 years, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) has affected every aspect of my life. Getting a diagnosis and treatment was a battle— GPs did not take my symptoms seriously until my asthma became severe enough to warrant referrals to an immunologist, ENT, and asthma specialists. 

Since my late twenties, I have undergone functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) every three years on average—that’s over 10 surgeries, yet my polyps always return. On bad days, I could go through an entire box of tissues in a single day. The constant congestion, sleep disruption, and difficulty breathing have left me exhausted, affecting my ability to work and my mental health, leading to depression and hopelessness. 

## **Social and Emotional Impact** 

CRSwNP has made everyday life and socialising incredibly difficult. Going out for meals felt pointless and embarrassing—I couldn’t taste or smell anything and had to constantly blow my nose. I also couldn’t tolerate alcohol, which further limited my ability to join in social activities. 

One of the hardest losses was missing out on the joys of family life. I never got to experience the smell of my babies, and I constantly worried about not being able to detect spoiled food, gas leaks, or smoke—a real safety concern. I lost confidence in my appearance and hygiene, never knowing if I had body odour or bad breath, which forced me to rely on others to tell me—an embarrassing and humiliating experience. 



<!-- page 469 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

I was once a keen musician, but congestion made it impossible to play woodwind instruments or sing in a choir. Even something as simple as speaking on the phone became difficult because my voice sounded perpetually congested, and people struggled to understand me. 

It has an enormous effect on my family, particularly my husband. We have taken to sleeping in separate rooms due to my snoring, which even mouldable earplugs couldn’t block. We tried sleeping top to toe, but eventually, we had to sleep separately, which has affected our relationship in many ways. Socialising has always been difficult—it’s tiring and frustrating constantly explaining why I can’t eat, drink, or enjoy food like everyone else. I also see how sad my family are, which upsets me deeply. 

My children have adapted and are thoughtful when choosing gifts, but wider family members often forget or don’t fully understand my limitations. I frequently have to ask others to check things for me, such as whether food is spoiled, which frustrates both them and me. 

I worry about the long-term effects of steroid use on my immune system and overall health. What am I storing up for my old age? 

## **The reality of NHS treatment for CRSwNP** 

My experience with functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) has evolved over the years. When I first started, the procedures were archaic—nasal packing felt like having tampons shoved up my nostrils, and removal was excruciating, feeling as if my brain was being pulled out. It often resulted in severe nosebleeds. 

Over time, the procedure has improved. Robotic surgery is now used as I have no sinus landmarks left due to repeated operations. Dissolvable gel packing is an improvement, though at first, it was uncomfortable as it ran down the back of my throat. I’m often sick after surgery due to swallowed blood, making the idea of day surgery unrealistic for me. Having undergone 13 surgeries, it is clear that this is not a long-term solution. 

Only prednisolone provides relief, though my GPs are reluctant to prescribe it due to the risks of long-term steroid use. Montelukast tablets, Budesonide nasal rinses, and Symbicort inhalers help manage day-to-day symptoms, but once the polyps start to worsen, I inevitably develop rhinosinusitis, which can last weeks or months. GPs do not always understand the impact of this condition, and sometimes I even develop a bad rash as a reaction. 

My current ENT consultant is excellent, and I was fortunate to be referred to a multidisciplinary team at hospital in the midlands. However, it has taken me years of battling to get this level of care. Their hands are tied when it comes to Dupilumab (Dupixent) due to NICE restrictions. We have discussed it many times, yet I have 



<!-- page 470 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

been told it is cheaper to keep performing surgeries than to prescribe Dupilumab on the NHS. 

## **Why Dupilumab would help me** 

Every time I ask about Dupixent (Dupilumab), I receive the same response: it’s too expensive and only available for asthma and eczema patients. However, my CRSwNP symptoms impact my quality of life more than my asthma does. The NHS has determined that repeated surgeries are cheaper than providing Dupilumab, yet this approach only prolongs my suffering. It could shrink and stop polyps from returning, breaking the cycle of surgery and steroids. It could relieve my migraines, facial pain, mucus buildup, hearing issues, and lack of sleep. It might even allow me to regain some smell and taste, even if only partially—which would be life-changing. 

I’ve read incredible success stories from patients in the USA and Europe who are already using Dupilumab. Yes, I understand that there are potential side effects, such as joint pain. However, the long-term damage from steroid use and repeated surgeries is likely far worse. I also know that injecting myself twice monthly won’t be pleasant, and I wish there were a tablet form. But at this point, I am desperate for anything that might offer lasting relief. 

Currently, there is nowhere to go but ongoing surgeries and steroid use. Dupilumab could be a life-changing treatment for people like me, yet access remains restricted. I, and so many others, deserve the chance to try it—before this disease takes any more away from us. 

## Case study 3 

## **Background** 

Over 60 years ago at the age of 17, I lost my sense of smell due to persistent sinus problems and nasal polyps. This condition had a profound impact on my early life and career. By 18, I had undergone multiple surgeries, including two Pattersons' Ethmoidectomies, leaving me with lasting scars and continued nasal issues. Frequent infections, blocked sinuses, and earaches disrupted my ability to work and socialise. My probation period in the Civil Service was extended due to repeated absences for treatments and recovery. 

I was born and brought up in Dudley in the West Midlands. At 17, when my problems were diagnosed, my ENT specialist advised me to go and live in Switzerland or Austria, alternatively to Torquay or Bournemouth. This was quite a dramatic change to contemplate. However, eventually, after much treatment outlined in my survey form, at 30 my husband got a job in Torquay and we moved. I had to take three years of unpaid leave from the Civil Service and couldn't get a transfer for nearly 



<!-- page 471 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

three years, and when I did, I had to accept one at a lower grade to stay on their books. Six months after we moved, my father decided to take early retirement, and my parents moved as well. 

Unfortunately, it didn't work out very successfully. My husband didn't like his job, and my mother hated Torquay and made herself ill. My parents returned to Dudley, and we ended up both living and working in Gloucestershire, where I still reside. There is a potentially longer, quite unhappy story that followed this move, which I won’t go into, but to summarise—my sinus problems had a monumental impact on my life and the life of my family, socially, emotionally, and financially. 

## **Challenges and impact** 

For over a decade, I had no sense of smell, though I was fortunate not to lose my sense of taste completely. During this period, I underwent multiple polyp removals and experimented with various treatments. The physical symptoms were debilitating, but the social and emotional toll was just as significant. I had to cancel plans frequently, struggled with hearing in professional training settings, and felt selfconscious in personal relationships. The fear of being unaware of dangers like gas leaks or fire added to the daily challenges of living with anosmia. 

In my mid-20s, my husband gave up smoking, and it was some time after (around the time we moved to Torquay) that I realised my general health and sinuses had improved. I attribute some of my better health over the last few decades to not living with or working with anyone who smoked. Some of the worst sinus periods and subsequent polyp removals occurred when I worked in an enclosed office with one or more smokers. I celebrated when smoking was finally banned from public places. 

## **Management and treatment** 

My condition improved in my 30s when I was prescribed a steroid nasal spray, Syntaris. Though it helped maintain my sense of smell, any attempt to stop treatment resulted in a rapid return of symptoms. Over the years, I have undergone further procedures, including Endoscopic Sinus Surgery at 60, but the effectiveness of surgical interventions has been inconsistent. Finding the right medication has been a struggle, with availability issues forcing me to source Syntaris from Italy at significant personal expense. More recently, I have found Nasacourt to be a suitable alternative. 

Despite these treatments, I still experience setbacks, particularly when I catch a cold, which can result in months-long periods of smell loss. Long-term concerns about the effects of steroid use, the need for ongoing sinus care, and hearing difficulties remain an ongoing struggle. 

## **My reflections** 



<!-- page 472 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

Looking back, I feel that some of the surgeries I underwent may have caused more harm than good. The lack of understanding from medical professionals has often left me feeling unsupported, and even now, few doctors take my concerns seriously. My experience has shown me that treatment for smell loss and sinus conditions requires persistence, trial and error, and often personal advocacy. I worry about the long-term effects of continued medication use, but after six decades of managing this condition, I have learned to adapt and seek solutions wherever possible. 

I had just got on with my life and not thought in depth about any of this until the Fifth Sense meeting last year. I could see that most of us have been suffering for years, often decades, with little understanding from the medical profession. It isn’t serious in the same way cancer and many other conditions are, so it doesn’t attract the attention and funding. Although I feel that not a lot can ever be done because of the structure of our sinuses and individuals’ own allergies or sensitivities that we are born with, it is good that an organisation like Fifth Sense has at last come to the fore, raising the profile of the condition and looking at the treatments available. 

## Case study 4 

## **Background** 

I have had CRSwNP for around 15 years -chronic rhinosinusitis and grade 4 polyps. I have been taking steroids for the same amount of time, nasally and occasionally orally. Due to the steroids allowing me to (or the most part) breathe through my nose, I am not having the operation. ENT have said when the drug becomes ineffective, I can have the operation. 

## **Social, emotional and physical impact** 

It is controlling my life and also heavily impacts the life and environment of my close family and friends. This is not a death sentence, but it is negatively life-changing. It not only has stolen any enjoyment of food and smells from me intermittently but when I have flair up and the steroids have become ineffective, it effects my hearing, which is by far the worst bit. I have diplacusis and this makes it almost unbearable to be around people and sounds. Even more unbearable when a sound is high pitched, coming from my young children (4 & 6). If I am having a flair and diplacusis occurs (voices sound like aliens/daleks and everything is out of tune), my life stops. I can’t live like this. Even though I wouldn’t commit suicide, nor feel that way inclined, the thought of it being easier to be dead has crossed my mind. I am a musician for pleasure and the hearing issues ruin any chance of that. All music sounds off key and it just feels like being in a horror film with all the sounds clanging and clashing together. To deal with the diplacusis I put ear plugs in, which then stops a lot of sound, making it dangerous for my children while I am the main carer for them. 



<!-- page 473 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

When I have no smell at all, I fear that I wouldn’t be able to smell gas in our home or check for smells that would alert me to an issue. I also have vertigo from the polyps from time to time and this adds extra fear to looking after my children and living a normal life. All my symptoms create anxiety and stress which then spreads out into my relationship. It is impossible to live normally with this condition. I live in fear of having my steroids becoming ineffective. 

## **Problems with my current treatment** 

I do not want to take the steroids forever. I have just been given an emergency card by the NHS to signal that I am dependant on steroids in case of an emergency. Why is this ok? We all know the side effects of steroids on the body and how the drops and sprays could affect our eyesight. We are potentially going to lose more of our senses using these drugs. This is not ok. 

## **What it would mean to be prescribed Dupilumab** 

It would change my life if this medicine was effective and available. I would be able to not live in fear and enjoy the life pleasures that we all have a right to enjoy. My family would benefit and it would stop the need for potentially multiple surgeries in the future. 

Case study 5 (Dupilumab Patient) 

## **My sinus journey** 

I’m not exactly sure of time frames, but in my early 20s, I suffered terribly with hay fever to the point where I couldn’t go to work as the symptoms were horrendous and debilitating. 

The doctor decided to give me a yearly hay fever injection, and it was like a miracle cure. However, quite a few years later, I started suffering from blocked sinuses (completely different symptoms to hay fever). I lost my taste and smell, started getting headaches, and felt pain in my face. I spent a lot of time over a few years going back and forth to the doctors, which would result in a different nasal spray or a course of steroids. Eventually, I was referred to ENT, and after being seen by the consultant, I was given some more medication. 

I went away only to return a short time later as the medications hadn’t worked for any length of time. At this point, they decided to operate. I waited for an appointment, which was a few months later, and within six weeks of having the operation, I had lost all smell and taste again. A few weeks later, it started again with a blocked nose and all other symptoms returning. Apparently, I had been signed off at the hospital despite telling them my symptoms had returned. So it was back to the doctors again, where more medication was given. This went on for two to three years until I was eventually referred back to the ENT department at the hospital, where I saw a 



<!-- page 474 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

different consultant and nurse. I had several endoscopies, and the polyps I originally had removed had grown back but seemed much bigger this time. The consultant and research nurse were working on a trial at that time, and they asked me if I’d like to be part of it. 

This was one of several trials I took part in. One of the trials I was on cleared my symptoms. I didn’t know at the time, but during the other trials, I was part of the placebo process. After I had completed the trials and been off the medication for a little while, my symptoms returned, and I saw the consultant again. He performed another endoscopy and then decided to operate. This was done within a matter of weeks, and the experience compared to the first operation I had was completely different and much better. My smell and taste returned for a good while before my symptoms started again. It was then that the consultant informed me that because I’d taken part in this particular trial, I was eligible for a medication called Dupilumab, which required a fortnightly injection that I could do at home. 

I’ve been on this for roughly 12 months now (could be longer). I then had another endoscopy in December 2024, and my sinuses were completely clear with no sign of any polyps. Under the guidance of the consultant, I now do the injections every four weeks, and I’m hoping to increase it to every six weeks. 

## **The impact of having no smell or taste** 

Having no smell or taste had a huge impact on my life. If I was going out to eat with friends or family, it didn’t matter what I chose off the menu as I knew I wouldn’t be able to taste it. 

For me, the biggest impact was not having any smell, as there are so many wonderful scents in the world, and I felt I was missing out on them all. In addition to this, I found that I couldn’t consume any alcohol as this made my symptoms even worse than they already were, and it then took days for it to calm down. 

It felt like my symptoms took over my life. I couldn’t enjoy socialising and found myself withdrawing from doing this. On the surface, I tried to stay positive, but I was suffering mentally with it all as I couldn’t see any end to it. On one occasion, I had been poorly, and being sick caused me real anxiety as I couldn’t breathe through my nose, which in turn caused me to panic. This was very scary, and after this event, I was paranoid about being sick again. This played on my mind constantly, especially as my husband worked away, which left me at home on my own. 

## **The transformative effects of dupilumab** 

Since starting with Dupilumab, my symptoms have improved to such an extent that they are no longer present. My sinuses are completely clear, I can breathe through my nostrils normally, I no longer suffer from mental health issues, socialising is no longer a problem, and life is as good as it can be. 



<!-- page 475 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

I cannot stress just how much taking Dupilumab has changed my life in every aspect because CRSwNP is a debilitating condition. In this day and age, with such advancements in medicine, there really shouldn’t be any reason why people suffer from CRSwNP like they do. Dupilumab should be made available for sufferers. The symptoms that come with this condition are life-changing for many people, including myself. If Dupilumab helps people like it has helped me, then it really does need to be made available on the NHS. 

## **My Experience** 

My personal experience of chronic sinus problems has been one I wouldn’t wish on anyone—it affects every part of your life. My sinuses were completely blocked, and even blowing my nose didn’t really help, as the mucus would return as quickly as I could blow it out. Sometimes, even though I was so blocked up, I couldn’t blow anything out, and there was a constant nasal drip down the back of my throat, which made me cough all the time to the point of retching and sometimes being sick. 

I had no smell or taste at all, and when my sinuses were badly blocked, they used to make a whistling noise that colleagues in the office would comment on, which in turn caused me a lot of embarrassment. I had lots of different nasal sprays, but being so blocked up, as soon as I sprayed them, it would just run out as it couldn’t go anywhere else due to the amount of mucus that was there, and I couldn’t get rid of it. Sleeping wasn’t good, as I would wake with a start, not being able to breathe and having to sleep with my mouth open, which wasn’t pleasant. This had a knock-on effect on my husband, as my snoring kept him awake. 

All of this had a huge impact on my life, as at the time, I had a physical job and struggled with the day-to-day tasks that were expected. I also felt that I didn’t want to socialise, partly due to constant tiredness and pain but also due to the symptoms I had that caused embarrassment. 

Now, after being on Dupilumab, I can honestly say it has been the best thing for my sinuses. I can breathe clearly, I have my smell and taste, my hearing isn’t impaired, and I have no facial pain or headaches. There are no disadvantages to taking this medication—only advantages. I have experienced and am still experiencing 100% improvement in all aspects of my life. I fully attribute these improvements to the medication I am taking.

Focus group notes 

## **Summary of conversations from CRSwNP focus** 

## **groups** 

Fifth Sense held two focus groups at the end of 2024 to provide time and space for people with Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. 

## **Focus group 1: 26 November 2024 7pm – 8pm** 

## **Discussion questions:** 

- What are the most significant ways that your CRSwNP impacts on your life?  Think about: What symptoms affect you the most (i.e. loss of smell and taste, breathing difficulties etc)? 

- Do you feel the form adequately captures the impact that CRSwNP has on your lives? 

- Are there any other things you think it should be asking? 

- Do you think there is enough information and support available to help people living with CRSwNP? 

- What more would you like to see? 

- Has your GP been helpful? 

## **Summary of discussions:** 

## Challenges of smell and taste disorders 

- Lack of pleasure from food 

- Smell memories and the emotional connection with friends and loved ones 

- Concerns about personal hygiene 

- Significant effects on mental health and overall well-being 

- More impactful than other health conditions for some individuals, leading to emotional exhaustion 

- Social anxiety due to noticeable symptoms (e.g., sniffing) 

- Disrupted sleep patterns and associated consequences 

- Waking up with a dry mouth 

- Difficulty engaging in physical exercise 

- Challenges with treatment adherence (e.g., requiring specific positions for administration) 

- Variability in treatment effectiveness 



<!-- page 477 -->

**==> picture [63 x 63] intentionally omitted <==**

- Inability to detect dangers (e.g., gas leaks, spoiled food, or signs of illness) 

- Common co-occurrence with asthma 

- Perception that ENT specialists show limited interest 

- Side effects of steroids, such as eye issues detected by opticians 

- Multiple surgeries often with limited long-term success 

## Personal experiences 

- One participant has had no sense of smell for nearly two decades, leading to social withdrawal, lack of interest in food, and feelings of isolation. Regular steroid use has resulted in asthma and skin conditions, while hearing has also been affected. Symptoms are currently managed but persist. 

- Another participant has undergone multiple surgeries with no lasting improvement and experiences severe congestion, hearing difficulties, and sleep disturbances. Steroid side effects include an itchy rash, and mobility is also impacted. 

- A different participant experiences temporary recovery of smell with steroid use, but the effect fades after a few weeks. Due to breathing difficulties, hearing issues, and the lack of long-term solutions, they have discontinued treatment. 

- Another individual experiences intermittent taste and smell function but suffers from chronic congestion, sore throats, headaches, and facial pain. Long-term steroid use has led to weight gain. 

- A participant shared experiences of undergoing a clinical trial, completing regular assessments, and suspecting involvement in a placebo-controlled study. 

## Key themes from group discussion 

- Smell and taste loss is mentally challenging and affects all aspects of life. 

- Social interactions, especially meals, become sources of anxiety. 

- Frustration with frequent comments about appearing to have a cold. 

- Embarrassment about the condition leads to reluctance in discussing it. 

- Persistent anxiety and depression directly linked to the disorder. 

- Prolonged use of steroid sprays raises concerns about glaucoma. 

- Hearing issues, including distortion (diplacusis), muffled sounds, and blocked ear tubes, are common.

- Safety concerns regarding gas, fire, wounds, and food spoilage. 

- Heightened focus on personal hygiene due to an inability to detect body odor. 

- Feeling isolated and left out of social activities. 

- Avoidance of activities like singing or choir participation due to nasal tone and hearing difficulties. 

- Career limitations in fields such as food preparation and fragrance-related work. 

## Poll results 

- All participants reported regular steroid use. 

- Some noted inconsistencies in asthma treatment due to unclear prescribing guidelines. 

## Macro patient discussion 

- The need for a clear care pathway was emphasised. 

- Long waiting lists (up to three years) for specialist consultations were highlighted.

1. Qualitative Insights: In December 2024, Sinus UK carried out two online insights workshops and one 1:1 interview with patients to gain a better understanding of the impact of living with severe CRSwNP. Sinus UK was engaged by Sanofi UK in a paid consultancy for this work. 

- Sinus UK engaged with 7 NHS ENT consultants to support the recruitment of patients, as well as using its own existing patient contacts. 

- 11 patients were recruited who had a confirmed diagnosis of CRSwNP by a healthcare professional, had undergone at least one sinus surgery and whose CRSwNP was ‘uncontrolled’. 

- A mixed methodology was used to gather data consisting of one, semi-structured, 1:1 phone interview and two semi-structured qualitative insights workshops between 20 November and 17 December 2024. 

- The phone interview lasted 1 hour. The 2 workshops were both online, 3 hours in length, with 5 patients at each. The same experienced facilitator conducted all 3 sessions. 

- The data was analysed by one author using inductive thematic analysis. An AI transcript, with 90% accuracy, was produced for each session, the transcript and audio recording were analysed to establish key themes. 

- A report was compiled based on these interviews and workshops and submitted to Sanofi UK as well as being used to inform this submission. 

2. Quantitative Insights: In February 2025, Sinus UK conducted an online survey of UK based patients with severe CRSwNP, with the aim of better understanding patient experiences. 

- The survey was open to UK based patients with a confirmed diagnosis of CRSwNP, who had undergone at least one sinus surgery and were still under the care of an ENT consultant (or waiting for an appointment with an ENT consultant). 

- 51 patients completed the online survey. 

- The survey questions and summary data are submitted as Appendix 1.

## **Living with the condition** 

**6. What is it like to live** Living with severe CRSwNP is not like having a common cold. But unfortunately this is how many patients feel **with the condition? What** their condition is perceived. CRSwNP is a long-term inflammatory condition which, at its worst, leaves patients in **do carers experience** a _“desperate state”_ and feeling like they _“can’t carry on this way”_ . Despite the fact the impact of CRS on a **when caring for someone** patient’s life may be greater than other chronic illnesses such as congestive heart failure, angina and COPD[1] , **with the condition?** Sinus UK feel it is still a greatly underappreciated condition. 

The patients this section primarily focuses on are those who have severe CRSwNP. Individuals, as our submission outlines, who have reached the limits of what modern medicine in the UK can currently offer, but who are forced to live with severely impaired quality of life. The accepted way to measure the impact of CRSwNP on the lives of patients is SNOT22. We feel this provides a truer reflection of the disease impact we describe in this section than the broader instrument used by NICE (EQ-5D). We would like to see SNOT22 used as part of this technology appraisal. **Symptoms** 

The symptoms most commonly reported by patients with severe CRSwNP include: 

|Blocked nose|Poor sleep|Pain(facialpain / headaches)|
|---|---|---|
|Runnynose|Fatigue|Post nasal drip|
|Loss of smell (and taste)|Impaired hearing|Depression|
|Social anxiety|Dizziness / balance issues|Loss of voice / difficultyspeaking|
|Work anxiety|Reducedproductivity|Difficultyeating|
|Mental Health Issues|Recurringsinus infections||
||||



Not every patient will have all of these symptoms, and some may have others not listed here. For some patients, their symptoms are constant, whilst for others their symptoms may come and go, depending on the treatment received.

CRSwNP patients will have a significant amount of this type of mucus. When the nose is blocked with polyps it makes it almost impossible to clear, leaving a permanent sense of fullness. 

This blockage has the following effects: 

- (i) Treatment being rendered ineffective: Nasal sprays are a common treatment for managing CRSwNP, as well as daily rinsing of the sinuses with saline solution. However, when your nose is blocked neither can get up the nasal passages and into the sinuses, potentially making them ineffective as a form of treatment. This has potential implications for the efficacy of these treatments and their capacity to manage symptoms effectively. Which is all the more serious given that when a patient has reached this stage in being blocked, they are most likely at the severe end of CRSwNP and therefore in greater need of treatment. 

“… _because I was that blocked and that bunged up I’d squirt the rinse up my nostril and it’d come straight back out again because it couldn’t go any further”_ (workshop participant) 

- (ii) Panic attacks due to not being able to breathe: 3 patients described in detail how frightening it is to have a blocked nose and the panic it causes them. For 2 of them the panic came at the point at which they were falling asleep. As the body relaxes you instinctively breath through your nose but you are not able to. 

_“I was almost having panic attacks at night because of drifting off to sleep and instinctively trying to breathe through my nose and remembering that I couldn’t”_ (workshop participant) 

2. Runny nose 

Paradoxically, despite having blocked noses, patients report also having a ‘runny nose’. Everyone in our workshops referred to the fact their noses constantly ran with more liquid-like mucus. 

_“the combination of the blocked and yet runny nose makes no logical sense, how can you be blocked and runny at the same time”_ (workshop participant) 

3. Loss of smell (and taste) 

Loss of smell, and the resulting diminished sense of taste, is a symptom that impacts quality of life for most patients. When asked to identify the 3 symptoms which most impact their quality of life, from a list of 15 

Patient organisation submission **Dupilumab for Treating Severe Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyposis [ID6480]**

**==> picture [269 x 49] intentionally omitted <==**

symptoms, loss of smell or taste had the most impact amongst the survey respondents (33 out of 51 respondents said that this was one of the 3 symptoms most impacting their quality of life). 8 of the 11 patients from our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions had no sense of smell for many years – several for over 10 years and one for more than 20 years. 

_“One of your five senses is gone, isn't it? Two if your taste is affected as well”_ (workshop participant) 

Quality of life for patients is severely restricted, not just because of the loss of enjoyment of smelling and tasting food or the pleasure of the scent of flowers, but also from a practical perspective of not knowing when action is needed. Patients are unaware of the signs that smell gives them in daily life, such as needing to change their baby’s nappy, or possible danger, like the smell of smoke or gas. 

Some patients are fortunate to get their sense of smell back after a course of steroids or surgery. Although this is often temporary. With the exception of 1 patient from our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions, they all lost their smell again after a few weeks or months. 

_“I remember when I got mine back after the operation, it was amazing. It was like I was a child again”_ (workshop participant) 

4. Poor Sleep & Fatigue 

The widespread impact of poor sleep on patients living with severe CRSwNP is evident from our research. Factors including a blocked nose and only being able to breathe through the mouth mean that patients struggle to get to sleep and stay asleep. Both poor sleep and fatigue were ranked highly by the survey respondents as impacting their quality of life (15 out of 51 respondents identified poor sleep and 16 out of 51 respondents identified fatigue as one of the 3 symptoms most impacting their quality of life). 

_“I was so exhausted from lack of proper sleep”_ (workshop participant) 

Sleep is crucial to being able to function in daily life. It can be influenced by many factors and what is deemed to be a good night’s sleep differs from person to person. However, it was clear that all the patients we spoke to in our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions had suffered from periods of very poor sleep as a result of their CRSwNP. One patient likened it to _“the first year after you have a baby”._ Another referred to it as _“sleep deprivation”_ . Patients spoke about being _“constantly tired”_ , sleeping separately from their partner and even
