6. Depression & Mental Health Issues 

It is widely understood that many people living with chronic conditions experience mental health problems at some stage. We did not explore this formally in relation to CRSwNP during our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions, yet it was spontaneously mentioned by 2 patients. One patient spoke about how CRSwNP _“…can be a bit depressing because it's relentless. There's no escape from it”._ 

As a result we included a question about the impact of CRSwNP on patients’ mental health within our online survey. 50 out of 51 respondents said that their CRSwNP had an impact on their mental health and for over 75% of respondents this was more than half the time or nearly all of the time. 

7. Hearing Loss, Dizziness & Balance Issues 

As the sinuses are located close to the ear canal, when they become congested it can affect hearing function. This is not an issue which affects all people living with CRSwNP, or at least it is not a symptom which patients highlight as causing the most impact, but hearing issues were mentioned by at least 6 patients during our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions. 

_“My ears are constantly blocked. I work with children. It's hard to hear what they're saying. I'm always saying, pardon”_ (workshop patient) 

As well as a loss of hearing, at least 4 patients at our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions spoke about suffering from dizziness and balance issues due to the impact their blocked noses had on their ears: 

_“I had it for six months and felt dizzy all the time”_ (workshop patient) 

8. Pain 

In our survey, 13 out of 51 respondents listed pain as one of the top three symptoms which had the most impact on their quality of life. Patients describe the pain as facial pain caused by pressure in the sinuses and headaches

We did not specifically raise the question of recurrent sinus infections with patients in our workshops, discussions or survey, however if was mentioned by some patients. The regularity with which some patients need to take antibiotics for sinus infections is clearly a concern.

These symptoms mean a continuation of poor quality of life and an inability to function anywhere close to their ‘normal’. 

**Care** 

Many patients describe a _“convoluted process”_ to getting a diagnosis of CRSwNP, with a long time spent going _“backward and forwards”_ to the GP. In many cases primary care is not very proactive in referring them to secondary care, and nearly half the patients from our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions paid privately to see an ENT consultant as they had _“had enough”_ and needed urgent help. Patients often have a long and difficult journey before they are able to receive more effective treatment from an ENT consultant and can be in a poor state of health by the time they reach the secondary care setting. 

Postcode Lottery: Owing to the great differences across the UK in the availability and quality of ENT services, we observe that some patients are in a worse position than others simply because of where they live. One patient spoke of how she was without any secondary care support as her local ENT service did not currently have an ENT consultant. 

Time to Diagnosis: The amount of time people wait from first experiencing symptoms to being diagnosed with CRSwNP varies. From our online survey we can see that a minority waited less than 12 months (21.57%) whilst the majority waited over 12 months (78.43%), with almost a quarter waiting over 4 years (23.53%). The situation was similar for the patients from our insights workshops and 1:1 discussions. Patients feel frustrated at having to wait so long just for a diagnosis, without the correct care or treatment. 

Time to Surgery: Once patients are diagnosed and under specialist care, they do not appear to encounter such lengthy wait times. The majority of patients do wait over 6 months for their first surgery, but over 45% of survey respondents waited 12 months, and over 30% waited more than 18 months.

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

Nasal polyps are a common chronic condition affecting about 4% of the UK adult population, and a point prevalence of approx. 1% undergoing active care. 

70% may be managed by medical treatment alone; surgery is effective at relieving symptoms but some patients, especially those with asthma and aspirin exacerbated respiratory disease, fail to achieve significant benefit and/or suffer early recurrence requiring multiple revision surgeries 

Surgery carries a small but important risk of major complications and waiting lists are lengthy while oral corticosteroids usually only achieve transient improvements and carry a risk of cumulative harm with repeated use. 

Dupilumab has been shown to achieve significant, sustained improvements in symptoms scores and obviate the need for surgery or oral corticosteroids, with low rates of adevrseevents.. 

This would be lifechanging for the relatively small proportion of patients with severe uncontrolled nasal polyps – while rhe majority should continue to be treated with medical and surgical treatment. This is an opportunity to refine treatment pathways across all aspects of care of nasal polyps and develop specialist centres to ensure improved clinical and cost-effectiveness of treatments offered. 

Thank you for your time.

Despite this I still live in<br>constant fear that my condition will regress again and there is nothing I can do<br>about it. How do your views on these current treatments**<br>**compare to those of other people that you may be**<br>**aware of?**||**a) My Views on Current Treatment**<br>CRSwNP has suffered from a severe lack of treatment innovation for a long time.<br>Once the first line treatment option of different nasal sprays hasn’t worked for you,<br>you are left with two options – Surgery or oral corticosteroids (OCS).<br>**Surgery –**I have had mixed experiences with surgery. From having symptom relief<br>for as little as 3 months, to having symptom relief last about a year before my<br>symptoms fully returned, and for my latest operation I had symptom relief for about<br>2.5 years before they returned. Surgery takes a long time to get booked in, leaving<br>you in a very poor state of health whilst you wait (no one puts themselves forward<br>for surgery when they are in a good state of health, you’re normally at a very low<br>point and then have to wait upwards of 12 months to have it). The operation takes a<br>minimum of two weeks to get over before you can return to work and then 3-6<br>months for your nose to properly calm down and get back to ‘normal’. One<br>operation or two you can understand, but having 4 doesn’t feel a sensible treatment<br>pathway.<br>**OCS –**I have taken so many courses of OCS I couldn’t begin to recall how many,<br>and to be honest, I don’t want to. I know there is lots of evidence of the long-term<br>impact of OCS. But you will take them if you are desperate for some temporary<br>relief from your symptoms. I have probably taken on average 2 courses a year over<br>the 24 years, with a minimum course of 5 days and a maximum of 3 weeks. They<br>are horrible things to take. I feel like I’ve had too much caffeine all the time, really<br>struggle sleeping and am permanently anxious.|

||It is a sad situation that the only options available to me at the severe end of<br>CRSwNP are surgery or steroids. Neither could be described as a ‘new’ innovation<br>in treatment.<br>**b) Other People’s Views on Current Treatment**<br>I’ve found my experience to be echoed by those of other patients.<br>**Surgery –**There is a range of experiences here. Some people hated surgery and<br>the facial pain you’re left with, whereas others seemed to take it more in their stride.<br>However, of the many patients I have spoken to, two themes come out. Firstly, it<br>can take a long time to wait for an op during which people they are at their lowest<br>ebb symptom wise. Secondly, surgery doesn’t work for everyone. If there are disadvantages for patients of current**<br>**NHS treatments for severe chronic rhinosinusitis with**<br>**nasal polyposis (for example, how they are given or**<br>**taken, side effects of treatment, and any others)**<br>**please describe these**|**A) Nasal sprays –**Generally these are convenient to take, albeit people with limited<br>hand mobility or impaired movement may struggle to use them. The issue with<br>sprays is if your nose is really blocked the spray can’t get into your nose and just<br>runs out the nose, making them potentially ineffective for patients with severe<br>CRSwNP.|



## Patient expert statement 

Dupilumab for treating severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis [ID6480] 

7 of 12 



<!-- page 551 -->

**==> picture [268 x 48] intentionally omitted <==**

**B) OCS –** There is a body of evidence that highlights the long-term risks of taking OCS. In my experience some healthcare professionals are very cautious in prescribing them because of these risks. They are also not very pleasant to take causing sleep loss, anxiety and a general sense of ‘being wired’ which can make working and leading a normal life harder. In my experience, with the patients I speak to, OCS only really offer temporary relief from symptoms, as little as a matter of weeks for some people. This seems like an increased risk for limited benefit. **C) Surgery –** No surgery is pleasant and one that clears out the cavities in your face (your sinuses) can be really uncomfortable. For most of the people we speak to it requires at least two weeks off work and can take a number of months for the effects to settle down. Although surgery is effective for some people I have spoken to, it isn’t effective for everyone and is a lot of disruption to simply be back to where you were, with a poor quality of life, within as little as 6 months. I was in a poor state in less than 6 months after my first surgery. The main disadvantage of all of the above treatments is that when they don’t provide long term symptom relief for a patient, they have nowhere else to go. I have experienced this myself, spending many miserable years taking course after course of OCS whilst hoping the next surgery might work better than the last, only to find it didn’t and being left with no other options. It is currently a very short treatment pathway and there is a need for more treatment options to be available on it, for those patients for whom current treatments don’t work.

## **Part 2: Key messages** 

In up to 5 sentences, please summarise the key messages of your statement: 

- CRSwNP has dominated my life for over 24 years. Severely impacting how well I could work, socialise and perform everyday functions. I have suffered periods of very poor sleep, fatigue, facial pain and fullness and have had long stretches without any smell or taste. The impact on my overall mental health as a result of this has been noticeable. 

- Although there is a range of pharmacological treatments available, the only ways of effectively reducing my symptoms and those of other people with severe CRSwNP are corticosteroids and nasal surgery. 

- For severe CRSwNP patients, steroids may only provide a few weeks of relief and surgery a few months. Once steroids and surgery prove to be ineffective long-term solutions, patients have nowhere else to go treatment wise except to enter a recurring cycle of more steroids and more surgery, and simply hope for a different outcome. Whilst enduring very poor quality of life. I have had firsthand experience of this vicious cycle. 

- There is clearly a need for an additional treatment within the pathway for these severe CRSwNP patients to provide them with long-term relief from the debilitating symptoms they are living with day to day. 

- I, along with other patients, welcome the prospect of a new treatment option. Biologics have the potential to be a much-needed treatment to fill the gap where current treatments are not, or are no longer, effective. This could be a long-term solution instead of bouncing between invasive surgery, steroids and multiple courses of antibiotics to achieve even temporary relief. 

Thank you for your time.

## 1 Executive summary 

This summary provides a brief overview of the key issues identified by the External Assessment Group (EAG) as being potentially important for decision making. It also includes the EAG’s preferred assumptions and the resulting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs). 

Section 1.1 provides an overview of the key issues. Section 1.2 provides an overview of key model outcomes and the modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER. Sections 1.3 to 1.6 explain the key issues in more detail. Background information on the condition, technology and evidence and information on non-key issues are in the main EAG report. 

All issues identified represent the EAG’s view, not the opinion of NICE.

## 1.2 Overview of key model outcomes 

NICE technology appraisals compare how much a new technology improves length (overall survival) and quality of life in a quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is the ratio of the extra cost for every QALY gained. 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect QALYs by: 

- Increasing the proportion of patients with controlled CRSwNP; 

- Reducing the rate of surgery 

Overall, the technology is modelled to affect costs by: 

- Higher acquisition costs compared to current standard treatment of established clinical management alone; 

- Reduction in surgery and post-surgery related costs; 

- Lower management costs for CRSwNP. 

The modelling assumptions that have the greatest effect on the ICER are: 

- Method used to estimate health state utility values.

## 1.4 Other key issues: summary of the EAG’s view 

A number of additional issues were identified. These have a less significant impact on results than the key issues identified in Section 1.3 but they still represent areas of uncertainty or required the EAG to make changes to the economic model. 

1. The EAG’s clinical experts highlighted the importance of decisions about dupilumab being made in specialist centres, overseen by a multidisciplinary care team (MDT) who have experience in the treatment of patients with CRSwNP. This does not impact on the evaluation of clinical effectiveness, but following a clarification request, an MDT appointment was incorporated into the economic base case. The EAG notes that any requirements for prescribing to be made in clinical practice will need to be made clear in any NICE recommendation, if committee decides to approve dupilumab – Sections 2.2.1 and 4.2.8; 

2. Two of the subgroups in the NICE final scope (patients who have asthma and patients who have NSAID-ERD) were combined in the CS. The EAG’s clinical experts were uncertain whether there would be a difference in treatment response between these two groups and so the EAG requested the results for each group separately. The company provided the results for patients with NSAID-ERD, but not for those who only had asthma – Section 2.3.5 and 3.3.5; 

3. In line with the primary outcome analysis of the clinical trials, in the company’s economic analysis, patients who required a course of rescue therapy were classed as non-responders. Clinical experts to both the company and EAG noted that they would not necessarily discontinue patients if only one course of oral corticosteroids (OCS) was required during treatment and that timing from treatment initiation would be a factor to consider. While the EAG is unable to comment on the ICER impact, if patients would not be considered nonresponders in clinical practice after requiring one course of rescue therapy, then the results of the model are unlikely to represent clinical practical – Section 4.2.4.1; 

4. No inclusion of mortality or cost benefits due to dupilumab on asthma patients – Section 4.2.6 and 4.2.8;

5. Utility values for post-op controlled disease do not differ between treatment arms, i.e. no prolonged treatment benefit following loss of control – Section 4.2.7.4; 

6. 5% of patients receive assistance with dupilumab administration, provided by a nurse home care visit – Section 4.2.8.5; 

7. Inclusion of two year follow-up costs post-surgery – Section 4.2.8.5.

## 2 Introduction and background 

## 2.1 Introduction 

This report contains the External Assessment Group (EAG)’s critique of the clinical and costeffectiveness evidence submitted for the Single Technology Appraisal (STA) of dupilumab (Dupixent[®] , Sanofi) for the treatment of people with uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis (CRSwNP). The marketing authorisation for dupilumab in this indication is, “as an add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control”.[1, 2] 

## 2.2 Background 

The company submission (CS) provides an overview of CRSwNP, including the causes, prevalence, diagnosis, pathology, and symptom burden (Section 1.2 of the CS). It also provides a description of dupilumab, its mechanism of action, indication, and methods of administration and dosage (Section 1.1 of the CS). Included below is the EAG’s summary of the key background information presented in the CS, supplemented by information provided by the EAG’s clinical experts. 

Chronic rhinosinusitis is predominantly a form of Type 2 inflammatory disease, resulting in symptomatic inflammation of tissues in the paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity, with symptoms that last longer than 12 weeks. For some people, chronic rhinosinusitis occurs alongside nasal polyps (CRSwNP), which are non-cancerous soft tissue growths that develop along the mucosal layer of the sinonasal passages or sinuses. Nasal polyps occur bilaterally for most people and can cause partial or total obstruction of the nasal cavities. CRSwNP can cause a range of symptoms including loss of smell and taste, sinonasal congestion and discharge, impaired breathing, facial pain or pressure, fatigue and sleep disturbance, recurrent respiratory infections, eustachian dysfunction, hearing impairment and post-nasal drip. CRSwNP most commonly occurs in adults between 45 to 60 years, with an estimated prevalence of 4.76 per 100,000 individuals in the UK adult population in 2018.[3] 

Diagnosis of CRSwNP begins when patients present to a GP with symptoms of sinonasal inflammation. The diagnostic criteria commonly used for CRSwNP is based on the 2020 European Position Paper on Rhinosinusitis and Nasal Polyps (EPOS).[4] This includes: 

- Two or more symptoms present for over 12 weeks, one of which must include sinonasal blockage, obstruction, congestion, or nasal discharge. This can also include facial pain or pressure, and reduction or loss of smell; 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 25 



<!-- page 581 -->

And either: 

- Endoscopic signs, such as presence of nasal polyps, mucopurulent discharge from the middle meatus, or oedema or mucosal obstruction primarily in the middle meatus; or 

- CT changes, shown as mucosal changes within the ostiomeatal complex and/or sinuses. 

CRSwNP is a disease with a high symptom burden, with the company reporting that loss of sense of smell and taste is the symptom that has the greatest impact on a patient’s quality of life. This view was supported by the EAG’s clinical experts, although they highlighted that this can also be one of the most difficult symptoms to resolve. Other important symptoms raised in the CS include nasal blockage, post-nasal discharge, thick nasal discharge and poor sleep quality. In addition to the symptoms directly associated with CRSwNP, patients often have comorbidities associated with Type 2 inflammation, including asthma, allergies, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug-exacerbated respiratory disease (NSAID-ERD). The most common comorbidity is asthma, which is estimated to affect 46.9% to 62.3% of patients who have CRSwNP.[5-7] The CS reports that the presence of comorbidities correlates with an increased severity of CRSwNP symptoms, and often results in an increased need for revision surgery.[8] 

The severity of CRSwNP can be determined based on the level of disease control, as defined in the EPOS 2020 paper.[4] It can either be controlled (patients either have no symptoms, or their symptoms do not affect quality of life, in addition to a healthy or almost healthy mucosa and only the need for local medication) or uncontrolled (patients have symptoms of nasal blockage, discharge, facial pain or pressure, reduced sense of smell, sleep disturbance, nasal endoscopy findings and the need for rescue medication). Patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP are referred to an Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) or Rhinology clinic for further treatment. These patients are the focus of this submission. 

## _2.2.1 Current treatment pathway_ 

Current UK management of CRSwNP is based on the EPOS 2020 recommendations.[4] Inhaled nasal corticosteroids (INCS) are recommended throughout the treatment pathway to reduce symptoms, while short-term systemic corticosteroids (SCS) are recommended for treatment of acute exacerbations to reduce polyp size and provide rapid symptom relief. For people who meet the criteria for uncontrolled CRSwNP there are currently three main treatment options: 

- Endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) — involving the removal of polyps, ESS is recommended to alleviate the symptoms of CRSwNP and improve the delivery of INCS; 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 26 



<!-- page 582 -->

- Saline rinses and INCS — these are recommended following ESS to maintain the benefits of surgery; and 

- Short courses of SCS — these are used to treat acute exacerbations both before and after ESS for patients who do not respond to INCS. 

Some patients will continue to experience symptoms despite the above treatment options, and the EPOS 2020 recommendations state that either revision surgery, aspirin desensitisation (for patients with NSAID-ERD) or treatment with a biologic should be considered.[4] The CS highlights limitations to these existing treatment options, such as surgery, which does not target the driver of the disease (Type 2 inflammation), and therefore while it provides temporary symptom relief, it does not guarantee that polyps will not recur. Aspirin desensitisation is only offered in a few UK centres and therefore not currently considered established clinical management (ECM), and while biologics have regulatory approval for CRSwNP in the UK, these are not yet available in the NHS. 

The proposed positioning of dupilumab for people with CRSwNP is after initial surgery, but prior to revision surgery (Figure 1). The company expects that dupilumab will be used alongside INCS, with the aim of reducing inflammation and symptoms, thereby reducing the need for revision surgery and SCS that may otherwise be needed later in the treatment pathway. 

Figure 1. Proposed positioning of dupilumab for patients with uncontrolled CRSwNP (reproduced from Figure 8 in the CS).

PAGE 27

The company’s suggested positioning of dupilumab broadly matches that expected by the EAG’s clinical experts. Some of the clinical experts highlighted subgroups of patients with more severe disease who they thought may benefit from revision surgery prior to dupilumab. One group comprises patients who have initial surgery which is inadequate relative to the severity of disease and could therefore benefit from comprehensive revision surgery. The other group includes patients with very high SNOT-22 scores and high polyp disease burden, such as those with the Samter's triad or NSAID-ERD, and those who are refractory to nasal steroid or oral burst therapy. However, another of the EAG’s clinical experts thought that this second group could still benefit from dupilumab after initial surgery, but prior to revision surgery. Randomisation of the key trials in the CS (SINUS-24 and SINUS-52) was not stratified on the characteristics outlined above, and so it is not possible to determine whether there are any differences in the treatment response for this group, but the EAG considers it an important issue to highlight. However, the EAG’s clinical experts agreed that the positioning in Figure 1 is expected to be appropriate for the majority of patients. 

An additional consideration highlighted by the EAG’s clinical experts is how decisions about prescribing dupilumab will be made. The experts stressed the importance of these decisions being made in specialist centres, overseen by a multidisciplinary care team (MDT) who have experience in the treatment of patients with CRSwNP (additional issue 1 in section 1.4). This was considered preferable to decisions being made by a single clinician, such as a rhinologist, and is similar to the way in which biologics are prescribed for patients with asthma. While this does not impact the interpretation of the results of the clinical analysis, the EAG considers this an important point to highlight, given the importance that the clinical experts placed on this point. Following a clarification request from the EAG, the inclusion of an MDT appointment has also been considered by the company and is incorporated in the base case, which is discussed in more detail in Section 4.2.8. 

## 2.3 Critique of the company’s definition of the decision problem 

The company provided a summary of the final scope issued by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), together with a rationale for any deviations from the decision problem. The CS covers most patients who are indicated in the marketing authorisation for dupilumab and matches the majority of the NICE final scope, with some differences in the population and subgroups. Overall, the EAG considers that the CS appears appropriate and justified. A summary of the final scope issued by NICE, the decision problem addressed in the CS, and the EAG’s critique of this is provided in Table 8. Further detail about the EAG’s critique is provided in Sections 2.3.1 to 2.3.5.

## _2.3.1 Population_ 

The NICE final scope focuses on all people who have previously treated severe CRSwNP, while the marketing authorisation states that dupilumab is indicated as an add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control. The CS states that while the NICE scope includes the relevant population, it does not specifically state that previous treatments should have failed to control the disease. In addition, the company notes that their clinical experts recommended that people should have surgery prior to being prescribed dupilumab, as this is an effective treatment option for some people. One of the company’s clinical experts estimated that less than 10% of patients with CRSwNP would be ineligible for surgery (CS, Appendix R.2). This was supported by the EAG’s clinical experts who indicated that the company’s definition coves most of the population who would be seen in clinical practice in England. As such, the company’s decision to focus on patients who have had previous surgery appears reasonable, and in line with clinical practice. 

The EAG noted that while the company’s proposed positioning of dupilumab focused on only patients who had previous surgery for nasal polyps (NP), the clinical section of the submission was based on the pooled ITT population (including both those who had, and had not, had prior NP surgery) ( **Key issue 1** in section 1.1). Given the company’s case for the prior NP surgery subgroup, and the views of both the company and EAG’s clinical experts that surgery should take place before dupilumab is prescribed, the EAG requested the pooled clinical outcomes from SINUS-24 and SINUS52 solely for the subgroup of patients who had prior NP surgery. The EAG’s assessment of the clinical data for dupilumab is therefore based primarily on this subgroup of the population in the NICE final scope, rather than all patients in the ITT population. 

The inclusion criteria for the key trials in this appraisal (SINUS-24 and SINUS-52) were discussed with the EAG’s clinical experts. Both used the same criteria, including patients with bilateral sinonasal polyposis that persisted despite prior treatment with SCS within the past 2 years; and/or had a medical contraindication/intolerance to SCS; and/or had prior sinonasal surgery for nasal polyps, and had: 

- An endoscopic bilateral NPS ≥5 at Visit 1 (maximum score of 8) with a minimum score of 2 in each nasal cavity; and 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 33 



<!-- page 589 -->

- Ongoing symptoms (for at least 8 weeks before Visit 1) of nasal congestion or obstruction (moderate or severe: score 2 or 3 at Visit 1 and a weekly average severity of >1 at Visit 2), and either loss of smell (partial or total) or rhinorrhoea (anterior or posterior). 

The EAG’s clinical experts thought the inclusion and exclusion criteria accurately reflected the patients they see in clinical practice, and represented those they would expect to be eligible for dupilumab treatment. As discussed above, they also agreed with the restriction of the trial population in the CS to only those who had prior NP surgery, as they considered this to be the group who would gain the most benefit from treatment with dupilumab. 

One potential limitation of the SINUS trials is the limited number of patients from England. Only the SINUS-24 trial included any patients from the UK (19 patients from 6 sites), with 64% of patients in SINUS-24 from the EU, compared to 19% in SINUS-52. This could limit the generalisability of the results if patient characteristics or clinical practice differ considerably between the countries included in the trial and those in the NHS. However, the EAG’s clinical experts considered the populations in both trials to be generalisable to the patient population that would be eligible for dupilumab in England. They noted that there may be some differences in practice, such as earlier surgery offered in the USA. However, they did not expect the differences in practice between countries to be sufficient to affect a patient’s response to dupilumab. As such, the location of the trials does not appear to be a major concern. All other inclusion criteria and baseline characteristics appeared reasonable and so the EAG considers that the submission reflects the patient population in the decision problem. 

## _2.3.2 Intervention_ 

The intervention matches that stated in the NICE final scope. Dupilumab (brand name Dupixent®) has a marketing authorisation for adults as add-on therapy with intranasal corticosteroids for the treatment of adults with severe CRSwNP for whom therapy with systemic corticosteroids and/or surgery do not provide adequate disease control. 

Dupilumab is a recombinant human IgG4 monoclonal antibody that inhibits IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, both of which are drivers of Type 2 inflammatory disease, including CRSwNP. By inhibiting the action of IL-4 and IL-13, dupilumab decreases the mediators of Type 2 inflammation. The recommended dose for dupilumab is 300 mg every other week, administered using a subcutaneous injection via either a pre-filled syringe or pen. Most people can self-administer dupilumab at home, although 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 34 



<!-- page 590 -->

some may need a carer or healthcare worker to administer the injection for them. The EAG’s clinical experts expected that the number of people who would need assistance in delivering dupilumab would be very small. 

The SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials assessed the use of dupilumab over 24 and 52 weeks, respectively, and the EAG’s clinical experts considered this to be an acceptable time over which to assess someone’s response to treatment. They noted that patients would likely remain on treatment beyond 52 weeks if they did show a response, and these longer-term effects are not reflected in the existing evidence base. Given that the dose, method of administration and assessment time points reflect what the clinical experts would expect to see in practice, the intervention used in the trials appears suitable to address the decision problem, although it is important to note the lack of longerterm data ( **Key issue 3** in section 1.1). 

The AROMA trial was discussed in the CS as a source of longer-term data for dupilumab for CRSwNP. This was an observational, open-label, single-arm, real-world registry study, with results currently available up to 24 months. AROMA assessed most of the outcomes that were reported in the SINUS trials, although only the results of one measure (SNOT-22) was reported in the CS. Although AROMA included a relevant intervention, the difference in trial design, with no comparator treatment, meant that it could not be incorporated into the pooled analysis. Other limitations included a lack of restrictions on rescue medication or concomitant medications during the trial, which could affect response to treatment. These limitations, alongside the limited reporting of the outcomes in the CS, limits the ability to assess the effects of dupilumab beyond the 52-week period covered by the SINUS-52 trial. With the lack of effectiveness data beyond 52 weeks, during clarification, the EAG requested a scenario analysis using the AROMA data to explore uncertainty in the long-term treatment effectiveness in the economic model. Although no justification was provided, the company updated their base-case analysis to use the analysis undertaken on AROMA. The EAG notes that no formal matching methods were used to account for differences in the patient population between the AROMA and SINUS studies (see Section 4.2.1 for further details). 

## _2.3.3 Comparators_ 

The comparator matches that in the NICE final scope of established clinical management (ECM) without dupilumab, including surgery. As discussed in Section 2.2.1, ECM for CRSwNP includes the use of INCS throughout the treatment pathway (before and after surgery), and the option of short courses of SCS if people have acute exacerbations. If a patient continues to have uncontrolled 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 35 



<!-- page 591 -->

symptoms following initial INCS, they can also be offered ESS. This is followed by a combination of INCS and saline rinses to maintain the benefits gained from surgery. The EAG’s clinical experts confirmed that the clinical management used in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials reflected clinical practice in England, and the results are therefore considered generalisable to the NHS. 

## _2.3.4 Outcomes_ 

The outcomes in the CS match those in the NICE final scope (see Table 8). Change in nasal congestion (NC) and nasal polyp score (NPS) were the co-primary endpoints in the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. The EAG’s clinical experts confirmed that these outcomes are often used in clinical practice to assess whether a patient is responding to treatment, although it was noted that these measures can be variable. Similar concerns about the variability of these outcomes were also reported by some of the company’s clinical experts (CS, Appendix R.2). In addition, the EAG’s clinical experts noted that while patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are often considered important outcomes when determining the effects of treatments for CRSwNP, NC score is not always considered the most reliable PRO. 

An additional PRO highlighted by the EAG’s clinical experts as commonly used in clinical practice was the 22-item Sinonasal Outcomes Test (SNOT-22), which was a key secondary outcome in the CS and the SINUS trials. SNOT-22 is used to assess a person’s HRQoL based on a range of symptoms associated with CRSwNP. The EAG notes that there appears to be some variation in practice in relation to the preferred measures used to assess response to treatment for people with CRSwNP. As such, all three outcomes (NPS, NC and SNOT-22) should be considered when assessing the effectiveness of dupilumab in this population. 

The NICE final scope also included outcomes relating to sense of smell and sinus opacifications. These were reported by the company as key secondary outcomes, with sense of smell measured using the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT) and the loss of smell test (LoS), and sinus opacification measured using Lund-Mackay Computed Tomography (LMK-CT). The EAG’s clinical experts discussed how loss of sense of smell is one of the most concerning outcomes for patients but noted that the results of the tests can be variable. As many patients never regain their sense of smell, it is not considered one of the main aims of treatment. Sense of smell outcomes are also covered to some degree as part of the SNOT-22 questionnaire. When discussing sinus opacification, the EAG’s clinical experts highlighted that while LMK-CT was once a common measure in clinical practice, it is no longer consistently used and, while it can be useful for guiding decisions on surgery, it is a less useful method of assessing treatment outcomes. LMK-CT outcomes are, 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 36 



<!-- page 592 -->

therefore, potentially less useful for assessing the effectiveness of dupilumab than the NPS, NC and SNOT-22. As such, the focus of the EAG’s assessment of clinical effectiveness is primarily on the coprimary endpoints (NC and NPS) and the outcomes from SNOT-22, rather than those associated with sense of smell or sinus opacifications. 

Of note is the different combination of outcomes used to assess clinical effectiveness compared to those used to define response to treatment in the economic model ( **Key issue 2** in section 1.1). While the clinical trials’ results focused on NPS and NC, the economic model used a response criterion based on a combination of NPS and SNOT-22 scores. This choice of outcomes appears reasonable, based on the feedback from the EAG’s clinical experts (outlined above), but there is a lack of clarity over the decision to use different outcomes for the clinical and economic analyses. For this reason, the EAG requested alternative economic analyses based on NPS alone and SNOT-22 only, to better align the clinical and economic comparisons, and to identify the impact of the alternative measures used in the base case. More information on the outcomes used for the assessment of cost-effectiveness is provided in Section 4.2.4. 

## _2.3.5 Subgroups_ 

Two of the subgroups stated in the NICE final scope (people who are ineligible for surgery and people who are ineligible for SCS) were not included in the CS. As noted in Table 8, the EAG considers the rationale for the exclusion of both subgroups to be reasonable. Given that the company’s proposed positioning of dupilumab and the EAG’s assessment of the clinical evidence focuses on people who had prior NP surgery, no one in this group would meet the criterion to be included in the subgroup of people who are ineligible for surgery. 

The EAG’s clinical experts discussed how very few patients would be ineligible for SCS, and this was reflected by the small number of patients who met the criterion for this subgroup in the SINUS trials (5.25%). The EAG therefore agrees with the company’s statement that there are insufficient data to allow for meaningful subgroup analysis. As this group is rarely seen in clinical practice, the EAG does not consider it a major concern that this subgroup could not be included in the analysis. 

The company combined two of the subgroups from the NICE final scope (people who have asthma and people who have NSAID-ERD). The EAG’s clinical experts discussed how people in both groups tend to have more severe disease than other people with CRSwNP and agreed with the company’s statements that many patients have both comorbid asthma and NSAID-ERD. Additionally, they noted 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 37 



<!-- page 593 -->

that patients who have NSAID-ERD and those who have asthma without NSAID-ERD are often treated in the same way in clinical practice. However, they also noted that patients who have NSAIDERD can have more severe disease than those who only have asthma and they were unsure whether this would affect the magnitude of their response to treatment. The EAG, therefore, requested separate results for the two subgroups in a clarification question, to determine whether there are any differences in treatment response. The company provided results for the NSAID-ERD subgroup but stated that, because the presentation of NSAID-ERD includes asthma, removing NSAID-ERD patients from the asthma only subgroup would introduce bias to the results (additional issue 2 in section 1.4). It is therefore difficult to assess the extent to which treatment response differs between patients who have asthma (without NSAID-ERD) and those who have NSAID-ERD. It is unclear to the EAG why removing NSAID-ERD patients from the asthma subgroup would introduce bias, given that some patients who have asthma do not have NSAID-ERD. However, the company did provide the results for a subgroup who have asthma (including both those who do and do not have NSAID), and so this can be compared against the overall results for patients who had prior NP surgery to provide an indication of any potential differences in response.

## 3 Clinical effectiveness 

## 3.1 Critique of the methods review 

The company conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs), _post-hoc_ analyses or pooled analyses of RCTs that compared the efficacy and safety of dupilumab or other approved and recommended treatments in adults with uncontrolled CRSwNP. 

Methods used for the SLR are summarised in **Error! Not a valid bookmark self-reference.** . The EAG considers the methods used to be appropriate to meet the NICE final scope. The SLR was updated in October 2024, three months prior to the submission, and so is unlikely to have missed any substantial, more recent, evidence.

The SLR identified 15,359 records after deduplication (Figure 1, CS Appendix D). A total of 465 fulltext articles were screened, with 141 publications representing 39 trials, identified as relevant. Of these, 19 assessed biologic treatments, four assessed surgery and 16 assessed other interventions, such as corticosteroids, leukotriene receptor antagonists and corticosteroid implants. 

While 39 trials reported on treatment in the population specified in the decision problem, only three included the intervention relevant to the scope. These were: 

- SINUS-24: Dupilumab vs placebo (ECM) (Phase III RCT); 

- SINUS-52: Dupilumab vs placebo (ECM) (Phase III RCT); 

- Bachert 2016: Dupilumab vs placebo (ECM) (Phase II trial). 

The interventions assessed by the other 36 trials were either not recommended by NICE for the treatment of CRSwNP or did not include the population of interest. Therefore, based on the available evidence, the EAG agrees that the direct evidence between dupilumab and ECM from the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials is the most appropriate method to assess the effectiveness of dupilumab. 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

<!-- page 596 -->

## 3.2 Critique of trials of the technology of interest 

Two RCTs (SINUS-24 [NCT02912468] and SINUS-52 [NCT02898454]), both comparing dupilumab to ECM without dupilumab, were the focus of this submission. Both were Phase III, placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomised multicentre trials. In SINUS-24, participants were randomised to either dupilumab 300 mg delivered subcutaneously once every two weeks (as specified in the marketing authorisation) or placebo over a period of 24 weeks (Figure 2). SINUS-52 was a 52-week trial, with participants randomised to one of three arms; dupilumab 300 mg delivered subcutaneously once every two weeks (as for SINUS-24), dupilumab 300 mg once every two weeks for the first 24 weeks, followed by once every four weeks for the final 24 weeks, or placebo (Figure 3). In both trials, all patients also received standard of care (mometasone furoate nasal spray, 100 µg in each nostril twice per day) throughout the trial period. The EAG notes that both trials included prior surgery as a stratification factor during randomisation, supporting the use of the prior surgery subgroup without the concerns associated with the breaking of randomisation. 

In addition to the treatment period, the SINUS-24 study included a 24-week post-treatment period (weeks 24 to 48), where treatment was withdrawn, and patient responses were monitored. Results of this period are summarised in Section 3.3.4 to inform what may happen to patients who discontinue treatment.

Both studies used the same methods for the imputation of missing data. A hybrid approach was used, with a combination of worst observation carried forward (WOCF) and multiple imputation (MI) methods. The EAG notes that WOCF can be considered a conservative approach to imputation in some situations. However, in other circumstances, such as when an intervention is effective and has few adverse effects, it can make comparisons against placebo appear more favourable. To identify the potential impact of this hybrid approach, the EAG requested further information about the quantity of missing data for each treatment arm. Alternative versions of the results were also requested using no data imputation and using only the MI approach. 

The company provided information on missing data for the ITT population for both trials, and the EAG notes that a considerably higher percentage of patients in the ECM group had missing data, resulting in more missing data being imputed using the WOCF method than in the dupilumab group (Table 10). The use of either no imputation, or MI without the addition of WOCF, resulted in marginally greater changes from baseline for bilateral NPS, NC score and SNOT-22 score in both groups. At 24 weeks, differences between groups were slightly smaller than when the hybrid approach with WOCF was used, suggesting that the WOCF method may have resulted in marginally worse scores for placebo. However, the alternative methods of imputing the missing data appear to have a very limited impact on the results and do not change the interpretation of any of the comparisons between dupilumab and ECM.

The matching trial design, population, interventions, comparators and outcomes meant that the company chose to pool the analysis of the two trials. The EAG’s clinical experts did not expect most of these differences to affect treatment response. This may indicate that the patients in SINUS-52 had more severe disease than those in the SINUS-24 trial, which could lead to a greater relative response to treatment than patients in SINUS-24. Overall, the EAG considers the pooling of results from the two trials to be an acceptable approach for outcome assessment. The pooled baseline characteristics were similar between the dupilumab and ECM arms, both in the ITT population and the prior NP surgery subgroup (Table 4 and Table 71 of company clarification responses). Most of the baseline characteristics in the prior NP surgery subgroup were similar to the full ITT population, with the exception of the percentage of patients with comorbid asthma or comorbid NSAID-ERD, which were slightly higher in the prior NP surgery subgroup (approximately 5% more with asthma and 6% more with NSAID-ERD). However, the percentage with each comorbidity was similar between trial arms in the prior NP surgery group, and

## 3.3 Critique of the clinical effectiveness analysis and interpretation 

Summaries of the individual trial results of SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 are presented in Appendix N of the CS, while the sections below focus on the results of the pooled analysis of the two trials, considering the effectiveness and safety of dupilumab compared to ECM. As outlined in Section 2.3, most of the clinical evidence in the CS is based on the full pooled ITT population of the two SINUS trials, while the company is positioning dupilumab for the subgroup of patients who had prior NP surgery ( **Key issue 1** in section 1.1). The EAG’s critique in the following sections will, therefore, focus on the prior NP surgery subgroup, in line with the company’s proposed positioning of dupilumab, and to ensure consistency between the assessment of the clinical and economic evidence. 

The CS reports the thresholds used to indicate a minimal clinically important difference (MCID) between dupilumab and ECM (Table 13). The company notes that most of the outcomes for CRSwNP are subjective and that the thresholds for patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are not well defined. As such, while SNOT-22 has a clinically validated threshold, all other MCIDs reported by the company are instead based on a _post-hoc_ analysis of the SINUS trials. These values were discussed with the EAG’s clinical experts, who considered them to be similar to those used in clinical practice. One exception was the UPSIT score, which the experts reported to be more variable between patients, and therefore more difficult to confidently assign a threshold for a MCID. The EAG’s clinical experts were not aware of any other validated MCIDs used for the outcomes reported in the trials for patients with CRSwNP. Therefore, with the exception of UPSIT, for which there is some uncertainty, the values presented by the company appear to be reasonable estimates of a clinically meaningful difference between dupilumab and ECM.

## _3.3.1 Primary outcome_ 

## _3.3.1.1 Bilateral NPS and NC score_ 

The co-primary endpoints for both trials were change from baseline in bilateral NPS and NC score at 24 weeks. Dupilumab resulted in improvements in both bilateral NPS and NC score over 24 weeks (Table 14), with the change from baseline for both outcomes exceeding the company’s thresholds for a MCID. While ECM also resulted in improvements in NC score, the change from baseline was smaller than that seen for dupilumab, and did not reach the MCID threshold. No improvements were seen for bilateral NPS with ECM, with an increase of 0.16 points instead reflecting a marginal increase in disease severity. 

Change from baseline for both outcomes was statistically significantly greater with dupilumab than ECM (Table 14), and a clinically meaningful difference was seen between groups for bilateral NPS. The difference between groups for NC score did not exceed the MCID, but was close to the 1-point threshold. As such, it appears that, following 24 weeks of treatment, dupilumab results in greater reductions in both polyp severity and patient-reported symptom severity than treatment with ECM alone.

While SINUS-52 indicates ongoing benefits of dupilumab over ECM for the first year of treatment, there are some limitations which should be considered when interpreting these results. As discussed in Section 3.2, patients in the SINUS-52 trial may have had more severe disease than those in SINUS24. However, as the response reported in the two trials was similar over the first 24 weeks, it may be reasonable to assume that the ongoing benefits seen for the patients in SINUS-52 may also be applicable to those in SINUS-24. Analysis of SINUS-52 was also based on the ITT population, rather than the prior NP surgery subgroup ( **Key issue 3** in section 1.1). However, given the similarities in results for the ITT population and prior surgery subgroup in the pooled analysis, the EAG considers the results likely to be a reasonable surrogate for response in the prior NP surgery group.

## _3.3.2 Secondary outcomes_ 

Key secondary endpoints reported in the CS related to changes in HRQoL (SNOT-22 score), sense of smell (UPSIT score, LoS score), overall symptoms (TSS) and sinus opacification (LMK-CT score) at 24 weeks. Based on feedback from the EAG’s clinical experts, as outlined in Section 2.3.4, the EAG considers the outcomes of the SNOT-22 questionnaire to be the most relevant to clinical practice, and this is therefore considered in the most detail in the section below. 

## _3.3.2.1 SNOT-22_ 

Both dupilumab and ECM resulted in statistically significant reductions in SNOT-22 scores from baseline, indicating improvements in HRQoL (Table 16). At 24 weeks, the mean difference between trial arms was -20.89 (95% CI -24.18 to -17.60), demonstrating that while both treatment options improved HRQoL, there was a statistically significant and clinically meaningful benefit of dupilumab over ECM. 

Initial improvements in HRQoL, as indicated by reduction in SNOT-22 scores, were seen in both groups by week 8 (Figure 8). While scores in the ECM group remained relatively stable from this point onwards, improvements were seen throughout the study period for dupilumab, albeit to a lesser extent than during the initial 8 weeks. These ongoing improvements, alongside those seen for the co-primary endpoints, highlight the benefits of dupilumab over ECM for both clinical outcomes and PROs during the first 24 weeks of treatment.

## _3.3.2.2 Other secondary outcomes_ 

As discussed in Section 2.3.4, the EAG’s clinical experts noted that the other secondary outcomes (LMK-CT, TSS, UPSIT score, LoS score) were less relevant to decision-making in clinical practice. However, the EAG notes that, as for the co-primary endpoints and SNOT-22 scores, dupilumab resulted in a clinically meaningful reduction from baseline for each of these outcomes (Table 18). In contrast, changes from baseline with ECM for each outcome were small, with none reaching the

MCID threshold. As a result, dupilumab resulted in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in each outcome compared to ECM alone (Table 18). ## _3.3.3 Safety_ 

The CS reported information on treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs), serious TEAEs, TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation and TEAEs leading to death (Table 20). The frequency of TEAEs was similar between ECM and dupilumab, suggesting no serious safety concerns. The EAG’s clinical experts stated that the frequencies reported are similar to those they would expect to see in clinical practice. Specific TEAEs that occurred in ≥5% of the patients in either group were also presented, with the frequency of TEAEs consistently lower for dupilumab than ECM (Table 21). 

In response to clarification questions, the company provided information on common serious TEAEs and TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation (Table 21). Very few of these TEAEs occurred in ≥5% of the patients in either group and none occurred more frequently with dupilumab than ECM. As such, there do not appear to be any major safety concerns regarding the use of dupilumab in

## _3.3.4 Post-treatment outcomes_ 

SINUS-24 included a 24-week post-treatment period, from week 24 to 48. Results for the co-primary endpoints were reported in the CS, demonstrating patient’s responses once treatment was stopped. While bilateral NPS remained relatively stable in the ECM group, there was a gradual increase in scores in the dupilumab group, reflecting worsening disease severity (Figure 10). Although scores in the dupilumab group remained lower than those recorded at baseline (LS mean difference -0.66, SE 0.12), the difference at week 48 was no longer clinically meaningful. The LS mean difference compared to ECM at week 48 was -0.80 (95% CI -1.11 to -0.48), also below the threshold for the MCID. 

NC score was relatively stable in the ECM group throughout the post-treatment period. Scores were also relatively stable in the dupilumab group between weeks 24 and 32 before beginning to rise from week 36 onwards (Figure 11), reflecting increasing severity of symptoms. As for bilateral NPS, scores remained lower than baseline, but the LS mean difference (-0.77, SE 0.07), and the difference compared to ECM (-0.26 (95% CI -0.46 to -0.06), were both below the threshold to be considered clinically meaningful.

In response to clarification questions, the company provided the results from the post-treatment period for the other outcomes. SNOT-22 scores showed a similar pattern of decline to NC and NPS, although the LS mean difference compared to ECM was -9.30 (no 95% CI reported), which is greater than the validated MCID. This suggests there were some residual benefits of dupilumab on HRQoL once dupilumab treatment was stopped. Other secondary outcomes (LMK-CT, TSS, UPSIT and LoS) showed a similar decline to the co-primary endpoints, with no clinically meaningful benefits compared to ECM by week 48. 

Result from the post-treatment phase indicate that, while there may be some residual benefits once dupilumab treatment is stopped, these decline over time. Although there may be some ongoing benefits for HRQoL, other outcomes indicate that patients reach a similar severity of disease to those on ECM within 6 months of the end of treatment. However, it should be acknowledged that the post-treatment outcomes reported are for the full ITT population and not the prior surgery subgroup ( **Key issue 1** in section 1.1).

## _3.3.5 Subgroups_ 

As for the main analysis, the EAG’s critique of the subgroup analyses focuses on the results for the prior NP surgery subgroup. As discussed in Section 2.3.5, subgroup analysis was not performed for either the patients who are ineligible for surgery (who are not relevant to the base case population) or those who are ineligible for SCS. However, as outlined in Section 2.3.5, the company provided results for the comorbid asthma and comorbid NSAID-ERD subgroups as part of their response to clarification questions. 

Results were similar between the comorbid asthma and comorbid NSAID-ERD subgroups, with neither group showing any major differences in response to treatment to the overall prior surgery group (Table 22 and Table 23). In both the asthma and NSAID-ERD subgroups, all outcomes demonstrated a clinically meaningful improvement with dupilumab, while for ECM, only SNOT-22 scores in the asthma subgroup met the MCID threshold. Change from baseline at 24 weeks was significantly greater with dupilumab than with ECM, with all outcomes apart from TSS meeting the company’s MCID thresholds. It therefore appears that, while patients who have a comorbidity of asthma or NSAID-ERD may have more severe disease, their response to dupilumab treatment, and its relative benefits over ECM, are similar to the wider patient population who have had prior NP surgery. 

As discussed in Section 2.3.5, no information was provided for the subgroup of patients who have asthma without NSAID-ERD (additional issue 2 in section 1.4). The benefits that this group of patients may experience in comparison to other patients therefore cannot be determined. However, as patients with NSAID-ERD are considered to have more serious disease than those who only have comorbid asthma, and results for this subgroup indicated similar benefits to the wider patient population, it may be assumed that the asthma subgroup would also show a similar response. This appears to be a reasonable assumption, as the EAG’s clinical experts highlighted that both groups tend to be treated in a similar way in clinical practice.

## 3.4 Critique of the indirect comparison 

The company highlighted how there are currently no targeted systemic treatments for patients with previously treated uncontrolled CRSwNP that are recommended by NICE. In addition, none of the comparators identified in the company’s SLR are recommended for current practice in the NHS in England. As a result, the company did not perform any indirect treatment comparisons. The EAG is satisfied with this approach, and with the company’s decision that the direct comparisons between dupilumab and ECM from the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials are the most appropriate against which to assess the clinical effectiveness and safety of dupilumab for CRSwNP. 

## 3.5 Conclusions of the clinical effectiveness section 

The EAG considers that the evidence provided by the company is appropriate to address the decision problem, and any differences between the NICE final scope and the CS are justified (Section 2.3). The SLR was performed using appropriate methods and is likely to have identified the most relevant and current evidence (Section 3.1). 

While the NICE final scope included all people with previously treated severe CRSwNP, the company chose to position dupilumab for patients who had prior NP surgery. This appears to be a reasonable decision, based on feedback from clinical experts for both the company and the EAG, who noted that surgery is an effective treatment option for some patients. However, the company’s assessment of the clinical evidence was based on the ITT population, including both patients who had, and had not had, prior NP surgery. To align the evidence used for the EAG’s clinical and economic evaluation, the company provided evidence for the prior NP surgery subgroup for all outcomes. This was the focus of the EAG’s assessment, although it should be noted that there was limited difference between the results of the overall ITT population and those who had prior NP surgery. 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 61 



<!-- page 617 -->

Two trials (SINUS-24 and SINUS-52) provided direct comparisons between ECM with dupilumab and ECM alone. The EAG considers both trials to be at low risk of bias, and with the identical methods used for each trial, alongside similar baseline characteristics for the two trials, the use of a pooled analysis for all outcomes appears appropriate. None of the comparators identified in the company’s SLR are currently recommended by NICE as treatment for CRSwNP and so no indirect treatment comparisons were performed. The EAG considers this to be a reasonable approach and therefore agrees with the company’s decision to focus on the direct evidence from the pooled analysis of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. 

For the assessment of clinical effectiveness, only one outcome (SNOT-22) had a validated MCID, but the EAG’s clinical experts considered that the MCIDs used for other outcomes appeared reasonable and reflective of clinical practice. Significant improvements were seen with dupilumab for both of the co-primary endpoints of bilateral NPS and NC score, resulting in greater improvements from baseline with dupilumab than with ECM alone (Section 3.3). SNOT-22, which is also considered an important outcome in clinical practice, demonstrated similar benefits with clinically meaningful improvements from baseline in comparison to ECM. Other secondary outcomes (LMK-CT, TSS, UPSIT score, LoS score) also demonstrated the benefits of dupilumab across the 24-week treatment period. When comparing change throughout the treatment period, outcomes with ECM either remained stable or showed an initial improvement during the first 8 weeks, before stabilising. In contrast, dupilumab resulted in gradual improvements in all outcomes throughout the 24-week period. These results indicate the ongoing, and increasing, benefits of dupilumab over ECM for both clinical and patient-reported outcomes in the first 24 weeks of treatment. While the pooled results were only available for the first 24 weeks of treatment, the SINUS-52 trial assessed response up to 52 weeks. Greater differences were seen between dupilumab and ECM at 52 than 24 weeks for bilateral NPS, NC score and SNOT-22 scores, indicating ongoing benefits of dupilumab throughout the first year of treatment. 

One limitation which should be considered when interpreting the results of the SINUS-24 and SINUS52 trials is the lack of long-term data. While dupilumab appears to have benefits over ECM over 52 weeks, the effects beyond this point are unclear. The AROMA trial indicates that the improvements seen in HRQoL may begin to decline between 12 and 24 months, but with no comparator arm in the study, it is unclear whether any benefits over ECM are maintained or also decline. It is also unclear whether this decline is evident for all outcomes, as only SNOT-22 scores were available from the 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 62 



<!-- page 618 -->

AROMA trial. As such, it is currently unclear how long the benefits of dupilumab may last beyond the 52-week period reported by the SINUS trials. 

Patients who tend to have more severe symptoms of CRSwNP were included as subgroups in the CS (Section 3.3.5), including patients with comorbid asthma, comorbid NSAID-ERD, or any comorbid type-2 condition. Results were similar to those of the wider patient population who had prior NP surgery, with all subgroups demonstrating greater improvements with dupilumab than ECM. Most of these differences were considered clinically meaningful, demonstrating consistent benefits of dupilumab over ECM across subgroups. 

Safety outcomes showed little difference between dupilumab and ECM (Section 3.3.3). Few serious TEAEs or TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation were reported, and common TEAEs (those occurring in at least 5% of either treatment arm) were consistently lower for dupilumab. As such, there do not appear to be any major safety concerns associated with the use of dupilumab for people with CRSwNP. 

Effectiveness and safety outcomes were also provided for the post-treatment period of the SINUS-24 trial (weeks 24-48). When treatment was stopped, bilateral NPS and NC remained relatively stable for the ECM group (Section 3.3.4), but gradually increased for the dupilumab group, reflecting increasing disease severity. By the end of the post-treatment period, outcomes remained better for the dupilumab than ECM group, but were not considered clinically meaningful, indicating that any benefits of dupilumab wane once treatment is stopped. 

For patients who have CRSwNP, dupilumab appears to result in reduced disease severity and improvements in patient-reported outcomes in comparison to ECM over the first year of treatment. In addition to clinical benefits, the evidence suggests there are few safety concerns associated with the use of dupilumab in this population. However, it should be noted that while the results of the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials demonstrate an effect of dupilumab up to 52 weeks after the start of treatment, a lack of long-term data means it is currently unclear how long the benefits are sustained beyond this point.

## 4.1 EAG comment on the company’s review of cost effectiveness evidence 

In June 2019, the company conducted a systematic literature review (SLRs) to identify existing evidence on cost-effectiveness, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and resource use and costs for treatments in patients with mild, moderate, and severe: chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps/polyposis. Updated searches were performed in September 2024. A summary of the External Assessment Group’s (EAG’s) critique of the methods implemented by the company to identify relevant evidence is presented in Table 26. 

The company also performed grey literature searches and hand-searching to identify relevant evidence, such as conference abstracts and health technology appraisals (HTAs) published after 2022.

In total (original search and September 2024 update), the SLRs identified 2,048 records (costeffectiveness, HRQoL and resource use studies were all searched for). Following title/ abstract and full text screening, the company included 96 unique reports (six of which were not selected for data extraction); 19 economic evaluations, 55 reports of cost and resource use and 16 were HRQoL studies. 

Of the 19 unique economic evaluations identified 10 were Markov/decision tree models, six were Markov/decision tree with microsimulation components and three took some other novel approach. Seven of the 19 papers used a 1-year cycle length. The company’s model is based on those used for prior submissions related to dupilumab (atopic dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, asthma and COPD), though the structure appears to be in line with prior models for this disease. 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 65 



<!-- page 621 -->

Of the 16 HRQoL studies, only five reported EQ-5D with SF-6D being more commonly used. Notably, these five studies all had relatively high utility scores compared to those used in the company’s model, this is further explored in Section 4.2.7. The paper used by the company, Crump, _et al._ 2017[9] , was excluded for being an “instrument design” study type (as opposed to a study explicitly trying to find HRQoL for health states) though the included paper Kumar _et al._ 2020[10] used the Crump mapping algorithm to derive health states. 

Of the 55 cost studies only four were based in England. Of these Benson _et al._ 2023[11] was used to help inform the cost of surgery in the company model and Wahid _et al._ 2020[12] was used in scenario analysis. 

Overall, the EAG considers the company’s SLR was thorough and comprehensive.

## _4.2.2 Intervention and comparator_ 

As noted in Section 2.3.2, the intervention evaluated in the economic model is dupilumab in combination with established clinical management (ECM). Dupilumab is given at a dose of 300mg subcutaneous injection every two weeks. 

The comparator in the economic model is ECM only. As previously discussed, ECM consists of nasal irrigation saline solutions, intranasal corticosteroids (INCS), systemic corticosteroids (SCS), antibiotics and endoscopic sinonasal surgery (ESS). Although ESS is included in the economic modelling as an event for a specified proportion of patients (see Section 4.2.3 for further details), it is not included as a standalone comparator. 

The company stated that the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials used to inform the effectiveness data for dupilumab in this appraisal were not designed to demonstrate a difference in the usage of INCS. Therefore, costs for INCS were not included in the economic model as they were assumed to be equal. This approach was also taken for nasal irrigation solutions, although the company did not state this explicitly in the submission.

PAGE 67 



<!-- page 623 -->

## _4.2.3 Modelling approach and model structure_ 

The company produced a cohort-level short-term decision tree leading to a Markov state transition model, programmed in Microsoft Excel®, to assess the cost-effectiveness of dupilumab plus ECM for the treatment of uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) following prior surgery. The analysis was carried out from an NHS and Personal Social Services (PSS) perspective. Costs and health effects are discounted at an annual rate of 3.5%, in line with the NICE Reference Case.[14] 

The company’s model structure was based on the published study by De Corsa _et al._ 2022,[15] which was developed by the company to assess the effectiveness of dupilumab for people with uncontrolled CRSwNP from the Italian national health service perspective. Amendments were made to model inputs for the current submission to reflect the specific population of interest. 

## _4.2.3.1 Short-term decision tree_ 

The short-term decision tree reflects the trial period of the longest available study (SINUS-52) of 52weeks. Response to treatment was undertaken at both 24 and 52 weeks in the key clinical trials (SINUS-24 and SINUS-52), which is reflected in the decision tree. Patients receiving dupilumab who are classed as ‘responders’ during the first 24-weeks of the decision tree continue to receive dupilumab, whereas those who do not respond discontinue treatment and receive ECM only. Patients who continued to respond to dupilumab between 24 and 52 weeks continue on dupilumab treatment into the long-term Markov model, whereas those who are no longer classed as responders are assumed to discontinue treatment with dupilumab and receive ECM only, as shown in Figure 12. 

Based on pooled data from both the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials, patients are assigned to one of three health states at the end of the decision tree, based on both the response to treatment during the trial period (either dupilumab + ECM or ECM alone) and surgery status. 

A small proportion of patients in both treatment arms underwent ESS during the key clinical trial periods (see Section 4.2.4). Therefore, the equivalent proportion of patients in each treatment arm receive the costs of surgery during the decision tree period. These patients then enter the long-term Markov model in the ‘post-op controlled’ health state. Patients who did not meet the response criteria at week 52 and did not have surgery enter the Markov model in the ‘inadequately controlled 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 68 



<!-- page 624 -->

disease health state’. Responders to treatment enter the Markov model in the ‘controlled disease’ 

health state.

## _4.2.3.2 Long-term Markov model_ 

The Markov model uses a lifetime time horizon with an annual cycle length and a half-cycle correction is applied. 

As noted above, patients enter the Markov state transition model in one of three health states: controlled disease, inadequately controlled disease or post-op controlled. The Markov model includes an additional health state for uncontrolled disease, which patients can either enter from the inadequately controlled disease health state, if ineligible for revision surgery, or from the postop controlled state, once control via revision surgery is lost, shown in Figure 13. Patients who are ineligible for surgery remain in the uncontrolled disease state until death, whereas patients eligible for revision surgery may undergo a further ESS before returning to uncontrolled once post-op control is lost. The data used to inform the transition probabilities in each cycle are described in further detail in Section 4.2.5. 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 69 



<!-- page 625 -->

The inadequately controlled disease health state is a temporary tunnel state which patients can only remain in for one model cycle (one year). This temporary state is included to capture any decline in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) prior to patients becoming uncontrolled. 

Patients may transition to death from any health state based on general population mortality. 

Figure 13. Diagram of Markov model structure used to estimate the post-trial period, reproduced from Figure 18 of CS

- _4.2.3.3 EAG critique_ 

Overall, the EAG is mainly satisfied that the model structure captures the main features of CRSwNP. Clinical experts to the EAG agreed with the model structure and confirmed that currently surgery is the only option available that would result in a patient moving out of the uncontrolled health state. They noted that although the surgery provides short-term improvement of symptoms, the main aim is to allow standard therapies such as INCS to work effectively, and therefore surgery alone does not provide full control of the disease. 

The EAG notes that a one-year cycle length is not in line with the regularity of dupilumab administration and may not capture the timings of key clinical events. During clarification, the EAG 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

<!-- page 626 -->

asked the company to justify the annual cycle length or adapt to a shorter cycle length. The company stated that the model is in line with the regularity of response assessments that will be undertaken in clinical practice and the initial decision tree captures response at both 24 and 52 weeks. In addition, the company noted that the one-year cycle length is consistent with clinical changes, such as discontinuation and disease progression. While the EAG considers that a shorter cycle length may have added to the accuracy of the economic model, it does not anticipate that this would have a substantial impact on any results. 

## _4.2.4 Treatment effectiveness_ 

The treatment effectiveness of dupilumab was informed by response rates observed in both the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials. In the model base-case, the company measured response using a combination of the objective nasal polyp score (NPS) measure **and** a patient reported outcome measure (PROM) using SNOT-22, using the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) discussed in Section 3.3 . Therefore, response was defined as: 

- NPS change from baseline of ≥1; and 

- SNOT-22 change from baseline of ≥8.9 points. 

The company stated that this criteria for response was tested with clinicians during an advisory board meeting who stated that the combined response criteria is in line with clinical practice. 

The proportion of responders at Week 24 was based on pooled data from the SINUS-24 and SINUS52 trials, resulting in ****% of responders in the ECM only (placebo) arm compared to ****% in the dupilumab arm, shown in Table 28. This was used in the decision tree model to inform responders and non-responders at Week 24 in both treatment arms. Data was only available from SINUS-52 on patients who responded at Week 24 and continued to meet the response criteria at Week 52; this was used to inform the proportion of patients classed as responders at the end of the decision tree and beginning of the long-term Markov model. In the ECM only arm, **% of patients showed a maintained response at Week 52 compared to ****% in the dupilumab arm. 

In the company’s original submission, the 28-week trial data on maintained response rates (week 24 to week 52) was converted to an annual probability to inform the long term probability of remaining in the controlled health state for each treatment arm (****% for the dupilumab + ECM arm versus ****% for the ECM only), and subsequently the annual probability of transitioning to the inadequately controlled health state (***% and ****%, respectively). However, during clarification,
