## _4.2.4.1 EAG critique_ 

As discussed in Section 2.3, the company has positioned dupilumab within the population of patients who have had at least one prior surgery. As this differs to the clinical trial ITT population, it reduced the number of patients available for the base-case analysis. This, in addition to the response criteria requiring patients to meet the MCID in both SNOT-22 and NPS resulted in very small patient numbers available for those who responded at both Week 24 and Week 52. This is particularly evident in the ECM only arm in which there were only * patients available, * of which were classed as responders. The EAG acknowledges that the small patient numbers are a limitation of the data available and that there is large uncertainty associated with this parameter. During clarification, the EAG asked for further detail on the small patient numbers and asked the company to explore the 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 73 



<!-- page 629 -->

impacts of this uncertainty in the model further. The company noted that all patients who required either a course of rescue therapy or surgery during the trial period were also classed as nonresponders. This, in addition to the dual response criteria needing to be met at both 24 and 52 weeks for the responder analysis resulted in low patient numbers available. 

The company’s base case analysis response criteria was chosen based on discussion with clinical experts who stated this would be used in clinical practice. While clinical experts to the EAG agreed with the response criteria used in the model, one noted that they would likely only use SNOT-22 response in clinical practice; i.e. if a patient was showing improvement in SNOT-22 outcomes and stated they felt better but had not met the >1 point change from baseline in NPS, they would not take them off treatment. The EAG notes that in the company clinical expert consultation, one expert also stated that symptom scores such as SNOT-22 are more important due to NPS (and LundMackay) scores being highly variable and unreliable to assess patient outcomes. They also noted that NPS can be less useful as a patient may still have multiple polyps but are more concerned about their loss of sense of smell. 

Therefore, the EAG requested an analysis in the model using only SNOT-22 outcome data to determine patient responder status. In addition, as the responder criteria used in the economic model is based on a _post-hoc_ analysis of the trial data that was not pre-specified, the EAG also requested an analysis in the model using the primary outcome of the clinical trials. The EAG notes that using the SNOT-22 response data improves the small patient numbers available, with the number of patients with response data available in the ECM only arm increasing from * patients in ** ** the base-case analysis to ** and from in the dupilumab arm to , shown below in Table 29. 

While the EAG considers the combined response criteria used in the company’s base case to be acceptable, it is noted that there is uncertainty associated if this is not what would be used in clinical practice and guidance may need to state that this is the criteria to be applied in order for any estimates of cost-effectiveness to accurately reflect the real world ( **Key issue 2** in Section 1.1). The EAG notes that a similar situation occurred with TA534 for atopic dermatitis and the subsequent recommendation specified the combined outcome required for determining an adequate response.[16] As the SNOT-22 only data increases the sample size available for the responder analysis and based on expert opinion from both the EAG’s clinical experts and the company’s, the EAG consider responder analysis based on SNOT-22 only to be a plausible scenario analysis (see Section 6). The EAG note that using SNOT-22 increased the company’s ICER by ≈£4,700.

As noted in Section 4.2.4, during clarification, the company updated the long-term effectiveness of dupilumab (beyond one year) to be based on an analysis of the AROMA data. The EAG has a number of issues with this being included in the base case, detailed below: 

- No formal matching of patients was undertaken, such as propensity score matching, to account for differences in the patient populations between the SINUS-24/52 RCTs and the AROMA observational study. 

- The response analysis of AROMA was based on SNOT-22 only, due to NPS being unavailable. If using responder data based on SNOT-22 to inform dupilumab effectiveness beyond the trial period, the EAG consider it inappropriate to use different criteria to assess response during the trial period in the base case analysis. 

- The company used data from the ITT population in the analysis from the SINUS trials as opposed to the prior surgery population. However, it is noted that the differences are minimal. 

- It is unclear from the company’s presented analysis if patients requiring rescue treatment and/or surgery were also classed as non-responders.

<!-- page 631 -->

- The ECM only arm is still informed by the SINUS trial data, i.e. the * patients classed as nonresponders in the clinical trials. The EAG considers it to be inconsistent to use the two alternative approaches for the different treatment arms. 

While the EAG considers there to be uncertainty with the company’s original base case approach, as previously stated, it does not consider using the analysis the company has undertaken on the AROMA data to reduce uncertainty and is more appropriate to be considered as a scenario analysis. The EAG notes that using the AROMA data analysis to inform the probability of moving to inadequately controlled in the dupilumab arm reduced the company’s ICER by £619. 

As previously noted, the company assumes no decline in the treatment effect of dupilumab over time. A clinical expert to the EAG considered that while they were unable to state how much effectiveness may decline in the long-term, it was likely that some decline in response would occur based on their experience with other biologics. As the longest randomised clinical trial (RCT) was only conducted for 52-weeks (SINUS-52), no RCT data are available to inform the long-term effectiveness of dupilumab for CRSwNP ( **Key issue 3** in Section 1). The EAG considers this to introduce uncertainty in the results of the economic model. In response to clarification (see response to B12), in addition to the analysis of the AROMA dataset mentioned above, the company also provided evidence of the sustained benefits of dupilumab observed in other disease areas (asthma and atopic dermatitis) and of dupilumab and other biologics in CRSwNP. The EAG notes that this is an uncertain feature of the economic model and the EAG does not consider evidence of a sustained effect in other therapy areas to be robust evidence for a sustained effect in CRSwNP. However, the EAG conducted an exploratory scenario of increasing the proportion of patients discontinuing dupilumab for any reason from year 5 onwards in the model to 15.6% 

(**********************% derived from the SINUS trials), to test the sensitivity of the results to a higher discontinuation rate due to lack of efficacy; this increased the company’s ICER by less than £1000. 

In line with the primary outcome analysis of the clinical trials, in the company’s base case analysis, patients who required a course of rescue therapy were classed as non-responders. A clinical expert to the company stated that when considering treatment response, the main criteria should be patients not requiring a course of rescue treatment in addition to symptom improvement. However, a second expert stated that they would not discontinue patients on dupilumab if one course of oral corticosteroids (OCS) was required during treatment. A clinical expert to the EAG suggested that

time from starting on dupilumab and then requiring a course of SCS would be a key factor to consider. For example, they would not consider a patient a non-responder if they only required one course of SCS in the first three months of treatment or two courses in the first six months; however, more courses of SCS in either time or frequency and would make them a non-responder. The EAG notes that if patients would not be considered non-responders in clinical practice after requiring one course of rescue therapy then the model may not be an accurate representation. Although classing patients who required SCS in the dupilumab arm will lower the proportion of patients in the model classed as non-responders, as more patients on ECM only required rescue therapy, this will have a greater impact on the ECM only arm. The EAG is unable to comment on the impact on the ICER that this will have as the data are unavailable for the EAG to run the analysis (additional issue 3 in Section 1.4). 

## _4.2.5 Transition probabilities_ 

Only transitions from the controlled health state are dictated by the clinical trial data and differ between treatment arms, as described above. All remaining transitions are informed by published literature, detailed below. 

## _**Inadequately controlled health state**_ 

As previously noted, the inadequately controlled health state is a temporary tunnel state that patients may only occupy for one annual cycle. Following this, patients may either enter the post-op controlled state or the uncontrolled health state. 

Based on pooled SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 data, the company stated that 23.7% of patients were ineligible for revision surgery. Therefore, these patients can only transition to the uncontrolled health state and the annual transition probability 100%. 

For patients eligible for surgery (76.3%), the probability of moving to the post-op controlled health state each year is 15.1%. In the CS, this figure is said to be sourced from Benson _et al._ 2023,[11] a retrospective cohort study of patients with CRSwNP in England which assessed the rate of surgery during a follow up period. This study used the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum database with Hospital Episodes Statistics (HES) linkage for the period of 2007–2019. The EAG was unable to replicate the 15.1% from the Benson _et al._ 2023 study.[11] During clarification, the company provided further detail of the calculations undertaken to produce the 15.1%, stating that this was derived by dividing the number of surgeries by year by the total eligible population, after accounting for the 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 77 



<!-- page 633 -->

average wait time in the UK (see response to B7b for further details). The number of surgeries and eligible patients for surgery used data from patients who had two or more surgeries during follow up and the average time between second and third surgery. 

All patients who are eligible for surgery, but who do not transition to the post-op controlled state, instead transition to the uncontrolled health state (100% – 15.1% = 84.9%). 

## _**Post-op controlled health state**_ 

As noted in Section 4.2.3.1, a proportion of patients in each treatment arm of the pooled SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trials underwent surgery, which is reflected in the decision tree and dictates the proportion of patients occupying the post-op controlled health state at the beginning of the Markov model. By Week 24, 1.2% of patients in the dupilumab arm and 5.5% in the ECM only arm had surgery. Between Week 24 and 52, 0% had surgery in the dupilumab arm compared to 4.7% in the ECM only arm. 

The probability of losing disease control following revision surgery and therefore moving to the uncontrolled health state is also informed by Benson _et al._ 2023.[11] The company stated that this was based on data provided on the mean time to third surgery for patients who have already had two surgeries during the study follow-up period. It was noted in the CS that data were adjusted to account for average wait times of two years in England following discussions with clinical experts during an advisory board. This was to account for the fact that the data from Benson _et al._ only provides average time from second surgery to third (875 days/2.4 years) and this does not account for the timing of loss of control, i.e. moving from post-op controlled to uncontrolled. Experts consulted by the company stated that they expect around 40% of patients to lose control quickly. The company stated that this adjustment, therefore, accounts for patients losing control following surgery and remaining on the surgical waitlist. Following this adjustment, it resulted in an annual probability of 42.8% moving to the uncontrolled state and the corresponding 57.2% remaining in the post-op controlled health state. The 42.8% was derived based on the following calculation: 

Annual probability = (proportion of patients having ≥3 surgeries/ proportion of patients having ≥2 surgeries) ÷ (average time from second to third surgery – average surgery wait time) 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 78 



<!-- page 634 -->

## _**Uncontrolled health state**_ 

The probability of having revision surgery in each cycle from the uncontrolled health state, for those eligible, is equal to that in the inadequately controlled health state (15.1%). Therefore, the probability of remaining in the uncontrolled health state is 84.9% for those eligible for surgery and 100% for those not eligible for surgery.

## _4.2.5.1 EAG critique_ 

Clinical experts to the EAG stated that they would not expect a high proportion of patients to be ineligible for revision surgery as it rarely occurs in their clinical practice, with an expected proportion of less than 10%. This is considerably lower than the 23.6% of patients ineligible in the company’s base case economic model based on the SINUS-24 and SINUS-52 trial data. The EAG also notes that a clinical expert consulted by the company, considered that while some patients may not be fit enough for surgery, it would not be as many as the 23% suggested by the company and estimated it to be lower than 10%. During clarification, the EAG asked for further details of the criteria used to determine eligibility for surgery; it was stated that this was based solely on expert opinion during baseline screening visits. The company noted the 23.7% is based on those with prior surgery and proposed an alternative lower value of 15.1%, which is based on the ITT population. In addition, the EAG requested that the company included a scenario analysis using an alternative value based on their experts’ feedback. The company included a rate of 10% in the economic model. This was then included in the company’s updated base-case analysis. Based on feedback from the company’s clinical experts, the EAG consider this lower value to be more reflective of UK clinical practice. The EAG notes that changing this parameter has a minor impact on the ICER. 

The company used the Benson _et al._ 2023[11] study to derive the transitions from both the inadequately controlled and uncontrolled health state to post-op surgery (15.1% applied in both health states) and from the post-op controlled to uncontrolled (42.8%). The study provides data on the average time from second to third surgery during follow-up. While the EAG agrees that this study is an appropriate data source that is applicable for the population in the appraisal, there are a number of uncertainties in the annual transition probabilities derived ( **Key issue 4** in Section 1.1). 

The Benson _et al_ study, as with other studies reviewed by the EAG, provides the average time from revision surgery to subsequent surgery for nasal polyps. This therefore represents the ‘loop’ from post-op controlled to uncontrolled and back to post-op controlled. However, due to the model structure, separate transitions are required to represent the proportion of patients who lose control in an annual cycle following revision surgery and then the proportion of patients who are classed as uncontrolled who have revision surgery each year. In order to account for these transitions required, the company used the average time patients in the UK spend on the surgery wait list (two years), informed by clinical experts, to adjust the average time from second to third surgery to represent time to patients losing control following surgery and remaining on a waiting list. The EAG notes that 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 81 



<!-- page 637 -->

there is uncertainty in adjusting based on waiting times, as this incorporates issues with service provision, which can vary significantly across different regions in England and therefore the resulting annual probability of 42.8% is uncertain. The EAG notes, however, that in a submission received from SINUS UK as part of this submission, of 51 patients surveyed with CRSwNP, 60% of patients indicated that their symptoms returned in 12 months or less following surgery for nasal polyps, highlighting the short time to loss of control as noted by the company’s clinical experts. A clinical expert to the EAG also noted that it is difficult to say how long a patient remains temporarily controlled post-surgery, particularly as this will be influenced by the type of surgery undertaken and surgeon expertise. 

In addition, the EAG considers the appropriateness of the methods used by the company to derive the 15.1% revision rate to be unclear but notes the company also applied the same adjustment of two years to these calculations. As a result, the EAG considers the annual transition probability to be uncertain. The EAG also noticed an error in the company’s calculation provided at clarification in which it is stated that the number of surgeries per year is 52, whereas based on the company’s calculations this should be 50.93. The EAG corrected this (see Section **Error! Reference source not found.** ) which resulted in an annual probability of 14.8% compared to the company’s 15.1%. 

The EAG notes that during the company’s consultation with clinical experts, they presented an annual rate of revision surgery of 1.9%. During clarification, the company clarified that this rate was based on an earlier draft of the model and based on French hospital discharge data and so not relevant to the current base-case model. However, this was provided as a scenario to show the impact of using this lower estimate. It had a minimal impact on the ICER, highlighting that while the EAG considers the rates used in the base case to be uncertain, transitions to the post-surgery controlled state are not a key driver of the economic model. While the EAG consider that the annual probability of revision surgery may be lower than that used in the company base case, as this will have a greater impact on the ECM only arm, the higher probability used by the company could be considered a conservative estimate and notes that the surgery rate is not a key driver of the ICER. 

While the EAG was unable to source an alternative value to inform the annual probability of moving from the post-op controlled to uncontrolled to explore the impact of any uncertainty on the ICER, a scenario analysis has been conducted by the EAG in which the transition probabilities used the same approach as the company (described in CQ B7b) but the adjustments made to account for surgery waiting time in the UK is changed from two years to one year (i.e. one model cycle). This results in an 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 82 



<!-- page 638 -->

annual transition probability from the post-op controlled to uncontrolled of 12.1%. The EAG notes that the same adjustment is not made to the uncontrolled to post-op controlled probability as the EAG consider this to result in much higher probabilities than the expected (41.3%) and, as previously noted, the value used by the company for the rate of revision could be considered a conservative option. Therefore, while the EAG considers these probabilities to also be uncertain, this scenario is included to show the impact of a lower probability in loss of control following surgery on the company’s ICER, which increased it by ≈£2,000. 

## _4.2.6 Mortality_ 

The economic model uses UK national life tables from 2021–2023[17] to represent general population mortality associated with age and no additional mortality risk specifically associated with CRSwNP is applied. However, the CS states that due to the increased risk of mortality with asthma, a relative risk (RR) for increased mortality is applied to all patients with comorbid asthma. The RR of 1.36 was sourced from a meta-analysis that aimed to evaluate the association of asthma on cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality. 

The EAG notes that the meta-analysis used to inform the relative risk for increased mortality in the company’s original submission for asthma patients was based on four studies, none of which were UK based and none were published recently, which the EAG considers may affect the applicability of the study to current UK practice. During clarification the EAG asked the company if any more relevant studies had been searched for. In response to clarification, the company updated this based on a targeted literature review. This identified a study by Zhang _et al._ 2022, which is a meta-analysis of 18 studies evaluating the association between asthma and all-cause mortality and produced a similar RR of 1.38. 

In the company submission, it is stated that there is an increased mortality risk with asthma;  the economic model applies the increased risk to all patients with comorbid asthma and not just patients with severe asthma. During clarification, the company stated that the mention of severe asthma in the CS was a typing error and, based on the literature source used, the company considers that this should be applied to all comorbid asthma patients. The company also updated the proportion of patients with comorbid asthma from 59.1% to 66.2%, based on the updated analysis. 

Due to the inclusion of increased mortality for asthma patients and the company applying separate rates of uncontrolled asthma for each treatment arm in the model, based on rates observed in the 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 83 



<!-- page 639 -->

pooled SINUS-24 and -52, this results in a difference in mortality between the two treatment arms and therefore in life years (LYs). 

## _4.2.6.1 EAG critique_ 

The EAG notes that dupilumab already has a positive NICE recommendation for treating severe asthma with type 2 inflammation, therefore patients with severe asthma and CRSwNP may already have access to dupilumab. In the published final guidance for TA751, it states, “ _... It [the committee] also heard that dupilumab is effective in people with comorbidities (such as nasal polyps and atopic dermatitis). It concluded that these additional benefits of dupilumab had not been adequately captured in the QALY calculation and took them into consideration in its decision making.”_[18] Therefore, the EAG considers that the crossover benefits of dupilumab for severe asthma and CRSwNP patients has already been accounted for in the decision making ICER threshold of the previous appraisal, and including them again may result in double counting of the benefit. In addition, the proportion of patients on ECM only with uncontrolled asthma in the clinical trials may be higher than in clinical practice as patients may be able to access alternative biologics approved by NICE for use in asthma. As a result, the EAG does not consider it appropriate to include the increased risk of mortality due to asthma in the base-case analysis (additional issue 4 in Section 1.4). 

The company's use of 2021–2023 life tables for age-matched general population mortality was identified as a minor issue by the EAG. Guidance in the NICE decision support unit (DSU) technical support document (TSD) 23 recommends using the ONS life tables from 2017–2019 due to the uncertainty about the long-term impact of COVID-19 on the latest estimates.[19] As such, the EAG ran a scenario using the ONS life tables for England from 2017–2019 (see Section 6.2).The EAG’s scenario had minimal impact on the ICER but it is included in the EAG base case for adherence to the guidance in NICE DSU TSD 23.[19]

There is a treatment-specific benefit for both responders and non-responders during the trial period (decision tree section) for patients receiving dupilumab. After this period (Markov section), there is assumed to be no difference in utility, within health states, between dupilumab and ECM pre-op patients (this is not the case for post-op patients, see Section 4.2.7.2). The inadequately controlled disease utility is intended to reflect the benefit of receiving optimised care, even if unresponsive to that care, as compared to uncontrolled disease, which reflects patients who lose any disease control. 

The Crump _et al._ 2017[9] paper used for mapping presents three model options based on a crosssectional Canadian population of chronic rhinosinusitis patients, awaiting bilateral endoscopic sinus surgery. Model 1 in the paper is a simple regression against the SNOT-22 global score, model 2 regresses against each component of SNOT-22 and model 3 is the same as model 2 but it also includes age and percentage female. Model 1 was selected as the company base case as models 2 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 85 



<!-- page 641 -->

and 3 appeared to be over-specified leading to implausible coefficients that meant loss of sense of taste/smell or waking up tired had a positive impact on a patient’s quality of life. In addition, model 1 appeared to have higher Spearman correlation coefficient levels with trial-observed EQ-5D. The EAG agrees with the company that of the models presented in the Crump paper, model 1 is the most appropriate. 

The SINUS trials directly recorded EQ-5D-5L data. The Crump model was selected as the base case, over the trial utility data, because responders at week 52 showed a score higher than the UK general population. The company also stated that a baseline EQ-5D of 0.782 is high considering the significant impact of this disease on patients. These values are suggested to be higher than expected, since EQ-5D does not explicitly account for items related to anosmia and sleep. The company further goes on to show the Spearman’s correlation coefficient between key disease-specific measures and EQ-5D is weak. 

A linear mixed model regression based on directly observed EQ-5D utility values collected up to week 52 in the SINUS trials was provided as scenario analysis. Hernandez-Alava[20] crosswalk was used in the creation of the dependent variable (converting EQ-5D-5L to EQ-5D-3L). Four models were tested, all models included age, sex, baseline EQ-5D score, and SNOT-22 total score, while models 2– 4 also included Nasal Polyps Score (NPS), and models 3 and 4 further tested interaction effects between SNOT-22 and NPS. Model 4 additionally included treatment as a coefficient. Model 1 was selected as the best-fit model because it had the lowest AIC (-3131.9) and BIC (-3122.8) values, indicating superior statistical performance. This model was preferred due to its simpler structure and better overall fit, focusing on the primary predictors of utility — SNOT-22 score, age, sex, and baseline utility — while excluding variables that did not significantly improve model accuracy. Notably, model 1 was selected despite it excluding NPS due to NPS not being a statistically significant factor, despite this being used to determine the definition of response. 

During clarification, the EAG requested that the company reran the four regression analyses using change from baseline in SNOT-22 score rather than total, in order to limit issues with multicollinearity between SNOT-22 and baseline EQ-5D. These were provided and incorporated into the company’s updated economic model, with models 5 to 8 being equivalent of 1 to 4, respectively, with the exception of SNOT-22, NPS and their interaction measured by change from baseline. The utility values by health state using the best fitting model (model 5) are shown in Table 32. Health state utilities derived from observed EQ-5D regression used in scenario analysis

## _4.2.7.2 Surgery and AE utility_ 

Post-operative patients experience a short-term disutility and a long-term utility gain, moving into the post-op controlled state. The short-term disutility comes indirectly from Scangas _et al._ 2017,[21] it is -0.150 applied over 14 days. The source paper is a cost-utility analysis of endoscopic sinus surgery for patients with chronic rhinosinusitis, both with (CRSwNP) and without nasal polyps (CRSsNP). It is unclear how the company derived this disutility from the paper as health states are recorded 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 87 



<!-- page 643 -->

annually in the reported model and no short-term disutility is directly mentioned (although probabilities relating to post-op complications, which would involve short-term disutility, are recorded). 

Long-term improvement in utility from surgery is 0.051, sourced from Soler _et al._ 2011.[22] As this is applied as a utility gain, as opposed to a standalone health state, the health state a patient transitioned from determines the patient’s utility in the post-op-controlled health state. Patients who are non-responders, inadequately controlled or uncontrolled can all require surgery and postsurgery, the health state they came from determines their subsequent utility. This means dupilumab non-responders who require surgery are expected to retain a treatment-specific benefit unless or until they transition from post-op controlled. ## _4.2.7.4 EAG critique_ 

The EAG notes that the company’s use of a disease-specific measure (SNOT-22) mapped to EQ-5D is a departure from the NICE reference case, particularly when EQ-5D(-5L) is available from the clinical trials and notes that mapping is commonly used to bridge an evidence gap when EQ-5D data are not available.[14] 

The EAG does not agree with the company view on observed EQ-5D being inappropriate. The issue of exceeding the general population is common in clinical trials and can be resolved by capping the responder utility values at general population for the baseline age and then applying a multiplier to subsequent health states in order to retain the proportional differences between states. The EAG requested that the company perform this analysis at clarification. The company provided this, producing a capping multiplier of 0.937 for the observed SINUS EQ-5D-3L crosswalked change from baseline data. This is the EAG’s preferred base case ( **Key issue 5** is Section 1.1; results are found in Section 5.2.2). In addition, Tashman _et al._ 2024, Wahid _et al._ 2020, Scangas 2018, Scangas 2017a and De Corso _et al._ 2022[12, 15, 21, 24] identified in the company’s SLR appear to show significantly higher utility values than used in the company’s base case. Therefore, the company’s statement about baseline utility being excessively high does not appear to be supported by the literature. The company reaffirmed their position on this at clarification by referring to the case they made in their submission, that the EQ-5D instrument performs poorly at capturing the quality of life for patients with CRSwNP, also noting that these papers appear to show baseline QoL close to age-related general population utility. The company emphasised that anosmia and sleep in particular are not explicitly covered by the EQ-5D measure. 

Usual activities and pain/discomfort should, to some extent, cover issues with sleep or lack of smell, although the EAG acknowledges that there may be a lack of sensitivity of measurement when compared to SNOT-22. This is commonly the case when a generic instrument is compared to a disease-specific measure of QoL. However, the EAG does not consider the company’s solution of using the Crump model’s SNOT-22 overall score to be more appropriate. Models 2 and 3 from Crump (which use individual components of SNOT-22 in the regression) show a positive statistically nonsignificant relationship between EQ-5D and the “anosmia” and “lack of sleep” components of SNOT22, which, as the company points out, implausibly suggests these negative health outcomes improve quality of life. Yet, by using model 1, this relationship is simply obscured by having these 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 89 



<!-- page 645 -->

components be combined with other components such as “facial pain/pressure” which have a large, statistically significant and negative impact on EQ-5D. 

Furthermore, the EAG considers the Crump model to have generalisability issues, which also make it inferior to using the company’s trial-based EQ-5D data. The Crump model population is exclusively chronic rhinosinusitis patients awaiting surgery, meaning it effectively only includes patients who would be in the uncontrolled disease health state. This makes it a worse representative sample for determining the quality of life of those other health states. The company responded to this issue at clarification by identifying that the SNOT-22 scores have a large standard deviation (SD) suggesting a reasonable spread across the population, attempting to demonstrate this by producing a sample histogram for illustrative purposes. The EAG does not agree with this explanation, as while the SD is high, the issue is that the population selected likely has constraints on their SNOT-22 score due to their position in the care pathway (waiting for surgery). It cannot be assumed that these patients have a standard distribution (as was done in the company’s illustrative histogram) as there is likely to be a SNOT-22 threshold below which a patient is eligible for/requires surgery. 

The EAG notes that the NICE reference case stipulates that in order to make the case that the EQ-5D is inappropriate, evidence should be derived from a synthesis of peer-reviewed literature. The EAG does not consider that this has been done. In addition, the validity of the argument made by the company that the EQ-5D instrument performs poorly at capturing the quality of life for patients with CRSwNP is also unclear as the company maps to the EQ-5D and therefore the utility values used in the model are still EQ-5D values, albeit derived from mapping. As noted in the NICE DSU TSD 22, “ _Mapping to EQ-5D is not appropriate if EQ-5D is considered inappropriate for measuring health benefits in the condition under consideration_ ”,[25] therefore, the company’s argument does not match their approach taken. 

The regression model provided by the company post-clarification alleviates some of the issues with Crump and using the trial data directly is preferable to using this external paper. However, the EAG notes that SNOT-22 is correlated to EQ-5D and other included variables and therefore including it as an independent variable in the regression analysis is likely to result in both multicollinearity and endogeneity. Although the EAG's preferred analysis would usually be EQ-5D from the trial derived from a regression analysis, the EAG consider the regression analysis to be methodologically flawed due to the inclusion of SNOT-22, however as the EAG was unable to perform an analysis without this included, the extent to which it is flawed in unclear. 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 90 



<!-- page 646 -->

For these reasons, the EAG’s preference is for the observed change from baseline in observed EQ5D-5L data crosswalked to EQ-5D-3L in the base-case analysis ( **Key issue 5** in Section 1). 

At clarification, the company was asked to justify why dupilumab non-responders who receive surgery would have a higher utility than ECM non-responders. No clinical justification was provided, the company instead made the case that the two papers sourced for surgery-related utility benefit suggest ESS provides a one-off quality of life improvement post-surgery. The EAG does not consider this to be evidence that a continued benefit from dupilumab is appropriate, as this appears to be a presentational preference for these studies. No evidence has been provided that, as a nonresponder, surgery will provide patients with a fixed benefit that improves the areas of the condition not affected by dupilumab. The EAG considers it more likely that surgery improves a patient’s QoL to a similar point irrespective of what their prior treatment was. In addition, the company’s assumption is inconsistent with the current model; it seems implausible that dupilumab provides no lasting benefit within health states after one year for non-surgery patients but it does if a patient has had surgery. Therefore, the EAG has assumed the surgery state is based on a fixed utility benefit applied to the post-decision tree ECM health states (additional issue 5 in Section 1). 

The EAG consider the source used for the utility gain of surgery in the company’s base case (Soler _et al._ 2011[22] ) to be inappropriate as it is based on SF-6D and uses data that the EAG considers relatively out of date (2004 – 2009). Therefore, the EAG prefers to use Remenschneider _et al_ . 2015[23] in the base-case analysis both because it contains more recent data (2011–2012) and as it is based on EQ5D-5L over SF-6D, which is more in line with the NICE reference case. The EAG acknowledges that the data in Remenschneider _et al_ . 2015[23] is still considered relatively out of date, however, in light of a lack of an alternative source this is the EAG’s preferred source ( **Key issue 5** in Section 1.1). 

Furthermore, the lack of confirmation of where the short-term surgery disutility came from in Scangas _et al._ 2017[21] represents a minor uncertainty. The EAG acknowledges that surgery will likely result in a short-term disutility and the value has minimal impact but the lack of clear origin introduces uncertainty.

## _4.2.8.2 Drug and administration costs_ 

Dupilumab is dosed at 300mg every other week and is provided by subcutaneous injection. The annual cost is £16,500, although there is a confidential patient access scheme in place with a discounted price of ******* A one-time administration cost of £49.39 is applied based on the PSSRU cost for a band 6 nurse to account for a one-off training in dupilumab administration. 

In the CS, dupilumab was assumed to have an adherence rate of 99.26% based on the average adherence between 300mg administered at Q2W-Q4W and Q2W arms from the SINUS trials. The company provided a scenario at clarification using just Q2W patients; they had an adherence of 99.34%. This was then updated as part of the company’s base-case. 

The EAG was advised that if dupilumab were to be recommended for routine clinical practice, the decision to start a patient on treatment would be made as part of a multidisciplinary team (MDT). A cost of £220.78 based on the NHS reference cost data for Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) serviceOutpatient Care national average unit cost (multiprofessional - Consultant Led) was included in the company base case following clarification. The EAG agree this should be included in the base case. 

Established clinical management (ECM) costs involve acute treatment of infections and inflammation using SCS and/or antibiotics; the unit cost of these treatments can be seen in Table 37. While ECM is provided to both arms, as treatment is acute and targeted means there are differences in drug use rates between the arms. These are recorded in Table 38 with unit costs found in Table 37. Following clarification, the company removed antibiotics drug use from the model as there was not a

## _4.2.8.3 Surgery costs_

Total per person NHS costs, from this paper, in the year following surgery, was estimated to be £2,547, which is used as the company’s base case. A scenario analysis was conducted using the component costs listed in the paper, which states surgery is priced at £2,284.63 with follow on outpatient costs of £76.78 in the immediate quarter after and 2-year follow up costs of £59.62 per quarter. This would result in a total cost of £2,540.27 for the year containing surgery. Costs in the paper were in 2017-18 UK pound sterling and so have been inflated to 2024 prices. The explanation provided by the company for why the component costs summed differs from the total first year costs is that the 2-year follow up cost of £59.82 is a per quarter average over 2 years while the first year per patient cost includes the true value. The EAG agrees that this explanation is plausible. 

Post-op costs are separated into first year and subsequent years. As previously shown Table 35, no additional healthcare resource use cost is applied in the first year as this is assumed to be accounted for in the cost taken from the Clarke _et al_ . 2022 paper.[27] In subsequent years, a single outpatient appointment cost is applied.

## _4.2.8.5 EAG critique_ 

At clarification the company was asked to provide the usage of SCS and antibiotics based on the decision problem as opposed to the ITT population. In response, the company has confirmed that the difference in antibiotic usage was not statistically significant between arms and has removed it from the model. Therefore, in the company’s updated model, only differences in SCS use are included. 

The company assumes that 100% of patients will be able to self-administer dupilumab but included a scenario analysis in which 5% of patients receive administration by a nurse. Based on clinical expert feedback, the EAG consider this to be more appropriate for the base-case analysis as it is unlikely that 100% of patients will be able to self-administer. The EAG notes that this has a minor impact on the ICER (additional issue 6 in Section 1.1). 

The company provided two scenarios for surgery costs, one based on the sum of component costs for the first year of surgery for patients and the other, which is stated in the paper to be the total 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 97 



<!-- page 653 -->

per-person NHS costs for 1 year in patients receiving surgery. However, the paper lists per quarter follow-up costs of £59.62 up to 2 years that do not appear to have been incorporated into the model, with patients in subsequent years (post op) only receiving one outpatient appointment. The EAG base case incorporates these 2-year follow-up costs into its base case, subtracting the cost of 1 outpatient appointment to avoid double counting of resource use. Second year costs are discounted 3.5% and the costs are inflated to 2024 prices. This results in an overall cost of £3,205. The impact of incorporating this increases the cost of surgery, which improves the cost-effectiveness of dupilumab as fewer dupilumab patients receive surgery (additional issue 7 in Section 1.4) . 

As previously discussed in relation to mortality, the EAG consider that some of the benefits of dupilumab in patients with comorbid asthma will have already been captured in the previous appraisal. Therefore, differences in asthma costs have been excluded from the EAG base case and provided as a scenario analysis only.

## 5.2 Company’s sensitivity analyses 

## _5.2.1 One-way sensitivity analyses_ 

The company conducted one-way sensitivity analyses (OWSAs) to assess the impact on the ICER of varying specific parameters in isolation and to identify the main model drivers. Parameters were varied by 95% confidence intervals (CIs) when available and ±10% when these were not available. 

The results are illustrated in the tornado diagram presented in Figure 16, which depicts the change in the ICER from baseline. The ICER was most sensitive to the utility values for the controlled and uncontrolled disease health states, the proportion of patients with sustained response on dupilumab at week 52 (as this informs the long-term Markov model transition probabilities) and compliance rate of dupilumab.

## 6 Additional economic analysis undertaken by the EAG 

## 6.1 Model corrections 

As noted in Section 4.2.5.1, the EAG corrected an error in the company’s calculation of the annual probability of revision surgery. Therefore, this was amended by the EAG to an annual probability of 14.8% compared to the company’s 15.1%. 

The EAG also amended the probabilistic values sampled for the proportion of patients with asthma as this was incorrectly sampling from the proportion of patients with severe asthma. 

All additional scenarios performed by the EAG include these model corrections to the base-case. 

## 6.2 EAG scenario analysis 

As discussed in Section 4, the EAG identified a number of uncertainties that warranted further exploration in scenario analyses, in addition to the company’s own sensitivity and scenario analyses. The majority of these were conducted by the company in response to clarification, as previously shown in 

Table 42 in Section 5.2.2. The additional scenarios performed by the EAG are detailed below. 

1. General population mortality based on ONS life tables 2017-19, in line with NICE DSU guidance[19] (Section 4.2.6). 

2. Annual probability of patients transitioning from controlled to inadequately controlled in the dupilumab arm beyond 5 years in the model is equal to 15.6%. This is an exploratory scenario based on ***************** of discontinuation (including due to loss of response) at the end of the SINUS-52 trial *******in order to explore the impact of a reduced treatment effect over time (Section 4.2.4). 

3. Transition probabilities from post-op controlled to uncontrolled based on the company analysis of Benson _et al._ but using an adjustment of a one year wait time in the calculations as opposed to two years. This results in an annual probability of post-op controlled to uncontrolled of 12.1% as opposed to the company’s 42.8% (Section 4.2.5.1). 

4. Utility values for post-op controlled disease do not differ between treatment arms, i.e. no prolonged treatment benefit following loss of control (Section 4.2.7.4). 

5. Inclusion of two year follow-up costs post-surgery (Section 4.2.8.5).

## 6.3 EAG preferred assumptions 

In this section, the EAG presents its preferred analysis for the cost-effectiveness of dupilumab in combination with ECM for the treatment of uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) following prior surgery. The assumptions that form the EAG’s preferred base case are listed below, with the cumulative results of each analysis shown in Table 48. The EAG notes that the individual impact of each scenario on the company’s base-case ICER has been previously presented in either 

Table 42 or Table 47. The EAG ran probabilistic results over 1,000 iterations. It is noted that due to variability in the PSA, there may be small discrepancies in the incremental costs or QALYs between scenarios. 

The EAG notes that due to changes in the base case preferences, corrections were applied to the sampled PSA utility values to ensure that the utility multiplier was also applied in the probabilistic version of the model and that utilities followed the expected ordering across health states. For scenarios including no mortality or costs associated with asthma, these values were set not to vary in the PSA. 

- General population mortality based on ONS life tables 2017-19, in line with NICE DSU guidance[19] (Section 4.2.6). 

- Transition probability of controlled to inadequately controlled based analysis of responders from the SINUS 24/52 trials (***% annual probability) (Section 4.2.4). 

- Removal of difference in mortality between treatment arms due to uncontrolled asthma (Section 4.2.6). 

- Utility values based on observed EQ-5D SINUS trial data (change from baseline), with a cap applied to the responder utility values at general population for the baseline age and a multiplier applied to subsequent health states in order to retain the proportional differences between states (Section 4.2.7.4). 

- Surgery utility gain based on Remenschneider _et al._ 2015 (Section 4.2.7.4). 

- Utility values for post-op controlled disease do not differ between treatment arms, i.e. no prolonged treatment benefit following loss of control (Section 4.2.7.4). 

- Removal of differences in costs related to asthma control (Section 4.2.8.5). 

- 5% of patients receive assistance with dupilumab administration, provided by a nurse home care visit (Section 4.2.8.5). 

- Inclusion of two year follow-up costs post-surgery (Section 4.2.8.5).

## 6.4 EAG additional sensitivity analysis 

The following additional sensitivity analyses were also undertaken using the EAG’s preferred analysis to explore the sensitivity to alternative assumptions: 

1. Responder analysis based on SNOT-22 response only. This scenario applies data analysis on patients response from SINUS 24/52 based on SNOT-22 change from baseline of ≥8.9 points only, as opposed to the combined response. Based on feedback from clinical experts, the EAG considers it a reasonable alternative to the base-case analysis, dependent on the criteria that will be used in clinical practice. 

2. Annual probability of patients transitioning from controlled to inadequately controlled in the dupilumab arm beyond 5 years in the model is equal to ****%. This is an exploratory scenario to explore the impact of a reduced treatment effect over time given the lack of availability of long-term comparative data. 

3. Use of company’s analysis of AROMA to inform long-term treatment effectiveness and discontinuation rates of dupilumab (transition from controlled to inadequately controlled), as used in the company’s updated base case analysis post clarification. 

4. Inclusion of asthma-related mortality and costs. While the EAG considers that costs for asthma control and mortality benefit related to asthma should not be included in the basecase analysis for CRSwNPs, it is considered an appropriate scenario analysis to explore the impact on the ICER. The EAG notes that as patients in clinical practice would have access to 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 111 



<!-- page 667 -->

other biologics for asthma that were not available during the clinical trials, the proportions of patients with uncontrolled asthma in the ECM arm may differ in the real world. In addition, some patients with severe asthma and CRSwNP will already have access to dupilumab. 

5. Utility values based on observed EQ-5D derived from the regression model. This analysis used utility values based on observed EQ-5D SINUS trial data (linear regression model controlling for age, gender, baseline utility and SNOT-22 change from baseline), as opposed to the change from baseline used in the EAG preferred analysis. 

6. Utility values based on the mapping of SNOT-22 to EQ-5D (-3L), as used in the company’s base analysis. 

7. Transition probability from post-op controlled to uncontrolled is based on the company analysis of Benson _et al_ . but using an adjustment of a one year wait time in the calculations as opposed to two years. This results in an annual probability of post-op controlled to uncontrolled of 12.1% as opposed to the company’s 42.8%. This exploratory scenario is included to explore the magnitude of the ICER impact when using a lower annual transition to the uncontrolled health state. 

As shown in Table 50, the use of responder analysis measured using SNOT-22 had the largest increase on the EAG’s ICER. The EAG notes that this scenario has a greater impact on the EAG’s preferred analysis compared to the company’s due to the smaller absolute QALYs in the EAG base case due to the utility values used and removal of survival benefit related to uncontrolled asthma (i.e. no difference in LYs). As previously discussed, the choice of method used to derive utility values has the greatest impact on the ICER, which is observed in additional analysis six, using the company’s mapping. The EAG notes that this scenario results in considerably higher incremental QALYs (****). As previously discussed, the EAG does not consider the company’s mapping to be appropriate (see Section 4.2.7.4). 

The reduced treatment effect beyond 5 years (additional analysis 2) had a small impact on the ICER as did the use of the AROMA study to inform the transition probability (additional analysis 3). The inclusion of asthma-related benefits reduced the EAG ICER by ≈£6,000, driven by both an increase in incremental QALYs due to a survival gain for dupilumab, and a reduction in incremental costs.

## 6.5 Conclusions of the cost effectiveness sections 

Generally, the EAG considers the company’s submitted cost-effective evidence to adhere to the NICE decision problem defined in the NICE final scope. The company compared dupilumab plus 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 114 



<!-- page 670 -->

established clinical management (ECM) to ECM only. Clinical experts to the EAG confirmed that endoscopic sinonasal surgery (ESS) is a component of ECM rather than a standalone comparator. 

The inputs used in the model in relation to utility values are the key driver of the ICER and consequently are considered to be a key issue in this appraisal ( **Key issue 5** in Section 1). As previously discussed in Section 4.2.7.4, the EAG does not consider the company’s departure from the NICE reference case and argument for the use of mapping SNOT-22 to EQ-5D, rather than using the trial-based EQ-5D, to be justified and also considers the model used for mapping (Crump _et al_ .) to be inappropriate due to generalisability issues). Therefore, the EAG considers the use of EQ-5D-5L (mapped to EQ-5D-3L) directly from the key clinical trials to be most appropriate. While the EAG preference would be trial EQ-5D derived from a regression model, as previously stated, the EAG considers the company’s regression to be methodologically flawed due to the inclusion of SNOT-22 as an independent variable. Therefore, the EAG’s preferred base case analysis used the trial observed EQ-5D change from baseline (CFB), resulting in a probabilistic ICER of £59,370 per QALY gained. As utility values produced using this approach for patients in the controlled health state resulted in a utility value higher than UK population norm, a cap on age-matched utility was used and a multiplier applied to subsequent health states in order to retain the proportional differences between states. The EAG notes that using the company’s mapped utility values substantially increases the incremental QALY gain for dupilumab, which can be clearly seen in the company’s scenario analysis using observed CFB utilities ( 

Table 42), whereby incremental QALYs reduced from **** to ****. As dupilumab has not demonstrated a survival benefit in patients with CRSwNP, the EAG considers an incremental QALY gain of *****considerably high. 

The EAG also considers the utility values used to represent the gain from surgery to be a key issue. The EAG’s preferred analysis includes a gain of 0.08, sourced from Remenschneider _et al_ . 2015.[23] This is considered more appropriate than the value used by the company (0.051 from Soler _et al._ 2011[22] ) due to it being derived from more recent data and as it is based on EQ-5D-5L rather than SF6D, which is more in line with the NICE reference case and other utilities used in the base-case. The EAG acknowledges that the data in Remenschneider _et al_ . 2015[23] is still considered relatively out of date (2011–2012); however, in light of a lack of an alternative source this is the EAG’s preferred option. 

While not changed in the EAG base-case analysis, the criteria used to measure response in clinical practice is an area of uncertainty if it differs to that used in the economic model (combination of SNOT-22 and nasal polyp score [NPS]). This is shown in the EAG’s additional sensitivity analysis 1, in which the use of responder status based on SNOT-22 only increased the ICER to £76,832 per QALY gained. As discussed in the analysis of the clinical evidence (Section 2.3.4), the response criteria used in the model also differed to the primary outcomes of the clinical trials and, therefore, that used to 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 115 



<!-- page 671 -->

assess clinical effectiveness (NPS and nasal congestion [NC]). While the EAG considers the combined criteria used in the base-case analysis to be appropriate, based on feedback from clinical experts, there is uncertainty regarding if this is what will be applied in clinical practice and, therefore, is considered a key issue. The EAG notes that there is also uncertainty regarding whether patients requiring a course of rescue therapy while receiving dupilumab will be classed as non-responders, as was applied in the company’s responder analysis. If patients would not be considered nonresponders in clinical practice after requiring one course of rescue therapy, it is unlikely that the results of the model are an accurate reflection of this treatment strategy. 

Based on patients only receiving dupilumab for the 52-week trial period (SINUS-52), no randomised controlled trial (RCT) data are available on the long-term treatment effect of dupilumab in CRSwNP patients, resulting in high uncertainty in this model input. Following the clarification stage, the company updated their estimates of the annual transition probability from controlled to inadequately controlled for dupilumab to be based on an analysis of the observational AROMA study. While the EAG consider these data to be useful to explore uncertainty in the long-term treatment effect beyond 52-weeks, the EAG has several concerns with the analysis undertaken and, therefore, deems it inappropriate for its base-case analysis (see Section 4.2.4.1 for further details). The EAG notes that using the same approach as the company to inform transition probabilities reduced the EAG’s preferred ICER by ≈£2000 (additional sensitivity analysis 3). 

In order to further explore the uncertainty in the long-term treatment effect of dupilumab, the EAG conducted an exploratory scenario in which the proportion of patients who lose control each year from year five onwards is ************** used in the base-case analysis. The EAG notes that while the ICER increased, this was not by a substantial amount. 

The EAG also considers there to uncertainty in the rate of loss of control following revision surgery and so the transition probability to the uncontrolled health state. As much of the identified data on rate of revision surgery is based on time from previous surgery, this is not fully applicable to the model structure. In addition, clinical experts to the EAG noted how the rate of loss of control and revision surgery is highly variable. Although the EAG has some concerns with the methods used to derive the transition probabilities, it is noted that the resulting estimates appear to be aligned with alternative data sources on loss of response and clinical expert opinion. The EAG’s exploratory additional sensitivity analysis 7 shows that the ICER increased by quite a large amount when using 

**==> picture [80 x 28] intentionally omitted <==**

PAGE 116 



<!-- page 672 -->

the lower probability; the EAG consider this to represent an upper boundary on what the ICER may be with a lower transition rate. 

The EAG considers the company’s base case analysis to overestimate the cost-effectiveness of dupilumab when taken in addition to ECM. The EAG notes that there are several uncertainties in the assumptions and inputs used in the model, as previously discussed. However, the main driver of the ICER is the method and corresponding estimates used for HRQoL in the model.
